studies.citation: Zhang F (2020; co-authors not visible in search results) Early warning signals of population productivity regime shifts in global fisheries. Ecological Indicators
studies.data_system: 191 global fisheries populations (source database not visible in search results)
studies.outcome_definition: Observed 'productivity regime shifts' of populations (shift detection method not visible in search results)
studies.baseline_comparator: None visible in search results (SD vs AR1 compared against each other only)
studies.key_finding: Evaluated SD and AR1 as EWS for observed productivity regime shifts in 191 global fisheries populations; 'successful' EWS gave >5 years warning for >50% of populations; SD and AR1 were simultaneously detected in <50% of regime shifts and SD had a higher positive likelihood ratio than AR1, which the authors read as suggesting critical transitions may not be the major cause of observed regime shifts.
studies.notes: Closest existing analogue to the proposed study for the EWS arm. Reports lead time and a positive likelihood ratio (so some false-positive accounting is implied), but whether origins were time-indexed, whether non-shifting stocks were included, and how series ends were treated is not visible in search results. First author Fan Zhang (Shanghai Ocean University page); full author list not visible.

studies.citation: Litzow MA, Mueter FJ, Urban JD (2013) Rising catch variability preceded historical fisheries collapses in Alaska. Ecological Applications
studies.data_system: Spatially resolved catch data from 14 Gulf of Alaska / Bering Sea crustacean fisheries (12 collapsing, 2 non-collapsing), 278 cumulative years
studies.outcome_definition: Historical fishery collapses (exact threshold not visible in search results)
studies.baseline_comparator: Non-collapsing fisheries used as contrast; no state/trend forecasting baseline visible
studies.key_finding: Spatial variability in catches increased prior to collapse (random-effects trend across all 12 collapsing fisheries); pooling across fisheries allowed detection 1-4 years before collapse (one summary says 5 years for king crab); trends in variability differed significantly between collapsing and non-collapsing fisheries; no evidence of pre-collapse increase in skewness.
studies.notes: Journal is Ecological Applications (my query wrongly said PLoS ONE). Spatial (not temporal) variance of catch is the indicator. Includes only 2 non-collapsing controls, so false-alarm burden is thinly characterised.

studies.citation: Pélissié M, Devictor V, Jensen OP, Dakos V, et al. (2026) Abrupt declines in fish productivity often precede stock collapses in marine fisheries. Science Advances 12(36): eaed7911
studies.data_system: 315 agency-assessed fish stocks worldwide (productivity time series; RAM Legacy not explicitly named for this paper in snippets, but named for the companion PNAS paper)
studies.outcome_definition: Stock collapse (definition not visible in search results); abrupt productivity shifts classified via time-series shape analysis with breakpoint validation (asdetect, 5-year tolerance)
studies.key_finding: Abrupt productivity shifts detected in >25% of 315 stocks; abrupt declines over-represented where SST warming was largest, abrupt increases more likely under lower fishing intensity; abrupt productivity declines preceded stock collapses by roughly 10-20 years in about a quarter of shifting stocks, suggesting some collapses 'could be anticipated if abrupt shifts were more systematically detected'.
studies.notes: Retrospective detection framing (per snippets); whether detection was performed prospectively at sequential origins is not visible. Preprint title: 'Ocean warming drives abrupt declines in fish productivity at global scale' (EcoEvoRxiv).

studies.citation: Cano AV, Jensen OP, Dakos V (2025) Identifying fish populations prone to abrupt shifts via dynamical footprint analysis. PNAS 122(34): e2505461122
studies.data_system: RAM Legacy productivity time series; ICES Atlantic cod CPUE; FishGlob survey CPUE (three curated datasets)
studies.outcome_definition: Time-series shape classes: abrupt vs nonabrupt (linear, quadratic, no change), classified from dynamical-footprint metrics (variance, autocorrelation)
studies.key_finding: Proposes a mechanism-agnostic, context-specific workflow that uses dynamical properties (variance, autocorrelation) of fish population fluctuations to classify series as abrupt vs nonabrupt and to identify populations prone to abrupt shifts, applied across RAM Legacy, ICES cod and FishGlob datasets.
studies.notes: Pélissié is not an author of this paper (contrary to my query). Uses the same variance/autocorrelation statistics as classical EWS but as classifiers of series shape rather than sequential forecasts; evaluation design not visible. Directly relevant because it spans the candidate datasets (RAM Legacy, ICES, FishGlob).

studies.citation: Benerradi R, Dakos V, Cano AV (2026) Sensitivity of fish stock trajectories to climate forcing and human exploitation at a global scale. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 23(241): 20251040
studies.data_system: 155 fish stocks worldwide (productivity, harvest rate, SST)
studies.outcome_definition: Not a collapse study; causal links to productivity via empirical dynamic modelling
studies.key_finding: EDM causal analysis found fishing pressure the most prevalent driver of productivity (causal link in 71 stocks, 45.8%) and SST a driver in 39 stocks (25.2%).
studies.notes: Same Montpellier group as the abrupt-shift papers; useful as a driver-attribution reference, not a collapse-prediction design.

studies.citation: Pinsky ML, Byler D (2015) Fishing, fast growth and climate variability increase the risk of collapse. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 282(1813): 20151053
studies.data_system: RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database v1.0, 154 marine fish populations, biomass and fishing-pressure series 1950-2008
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse vs depletion (exact biomass thresholds not attributable in search snippets; an unattributed snippet in the same results mentions BMIN < 20% BMSY and B/BMSY < 0.5 as definitions used in 'some studies')
studies.baseline_comparator: Not an EWS study; predictors are fishing pressure (chronic/acute overfishing), growth rate, climate variability in boosted regression trees
studies.key_finding: Boosted regression trees across 154 populations: overfishing was the most important predictor of collapse (chronic overfishing correlated with depletion, acute overfishing with collapse); fast-growing species were more sensitive to collapse than slow-growing ones, particularly in variable climates.
studies.notes: Key precedent for a 'state-and-pressure' predictor set (U/UMSY-type variables) for collapse risk in RAM Legacy; whether BRT evaluation used held-out data or sequential origins is not visible. Data on Dryad.

studies.citation: Pinsky ML, Jensen OP, Ricard D, Palumbi SR (2011) Unexpected patterns of fisheries collapse in the world's oceans. PNAS 108(20): 8317-8322
studies.data_system: Two fisheries datasets: stock assessments and landings
studies.outcome_definition: Dramatic population collapses (threshold not visible in search results); cited by others as offering 'a more scientifically rigorous analysis and definition of collapsed'
studies.key_finding: Up to twice as many fisheries for small, low-trophic-level ('fast') species have collapsed compared with those for large predators.
studies.notes: Useful for collapse-definition and prevalence context in RAM Legacy-era assessment data.

studies.citation: Yletyinen J, Butler W, Ottersen G, Andersen K, et al. (2018 preprint; reported as later published in Fish and Fisheries) When is a fish stock collapsed? bioRxiv
studies.data_system: Literature review plus multi-stock analysis (stock database not visible in search results)
studies.outcome_definition: Proposes a process-based collapse definition linking an abrupt decline and an ensuing period, specified in terms of population turnover; contrasts with fixed-threshold definitions (10% of maximum biomass, 15%, 50% of average biomass)
studies.key_finding: Numerous collapse definitions exist and a stock's classification is sensitive to the definition's formulation; the proposed process-based definition distinguishes collapses from less severe depletions or natural fluctuations across diverse life histories.
studies.notes: Journal version (Fish and Fisheries) is asserted in a snippet but its DOI/year are not visible; cite the bioRxiv DOI 10.1101/329979. Essential for the study's outcome definition.

studies.citation: Worm B, Barbier EB, Beaumont N, Duffy JE, Folke C, Halpern BS, Jackson JBC, Lotze HK, Micheli F, Palumbi SR, Sala E, Selkoe KA, Stachowicz JJ, Watson R (2006) Impacts of biodiversity loss on ocean ecosystem services. Science
studies.data_system: Global catch records (FAO-type landings; exact source not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse = reported catch at 10% of the historical maximum; recovery = any post-collapse increase above the 10% threshold
studies.key_finding: Catch-based collapse definition (10% of historical maximum catch) underpinning the contested 2048 projection; critics argued the fixed-percentage-of-maximum definition conflates management-driven catch reductions with collapse.
studies.notes: Catch-based collapse definitions are widely criticised (Branch et al. 'Apocalypse in world fisheries?' ICES JMS 2011 appears in results); prefer biomass-based definitions for the proposed study.

studies.citation: Mullon C, Fréon P, Cury P (2005) The dynamics of collapse in world fisheries. Fish and Fisheries 6: 111-120
studies.data_system: 1519 main catch series from the FAO world fisheries catch database over 50 years
studies.outcome_definition: Catch-based collapse (details of the 'plateau/smooth/erratic' typology not visible in search results)
studies.key_finding: Analysed the dynamics of collapse across 1519 FAO catch series; widely cited as the source of a collapse-shape typology (details not visible in search results).
studies.notes: PDF hosted on Fréon's site; typology details should be confirmed from the full text.

studies.citation: Essington TE, Moriarty PE, Froehlich HE, Hodgson EE, Koehn LE, Oken KL, Siple MC, Stawitz CC (2015) Fishing amplifies forage fish population collapses. PNAS
studies.data_system: 55 forage fish stocks (stock-assessment biomass series)
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse = biomass fell to a quarter or less of the stock's average biomass (27 of 55 stocks collapsed at some point)
studies.key_finding: High fishing rates were maintained while productivity declined rapidly, so the magnitude and frequency (but not duration) of forage fish collapses far exceeded expectations from natural fluctuations.
studies.notes: Author list beyond Essington and Moriarty taken from the Semantic Scholar title string only partially; treat co-author list as medium confidence. Useful for the 'B relative to mean' collapse definition and for the fishing-during-decline mechanism.

studies.citation: Neubauer P, Jensen OP, Hutchings JA, Baum JK (2013) Resilience and recovery of overexploited marine populations. Science 340: 347-349
studies.data_system: Global meta-analysis of overfished stocks (RAM Legacy not explicitly named in snippets)
studies.outcome_definition: Overfished/collapsed stocks and recovery times (thresholds not visible in search results)
studies.key_finding: Resilience of stocks subjected to moderate overfishing is enhanced, allowing swift recovery, but prolonged intense overexploitation (especially collapsed stocks) delays rebuilding and substantially increases uncertainty in recovery times; exploitation history predicts recovery.
studies.notes: Recovery rather than collapse prediction; relevant to how post-collapse periods are handled in labeling.

studies.citation: Hutchings JA, Reynolds JD (2004) Marine fish population collapses: consequences for recovery and extinction risk. BioScience 54(4): 297-309
studies.data_system: >230 marine fish populations
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse definition not visible in search results; reports median 83% reduction in breeding population size from historic levels
studies.key_finding: Across >230 populations, median 83% reduction in breeding size; few recover rapidly and most show little or no change up to 15 years after collapse; Allee effects/depensation among factors limiting recovery.
studies.notes: Background for collapse prevalence and post-collapse persistence.

studies.citation: Vert-pre KA, Amoroso RO, Jensen OP, Hilborn R (2013) Frequency and intensity of productivity regime shifts in marine fish stocks. PNAS 110: 1779-1784
studies.data_system: Marine fish stock assessments (RAM Legacy not explicitly named in snippets)
studies.outcome_definition: Productivity regime shifts between low and high regimes (detection method not visible in search results)
studies.key_finding: First assessment of how frequent and intense productivity regime shifts are across marine fish stocks; drew a PNAS comment ('Production is a poor metric for identifying regime-like behavior in marine stocks', Szuwalski & Hilborn) and reply.
studies.notes: Quantitative results (fractions of stocks with regime-like productivity) not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Perälä T, Kuparinen A (2015) Detecting regime shifts in fish stock dynamics. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences
studies.data_system: Recruit-per-spawner time series; simulated Atlantic cod series used for testing
studies.outcome_definition: Productivity regime shift (change point in recruit-per-spawner series)
studies.key_finding: Applies a Bayesian online change-point detection algorithm to recruit-per-spawner series to detect productivity regime shifts, evaluated on simulated Atlantic cod series.
studies.notes: The 'online' formulation is sequential by construction (hence 'partial' for time-indexed), but a forecast-skill evaluation is not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Perälä T, Kuparinen A (2017) Detection of Allee effects in marine fishes: analytical biases generated by data availability and model selection. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 284(1861): 20171284
studies.data_system: Nine Atlantic herring populations; a snippet also mentions RAM Legacy SSBmsy/SSBmax for >130 stocks in the same results (attribution to this paper uncertain)
studies.outcome_definition: Demographic Allee effect (positive association between per-capita growth and abundance at low size)
studies.key_finding: Argues that failures to detect Allee effects in marine fishes stem from methodological and data limitations; evidence for Allee effects is strongly provisional on observations at low abundance; Atlantic cod gave the strongest Allee evidence while herring showed compensatory signals.
studies.notes: Relevant to whether depensation could be a mechanism producing critical-slowing-down-type dynamics before collapse.

studies.citation: Keith DM, Hutchings JA (2012) Population dynamics of marine fishes at low abundance. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences 69(7): 1150-1163
studies.data_system: 207 exploited marine fish stocks (104 species); meta-analysis
studies.outcome_definition: Standardised per-capita population growth vs abundance (Allee effect detection)
studies.key_finding: Considerable variability in how per-capita growth changes with abundance; some species (e.g. Atlantic cod) show evidence of Allee effects.
studies.notes: Meta-analytic Allee-effect evidence base for marine stocks.

studies.citation: Kuparinen A, Keith DM, Hutchings JA (2014) Allee effect and the uncertainty of population recovery. Conservation Biology 28(3): 790-798
studies.data_system: Not visible in search results (modelling of recovery dynamics)
studies.outcome_definition: Recovery of depleted populations under Allee effects
studies.key_finding: Allee effects can limit growth at low abundance and thereby increase uncertainty in recovery dynamics of collapsed populations.
studies.notes: Adjacent mechanism paper.

studies.citation: Hilborn R, Hively DJ, Jensen OP, Branch TA (2014) The dynamics of fish populations at low abundance and prospects for rebuilding and recovery. ICES Journal of Marine Science 71(8): 2141-2151
studies.data_system: Updated stock-assessment database with >100 stocks depleted to <20% of maximum observed stock size
studies.outcome_definition: Depletion to <20% of maximum observed stock size; depensation tested in surplus production and recruitment
studies.key_finding: Tested depensation in surplus production and recruitment and examined probability of stock increase as a function of stock size and fishing pressure; found little evidence for strong depensation though it could not be ruled out.
studies.notes: Counterpoint to Perälä & Kuparinen 2017 and Keith & Hutchings 2012; also uses 'probability of increase given state and fishing pressure', a state-based predictor akin to the proposed baseline.

studies.citation: Hutchings JA (2014) Renaissance of a caveat: Allee effects in marine fish. ICES Journal of Marine Science 71(8): 2152
studies.data_system: Not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: Not visible in search results
studies.key_finding: Title and venue visible only; argues (per title) for renewed attention to Allee effects in marine fish.
studies.notes: Only bibliographic details visible.

studies.citation: Vasilakopoulos P, Marshall CT (2015) Resilience and tipping points of an exploited fish population over six decades. Global Change Biology
studies.data_system: Barents Sea cod (Gadus morhua) population, six decades
studies.outcome_definition: Critical transitions/tipping points inferred from a fitted folded stability landscape (fold bifurcation)
studies.key_finding: Introduced a generic resilience measure (vertical distance from attractor plus horizontal distance from tipping point) from fold-bifurcation attributes; fitted landscape for Barents Sea cod resembled a hysteresis plot of alternative stable states.
studies.notes: Later extended to Integrated Resilience Assessment for Mediterranean, Atlantic and Pacific ecosystems (Sci Rep 2017; Hidalgo et al. J Anim Ecol 2022 in results). Single-stock, retrospective.

studies.citation: Sguotti C, Otto SA, Frelat R, Langbehn TJ, Ryberg MP, Lindegren M, Durant JM, Stenseth NC, Möllmann C (2019) Catastrophic dynamics limit Atlantic cod recovery. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 286: 20182877
studies.data_system: Atlantic cod stocks (North Atlantic; stock assessment series; count not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse and recovery as discontinuous transitions in a stochastic cusp (catastrophe theory) model
studies.baseline_comparator: Alternative (linear/logistic) models within cusp framework; not visible in detail
studies.key_finding: Stochastic cusp modelling suggests cod collapse and recovery are driven by the interaction of exploitation pressure and environmental drivers, with hysteresis limiting North Sea cod recovery after warming and the 2012 regime shift.
studies.notes: Data on Dryad and Zenodo. Retrospective mechanism attribution, not prospective warning.

studies.citation: Möllmann C, Cormon X, Funk S, Otto SA, Schmidt JO, Schwermer H, Sguotti C, Voss R, Quaas M (2021) Tipping point realized in cod fishery. Scientific Reports 11: 14259
studies.data_system: Western Baltic cod stock assessment and environmental series
studies.outcome_definition: Tipping point / shift to low-productivity state identified via changepoint analysis and stochastic cusp modelling
studies.key_finding: Combined changepoint analysis and stochastic cusp modelling to conclude Western Baltic cod is beyond a tipping point caused by unsustainable exploitation under changing environment, with climate change stabilising a likely irreversible low-productivity state.
studies.notes: Single-stock retrospective case study.

studies.citation: Blöcker AM, Gutte HM, Bender RL, Otto SA, Sguotti C, Möllmann C (2023) Regime shift dynamics, tipping points and the success of fisheries management. Scientific Reports
studies.data_system: Six strongly fished or depleted commercial fish stocks in the North Sea
studies.outcome_definition: Regime shift dynamics / tipping (positive or failed recovery) in response to fishing and temperature
studies.key_finding: Regime-shift dynamics found in all six North Sea stocks as responses to fishing pressure and temperature; context dependence determines whether management leads to failed recovery or positive tipping.
studies.notes: Same Hamburg group; retrospective.

studies.citation: Krkošek M, Drake JM (2014) On signals of phase transitions in salmon population dynamics. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 281: 20133221
studies.data_system: Recruitment dynamics of 120 stocks of three Pacific salmon species
studies.outcome_definition: Ecological phase transitions including populations approaching extinction (exact criterion not visible in search results)
studies.key_finding: Tested critical slowing down in salmon recruitment as an EWS of phase transitions; pink salmon exhibited increased variability and autocorrelation in populations approaching extinction, consistent with EWS; a Drake-lab summary notes that forecasting fish stock collapses via CSD 'has not yet been developed' and first requires demonstrating CSD in fish transitions.
studies.notes: Anadromous rather than strictly marine stocks; multi-stock comparison implies non-transitioning stocks are present, but design details not visible. Cited in debates on EWS reliability in field data.

studies.citation: Burthe SJ, et al. (2016) Do early warning indicators consistently predict nonlinear change in long-term ecological data? Journal of Applied Ecology
studies.data_system: Long-term abundance time series for 55 taxa (126 data sets) across trophic levels in marine and freshwater ecosystems (UK; specific marine sources not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Significant nonlinear change in abundance (test method not visible), scored against significant increases in variance and autocorrelation
studies.baseline_comparator: None (indicator classifications compared with presence/absence of nonlinear change)
studies.key_finding: Variance and autocorrelation consistently failed to predict nonlinear change: true positives were uncommon (8% for variance, 6% for autocorrelation), all but one series also contained false classifications, and 43% of series were classified differently by variance vs autocorrelation.
studies.notes: Strong precedent for reporting confusion-matrix-style outcomes including false positives on series without transitions; not fisheries stock assessments per se but includes marine taxa.

studies.citation: Litzow MA, Hunsicker ME (2016) Early warning signals, nonlinearity, and signs of hysteresis in real ecosystems. Ecosphere 7(12): e01614
studies.data_system: Review and meta-analysis of published EWS studies plus eight northeast Pacific Ocean time series
studies.outcome_definition: Ecological transitions with tested nonlinearity (definition per study)
studies.key_finding: Published studies demonstrating nonlinearity in ecosystem dynamics are more likely to support EWS predictions than studies with linear or undetermined dynamics; recommends testing for nonlinearity before applying EWS.
studies.notes: Implies the proposed study should stratify or report results by evidence of nonlinearity in stock dynamics.

studies.citation: Litzow MA, Urban JD, Laurel BJ (2008) Increased spatial variance accompanies reorganization of two continental shelf ecosystems. Ecological Applications 18: 1331-1337
studies.data_system: Trawl survey data spanning phase transitions in the Gulf of Alaska and Scotian Shelf
studies.outcome_definition: Ecosystem phase transitions between alternate states (criteria not visible)
studies.key_finding: Tested whether increases in ecosystem (spatial) variability accompany phase transitions in two shelf ecosystems, as potential early warning.
studies.notes: Community-level, survey-based; precursor to Litzow et al. 2013.

studies.citation: Clements CF, McCarthy MA, Blanchard JL (2019) Early warning signals of recovery in complex systems. Nature Communications 10
studies.data_system: Trait-based ecological model plus two real-world ICES cod stock survey time series (SSB, mean size, SD size)
studies.outcome_definition: Recovery of overexploited stocks (criterion not visible)
studies.baseline_comparator: Abundance-only EWS vs trait-based vs combined
studies.key_finding: Abundance-based and trait-based (body size) signals are independently detectable before recovery of overexploited stocks, and combining them gives the best predictions of recovery.
studies.notes: Author list inferred from the URL/host page ('Clements') and snippet; co-authors medium confidence. Recovery, not collapse, but uses ICES survey data relevant to the FishGlob/ICES arm.

studies.citation: Clements CF, Blanchard JL, Nash KL, Hindell MA, Ozgul A (2017) Body size shifts and early warning signals precede the historic collapse of whale stocks. Nature Ecology & Evolution
studies.data_system: Historical commercial whaling catch and body-size records
studies.outcome_definition: Global collapse of whale stocks (criterion not visible)
studies.key_finding: Whale body sizes declined by up to 4 m over 70 years during whaling and EWS were detectable up to 40 years before global collapse of whale stocks; combining abundance and body size can shorten the series needed and reduce false positives.
studies.notes: Co-author list beyond Clements not visible in snippets; treat as medium confidence. Marine mammals, not fish.

studies.citation: Clements CF, Ozgul A (2016) Including trait-based early warning signals helps predict population collapse. Nature Communications
studies.data_system: Not visible in search results (experimental/model populations)
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse (experimental)
studies.key_finding: Composite indices adding phenotypic traits (body size) to abundance-based EWS give more accurate inference of approaching transitions than abundance alone.
studies.notes: Methodological background for trait-augmented EWS.

studies.citation: Boettiger C, Hastings A (2012) Early warning signals and the prosecutor's fallacy. Proceedings of the Royal Society B
studies.data_system: Simulated systems that transitioned purely by chance
studies.outcome_definition: Simulated critical/stochastic transitions
studies.key_finding: Conditionally selecting systems known to have transitioned inflates false-positive rates of common EWS statistics (the prosecutor's fallacy); selection for forecasting must include systems that did not transition.
studies.notes: Core methodological justification for including non-collapsing stocks and prospective evaluation.

studies.citation: Perretti CT, Munch SB (2012) Regime shift indicators fail under noise levels commonly observed in ecological systems. Ecological Applications 22(6): 1772-1779
studies.data_system: Three-species simulation model under field-like noise
studies.outcome_definition: Simulated regime shifts
studies.key_finding: A suite of regime-shift indicators failed under noise levels commonly observed in open ecological systems.
studies.notes: Authors at Scripps (fisheries-oriented group); simulation only.

studies.citation: Hsieh C-h, Reiss CS, Hunter JR, Beddington JR, May RM, Sugihara G (2006) Fishing elevates variability in the abundance of exploited species. Nature 443: 859-862
studies.data_system: CalCOFI larval fish record (exploited vs unexploited species)
studies.outcome_definition: Not a collapse study (temporal variability of abundance)
studies.key_finding: Exploited species show higher temporal variability in abundance than unexploited species after accounting for life history, abundance, traits and phylogeny, likely via fishery-induced age truncation.
studies.notes: Important confound: variance increases can arise from fishing-induced age truncation, not critical slowing down. Co-author list beyond 'Hsieh, Reiss, Hunter et al.' from memory of the Nature listing is not fully visible; treat co-authors after Hunter as medium confidence.

studies.citation: Anderson CNK, Hsieh C-h, Sandin SA, et al. (2008) Why fishing magnifies fluctuations in fish abundance. Nature 452: 835-839
studies.data_system: 50-year CalCOFI larval fish record
studies.outcome_definition: Not a collapse study (variability of exploited populations)
studies.key_finding: Distinguished three mechanisms for elevated variability of harvested stocks (variable fishing pressure, environmental tracking by truncated populations, demographic instability from age truncation).
studies.notes: Mechanistic confound for variance-based EWS in exploited stocks.

studies.citation: Minto C, Myers RA, Blanchard W (2008) Survival variability and population density in fish populations. Nature 452: 344-347
studies.data_system: Large global compilation of marine, anadromous and freshwater fisheries data
studies.outcome_definition: Not a collapse study (survival variability vs adult abundance)
studies.key_finding: Interannual variability in progeny survival increases at low adult abundance in an inversely density-dependent fashion.
studies.notes: Mechanism by which variance rises at low abundance independent of critical slowing down; relevant to interpreting variance-trend EWS near collapse.

studies.citation: Ward EJ, Holmes EE, Thorson JT, Collen B (2014) Complexity is costly: a meta-analysis of parametric and non-parametric methods for short-term population forecasting. Oikos 123(6): 652-661
studies.data_system: Not visible in search results (my query assumed RAM Legacy and GPDD; not confirmed)
studies.outcome_definition: Short-term population forecast accuracy (not collapse)
studies.baseline_comparator: Parametric vs non-parametric forecasting methods compared
studies.key_finding: Meta-analysis of parametric and non-parametric short-term population forecasting methods; title indicates more complex models did not forecast better.
studies.notes: Candidate precedent for capacity-matched baseline forecasters; datasets and evaluation details not visible in search results and must be confirmed from the paper (a reproduction report exists at the RREEBES link).

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2024) Stock assessment models overstate sustainability of the world's fisheries. Science
studies.data_system: Global stock assessments (RAM Legacy-type retrospective assessment series; database not explicitly named in snippets)
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse = biomass below 10% of maximum historical biomass
studies.key_finding: Accounting for retrospective bias in assessments, 85% more stocks than currently recognised have likely collapsed below 10% of maximum historical biomass.
studies.notes: Highly relevant caveat: assessment-derived biomass series are revised retrospectively, so 'data available by time t' in a prequential design differs from final assessment series. Author list not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Free CM, et al. (2019) Impacts of historical warming on marine fisheries production. Science
studies.data_system: 235 populations, 124 species, 38 ecoregions (temperature-dependent surplus production models; RAM Legacy not explicitly named in snippets)
studies.outcome_definition: Not a collapse study (temperature-driven productivity/MSY change)
studies.key_finding: MSY declined 4.1% from 1930 to 2010 overall (up to 35% in some ecoregions); 12% of populations showed significant temperature-driven productivity change.
studies.notes: Productivity-regime context; a Science comment on the paper also appears in results.

studies.citation: Szuwalski CS, Vert-Pre KA, Punt AE, Branch TA, Hilborn R (2015) Examining common assumptions about recruitment: a meta-analysis of recruitment dynamics for worldwide marine fisheries. Fish and Fisheries 16(4): 633-648
studies.data_system: 224 stocks in the RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database
studies.outcome_definition: Not a collapse study (recruitment-spawning biomass relationships and regimes)
studies.key_finding: Recruitment and spawning biomass are not positively related over the observed range for 61% of 224 RAM Legacy stocks.
studies.notes: Relevant to the mechanism (regime-like recruitment) underlying productivity shifts.

studies.citation: Britten GL, Dowd M, Worm B (2016) Changing recruitment capacity in global fish stocks. PNAS 113: 134-139
studies.data_system: Global stock assessments (database not explicitly named in snippets)
studies.outcome_definition: Not a collapse study (time-varying recruitment capacity)
studies.key_finding: Recruitment capacity has been reduced by environmental change and overfishing, by about 3% of historical maximum per decade on average.
studies.notes: State-space trend estimation of productivity; adjacent to the 'trend' baseline concept.

studies.citation: Britten GL, Duarte CM, Worm B (2021) Recovery of assessed global fish stocks remains uncertain. PNAS 118(31): e2108532118
studies.data_system: Assessed global fish stocks (RAM Legacy-era; database not explicitly named in snippets)
studies.outcome_definition: Stocks below biomass targets / exploited above sustainable rates
studies.key_finding: Different averaging methods over high inter-stock variability yield divergent recovery trajectories; 4 of 10 methods suggest recovery not achieved, with up to 48% of stocks below biomass targets and 40% exploited above sustainable rates.
studies.notes: Shows sensitivity of aggregate status conclusions to aggregation choices; supports grouping by system.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2026) Nonlinearity in marine fish populations is amplified by temperature variation and fast life histories. Nature Ecology & Evolution
studies.data_system: 243 recruitment and 266 spawner time series of 143 marine fish species worldwide (database not explicitly named in snippets)
studies.outcome_definition: Not a collapse study (degree of nonlinearity in fluctuations)
studies.key_finding: Nonlinearity shown by 81% of populations and correlated with fluctuation magnitude; temperature variation amplifies nonlinearity and fast life histories elevate it.
studies.notes: Relevant to Litzow & Hunsicker's recommendation to condition EWS expectations on nonlinearity; author list and DOI not visible (URL only).

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2026) Large fisheries declines linked to compound and extreme climate events. Nature Communications
studies.data_system: 6659 catch time series for 1246 species across 254 regions (three decades)
studies.outcome_definition: Local extreme low catch events (risk-based analysis; threshold not visible)
studies.key_finding: Compound extreme high ocean temperature and low productivity events sharply increase the likelihood of local extreme low catch events, especially in tropical/subtropical regions.
studies.notes: Catch-based, climate-driver framing; not EWS.

studies.citation: Pedersen EJ, Thompson PL, Ball RA, Fortin M-J, Gouhier TC, Link H, Moritz C, Nenzen H, Stanley RRE, Taranu ZE, Gonzalez A, Guichard F, Pepin P (2017) Signatures of the collapse and incipient recovery of an overexploited marine ecosystem. Royal Society Open Science 4: 170215
studies.data_system: 33-year scientific trawl survey, Newfoundland/Labrador groundfish community
studies.outcome_definition: Early-1990s cod/groundfish collapse and subsequent phases (descriptive)
studies.key_finding: Groundfish community passed through four phases: rapid synchronous biomass collapse, regime shift in composition with loss of functional diversity, slow compositional recovery, and slow biomass growth.
studies.notes: Retrospective description of the canonical collapse; useful for survey-based (FishGlob-type) outcome characterisation.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (year not visible; PMC record 2021-era) Temperature increase drives critical slowing down of fish ecosystems. PLOS ONE
studies.data_system: Maizuru Bay (Japan) coastal fish community census 2002-2014
studies.outcome_definition: Community-level critical slowing down / shift toward oscillatory low-diversity state
studies.key_finding: A ~20% local temperature increase (2002-2014) was associated with ~25% diversity loss and analysis suggesting the fish community moves toward persistent oscillatory states with lower diversity and stock, framed as critical slowing down.
studies.notes: Community, not stock; authors/year not visible.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2026) Early Warning Signals in Ecological Time-Series. Entropy 28(6): 628
studies.data_system: Review (lakes, coral reefs, grasslands, forests, marine systems)
studies.outcome_definition: Review
studies.key_finding: Synthesis of EWS theory, indicators, empirical applications and ML/model-based extensions; stresses that neither presence nor direction of indicator trends is universal and that mechanism-specific false positives (N-, R-, S-tipping) require prior mechanistic context.
studies.notes: Recent review useful for the introduction's false-positive framing; cites the 2020 Ecological Indicators fisheries EWS study ('Zhang, 2020').

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2024) Empirical validation of integrated stock assessment models to ensuring risk equivalence: a pathway to resilient fisheries management. PLOS ONE
studies.data_system: Integrated stock assessment models (case stocks not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Prediction skill of abundance indices (not collapse)
studies.baseline_comparator: Naive forecast (MASE < 1 indicates skill over naive)
studies.key_finding: Hindcasting cross-validation (HCXval) removes data sequentially from the most recent years backward ('tail cutting') and scores forecasts of unseen observations with Mean Absolute Scaled Error relative to a naive forecast over specified horizons.
studies.notes: Provides a fisheries-native template for time-indexed origins and a naive baseline, but for index prediction rather than collapse classification. The related ResearchGate record 'Evaluation of the prediction skill of stock assessment using hindcasting' has no visible authors/journal in results.

studies.citation: Ricard D, Minto C, Jensen OP, Baum JK (2012) Examining the knowledge base and status of commercially exploited marine species with the RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database. Fish and Fisheries
studies.data_system: RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database (initially 331 stocks from 21 agencies; time series of total biomass, spawner biomass, recruits, fishing mortality, catch)
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable (database description)
studies.key_finding: Describes the RAM Legacy database core series (biomass, SSB, recruits, F, catch) assembled from 21 agencies for 331 stocks; a later snippet in the same results mentions 1,330 stocks in a subsequent version (attribution unclear).
studies.notes: Co-author list beyond Ricard is from the standard citation and only 'Ricard - 2012' is visible in the URL title; treat co-authors as medium confidence.

studies.citation: Trochta JT, et al. (2020) The highs and lows of herring: a meta-analysis of patterns and factors in herring collapse and recovery. Fish and Fisheries
studies.data_system: Not visible in search results (herring stocks meta-analysis)
studies.outcome_definition: Herring collapse and recovery (definitions not visible)
studies.key_finding: Title only visible: meta-analysis of patterns and factors in herring collapse and recovery.
studies.notes: Surfaced only as a link; no content visible.

notes: Search limitations: per instructions I relied solely on WebSearch result snippets (53 queries) and did not attempt WebFetch/curl against publisher, PubMed/PMC, Crossref or repository hosts. Design fields were filled only where a snippet showed the detail; most 'unknown' entries reflect snippet coverage, not paper content. Corrections to seed assumptions: Litzow et al. 2013 is in Ecological Applications (not PLoS ONE); Pélissié is not an author of the 2025 PNAS dynamical-footprint paper (Cano, Jensen, Dakos), but leads the 2026 Science Advances paper; the Ecological Indicators 2020 fisheries-EWS paper's first author is Fan Zhang, co-authors not visible. Unattributed snippet: a collapse definition of 'BMIN < 20% of BMSY' and 'B/BMSY < 0.5' appeared in the RAM Legacy collapse-definition query results without a clear source paper; do not cite it to Pinsky & Byler without checking. Author lists for the 2024 Science 'Stock assessment models overstate sustainability' paper, the 2026 Nature Ecology & Evolution nonlinearity paper, the 2026 Nature Communications compound-climate paper, the Maizuru Bay PLOS ONE paper, the Entropy 2026 review, and the 2024 PLOS ONE HCXval paper were not visible. Landscape summary relevant to the novelty claim (facts only, no EWS-outcome computation): (1) the closest prior EWS-in-fisheries evaluations are Zhang 2020 (SD/AR1 on 191 populations, lead time >5 y for >50%, positive likelihood ratio reported), Litzow et al. 2013 (spatial catch variance, 12 collapsing vs 2 non-collapsing fisheries, 1-4 y lead), Krkošek & Drake 2014 (CSD in 120 salmon stocks), Burthe et al. 2016 (126 marine/freshwater series; true positives 6-8%, false classifications ubiquitous) and Pélissié et al. 2026 (abrupt productivity declines precede collapse by ~10-20 y in ~25% of shifting stocks, retrospective); none of the visible snippets describe a design combining sequential time-indexed origins, fixed 1-5 y horizons, capacity-matched state/trend baselines, calibration to a common false-alarm budget, and explicit treatment of right-censored origins, which is consistent with (but does not prove) the intended novelty claim; (2) fisheries-native hindcast cross-validation (HCXval with tail cutting and MASE vs naive forecast) exists for abundance-index prediction and can serve as the template for the baseline arm; (3) collapse-definition heterogeneity is well documented (Worm 2006 catch <10% max; Essington 2015 biomass <=25% of mean; Hilborn 2014 <20% of max observed; Science 2024 <10% of max historical biomass; Yletyinen et al. process-based turnover definition), and the Science 2024 retrospective-bias finding implies assessment series available at time t differ from final series, which matters for a strict prequential design; (4) documented confounds for variance/autocorrelation-based EWS in exploited stocks include fishing-induced age truncation raising variability (Hsieh 2006; Anderson 2008), inversely density-dependent survival variability at low abundance (Minto 2008), prosecutor's-fallacy selection bias (Boettiger & Hastings 2012), noise sensitivity (Perretti & Munch 2012) and dependence on nonlinearity (Litzow & Hunsicker 2016; 2026 Nat Ecol Evol nonlinearity paper). No deep-learning EWS study specific to marine fish stock collapse surfaced in the ML query (results were generic bifurcation/flickering detectors or aquaculture disease systems).
