studies.citation: Litzow MA, Mueter FJ, Urban JD (2013) Rising catch variability preceded historical fisheries collapses in Alaska. Ecological Applications 23:1475-1487
studies.data_system: Spatially resolved catch data from 14 Gulf of Alaska / Bering Sea crustacean fisheries (12 collapsing, 2 non-collapsing), 278 cumulative fishery-years
studies.outcome_definition: Stock collapse of crustacean fisheries beginning in the 1970s; exact numerical collapse criterion not visible in search results
studies.baseline_comparator: Two non-collapsing fisheries used as a comparison group; no state/trend forecasting model visible
studies.key_finding: A random-effects model across all 12 collapsing fisheries found strong evidence of increasing spatial catch variability 1-4 years before collapse, and variability trends differed significantly between collapsing and non-collapsing fisheries; no evidence of pre-collapse increases in skewness. Authors concluded fishing effects, rather than critical slowing down, were the more likely cause of rising variability.
studies.notes: Retrospective pooled-trend test, not a sequential-origin forecast. Detection was only achieved by pooling across fisheries. Non-collapsing controls were few (n=2).

studies.citation: Zhang F (2020) Early warning signals of population productivity regime shifts in global fisheries. Ecological Indicators 115
studies.data_system: 191 global fisheries populations (database not explicitly named in snippets; the same search surfaced RAM Legacy productivity-regime-shift work)
studies.outcome_definition: Observed productivity regime shifts (not biomass collapse); shift-detection method not visible in search results
studies.key_finding: Evaluated standard deviation (SD) and lag-1 autoregressive coefficient (AR1) as EWS for observed productivity regime shifts in 191 populations; EWS tended to give warning more than 5 years in advance for more than 50% of populations, but performance was described as 'bumpy' and the author concluded critical transitions may not be a major cause of regime shifts in global fisheries.
studies.notes: Closest existing RAM-scale EWS evaluation, but outcome is a productivity regime shift rather than an abundance collapse. Search summaries gave conflicting article identifiers (106344 vs 106371); use the ScienceDirect PII URL. Whether non-shifting populations or false-alarm rates were analysed is not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Cano AV, Jensen OP, Dakos V (2025) Identifying fish populations prone to abrupt shifts via dynamical footprint analysis. PNAS 122(34): e2505461122
studies.data_system: Fish population biomass time series from three datasets (dataset names not visible in search results; search summary also links it to 315 agency-assessed stocks)
studies.outcome_definition: Time series classified into 'abrupt' vs 'nonabrupt' trajectory classes (shape/trend-based classification: no change, linear, quadratic, abrupt)
studies.baseline_comparator: None visible; classification accuracy reported for abrupt vs nonabrupt classes
studies.key_finding: A mechanism-agnostic, context-specific approach classifies biomass time series as abrupt vs nonabrupt and predicts class membership from a 'dynamical footprint' (variance, autocorrelation and related metrics); populations prone to abrupt shifts were detected with moderate accuracy in three datasets despite data limitations.
studies.notes: Whole-series classification (which stocks are prone to shifts), not a time-indexed forecast of when a shift occurs. Validation scheme (cross-validation vs holdout) not visible in search results. One search summary listed Pélissié as a collaborator on related work, not as author of this paper.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (Cano/Jensen/Dakos group per search summary) (2026) Abrupt declines in fish productivity often precede stock collapses in marine fisheries. Science Advances
studies.data_system: 315 agency-assessed fish stocks worldwide (RAM Legacy 'appears to' be the source per search summary); SST 1870-2020; U/UMSY as fishing-intensity proxy
studies.outcome_definition: Stock collapse (numerical threshold not visible in search results); productivity trajectories classified as no change / linear / quadratic / abrupt
studies.baseline_comparator: None visible (retrospective association between abrupt productivity shifts, warming, fishing intensity and later collapse)
studies.key_finding: Abrupt productivity shifts detected in more than a quarter of 315 stocks; abrupt declines over-represented where SST warming was largest, abrupt increases more likely under lower fishing intensity; abrupt productivity declines preceded stock collapses by roughly a decade (10-20 years) in about 25% of shifted stocks, so some collapses could be anticipated if abrupt shifts were detected systematically; authors propose productivity-based warning signals in harvest control rules.
studies.notes: Year and author list inferred from PubMed/PMC ID ranges and search context, not explicitly visible; the EcoEvoRxiv preprint 'Ocean warming drives abrupt declines in fish productivity at global scale' appears to be the related preprint. A search summary for the 'abrupt shift' query mentioned a Bayesian online change-point algorithm for mean and variance shifts, but its attribution to this paper vs. the ResearchGate item 'A systematic approach for detecting abrupt shifts in ecological timeseries' is not clear.

studies.citation: Pinsky ML, Byler D (2015) Fishing, fast growth and climate variability increase the risk of collapse. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 282(1813): 20151053
studies.data_system: 154 marine fish populations from RAM Legacy stock assessments
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse and long-term depletion (numerical criteria not visible in search results)
studies.baseline_comparator: Boosted regression trees on harvesting (magnitude and duration of overfishing), life-history traits and climate variability; no EWS
studies.key_finding: Magnitude of overfishing was the most important factor explaining collapses, duration of overfishing best explained long-term depletion; fast-growing species in climatically variable LMEs were about twice as likely to collapse when overfished.
studies.notes: Cross-sectional risk model using fishing-pressure covariates (U/UMSY-type information) rather than time-series EWS; relevant as a 'state' predictor benchmark. Data archived on Dryad.

studies.citation: Pinsky ML, Jensen OP, Ricard D, Palumbi SR (2011) Unexpected patterns of fisheries collapse in the world's oceans. PNAS 108(20):8317-8322
studies.data_system: RAM Legacy stock assessments plus catch data
studies.outcome_definition: Collapsed if minimum annual biomass (BMIN) < 20% of BMSY; BMSY estimated from Schaefer surplus-production fits when not reported
studies.baseline_comparator: None (descriptive comparison of collapse frequency by trophic level/body size)
studies.key_finding: Up to twice as many fisheries for small, low-trophic-level species have collapsed as fisheries for large predators, contrary to terrestrial expectations.
studies.notes: Primary value for this project: an explicit, widely used biomass-based collapse definition (BMIN < 0.2 BMSY) in RAM Legacy.

studies.citation: Yletyinen J et al. (2018) When is a fish stock collapsed? bioRxiv 329979
studies.data_system: Stock time series with diverse life histories (database not visible in search results)
studies.outcome_definition: Proposes a process-based, time-series-based collapse definition linking three phases of a collapse event, intended to separate collapses from less severe depletions and natural fluctuations
studies.key_finding: Numerous collapse definitions exist and a stock's classification is sensitive to the definition's formulation, contributing to contrasting perceptions of stock status; a process-based, time-series detection method is proposed.
studies.notes: Co-author list not visible in search results. A 2026 Stockholm University news item suggests related published work on avoiding stock collapses as a management objective; details not visible.

studies.citation: Essington TE et al. (2015) Fishing amplifies forage fish population collapses. PNAS 112(21):6648-6652
studies.data_system: Global dataset of 55 forage fish stocks (27 collapsed at some point)
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse = biomass falling to one quarter or less of the stock's average biomass
studies.baseline_comparator: Null model: simulations of natural, random fluctuations
studies.key_finding: High fishing rates were maintained while stock productivity was in rapid decline; magnitude and frequency (but not duration) of collapses far exceeded expectations from natural fluctuations; a minimum-biomass-threshold harvest rule at 50% of average observed biomass would have prevented 64% of collapses at <2% long-term catch loss.
studies.notes: Provides a null-model comparator and a biomass-based collapse definition; also documents that productivity decline precedes collapse under sustained fishing.

studies.citation: Krkošek M, Drake JM (2014) On signals of phase transitions in salmon population dynamics. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 281(1784): 20133221
studies.data_system: Recruitment dynamics of 120 stocks of three Pacific salmon species
studies.outcome_definition: Proximity to critical transitions (extinction) in fishery models, indexed by fitted growth parameter near zero
studies.baseline_comparator: Cross-stock comparison against fitted population-growth parameter; no forecasting baseline visible
studies.key_finding: Pink salmon showed increased variability and autocorrelation in populations with growth parameter near zero, consistent with EWS of extinction; for sockeye, models and data indicate portfolio effects from heterogeneity in age-at-maturity may obscure EWS.
studies.notes: Anadromous rather than marine stock assessment, but a direct test of CSD indicators across many stocks with a mechanism (age-structure portfolio effects) that can mask EWS.

studies.citation: Dakos V, Glaser SM, Hsieh C-h, Sugihara G (2017) Elevated nonlinearity as an indicator of shifts in the dynamics of populations under stress. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 14(128): 20160845
studies.data_system: Reconstructed attractors from observed population time series; companion bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/051532) used Ricker-type simulations of a stock transitioning to overexploitation
studies.outcome_definition: Shifts in population dynamics under stress / transition to overexploitation and collapse in simulated stocks
studies.baseline_comparator: Linear vs nonlinear EDM forecast skill comparison; unexploited vs exploited simulated populations
studies.key_finding: Nonlinearity (difference in forecast skill between nonlinear and linear models on reconstructed attractors) and variance increase similarly before shifts; in the fish-stock preprint, CV, AR1 and nonlinearity all strongly increased before collapse, suggesting elevated nonlinearity as an additional indicator.
studies.notes: Empirical datasets used in the Interface paper are not visible in search results; the fish-stock version appears to be simulation-based (bioRxiv, authors not visible).

studies.citation: Clements CF, Blanchard JL, Nash KL, Hindell MA, Ozgul A (2017) Body size shifts and early warning signals precede the historic collapse of whale stocks. Nature Ecology & Evolution 1: 0188
studies.data_system: Commercial whaling catch and body-size records for blue, fin, sei and sperm whales
studies.outcome_definition: Global collapse of whale stocks during commercial whaling
studies.key_finding: Mean body size of caught whales declined by up to 4 m over 70 years; EWS (abundance- and trait-based) were detectable up to 40 years before the global collapse of whale stocks.
studies.notes: Marine harvested-stock collapse, but not fish and only collapsing stocks appear to be analysed (Boettiger-Hastings selection concern applies).

studies.citation: Clements CF, McCarthy MA, Blanchard JL (2019) Early warning signals of recovery in complex systems. Nature Communications 10: 1681
studies.data_system: Trait-based (size-spectrum) ecological model plus real-world fisheries data (specific database not visible in search results)
studies.outcome_definition: Recovery of overexploited stocks (not collapse)
studies.baseline_comparator: Abundance-only EWS vs trait-based EWS vs combined
studies.key_finding: Both abundance-based and trait-based EWS were independently detectable before recovery of overexploited stocks; combining them gave the best predictions of recovery.
studies.notes: Direction is recovery rather than collapse; relevant as the only fisheries-data EWS study found that compares indicator sets.

studies.citation: Vasilakopoulos P, Marshall CT (2015) Resilience and tipping points of an exploited fish population over six decades. Global Change Biology
studies.data_system: Six decades of data on one exploited fish population (species not visible in search results)
studies.outcome_definition: Abrupt, possibly irreversible state shift in the 2010s identified via fold-bifurcation attributes
studies.key_finding: Empirical evidence of a fold bifurcation in an exploited fish population; declining fishing pressure in the 1990s gave a gradual transition, further decline in the 2000s eroded resilience leading to an abrupt shift in the 2010s; introduces a resilience measure based on fold-bifurcation attributes.
studies.notes: Retrospective single-stock abrupt-shift detection; no out-of-sample prediction.

studies.citation: Sguotti C, Otto SA, Frelat R, Langbehn TJ, Ryberg MP, Lindegren M, Durant JM, Stenseth NC, Möllmann C (2019) Catastrophic dynamics limit Atlantic cod recovery. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 286: 20182877
studies.data_system: Atlantic cod stocks across the Atlantic (assessment time series; data on Dryad)
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse and (failed) recovery modelled as discontinuous transitions in a stochastic cusp model
studies.baseline_comparator: Stochastic cusp (catastrophe) model vs linear alternatives (comparison details not visible)
studies.key_finding: Collapse and recovery of cod stocks are potentially driven by the interaction of exploitation pressure and environmental drivers; ocean warming can induce a discontinuous relationship between fishing pressure and stock size, explaining hysteresis and limiting recovery.
studies.notes: Retrospective mechanism/hysteresis paper; useful for the 'abrupt shift' outcome literature, not for forecast evaluation.

studies.citation: Möllmann C, Cormon X, Funk S, Otto SA, Schmidt JO, Schwermer H, Sguotti C, Voss R, Quaas M (2021) Tipping point realized in cod fishery. Scientific Reports 11: 14259
studies.data_system: Western Baltic cod stock assessment and environmental time series
studies.outcome_definition: Tipping point / shift to a low-productivity state detected via changepoint analysis and stochastic cusp modelling
studies.key_finding: Statistical changepoint analysis and stochastic cusp modelling indicate Western Baltic cod is beyond a tipping point caused by unsustainable exploitation that ignored changing environmental conditions; climate change stabilizes a novel, likely irreversible low-productivity state.
studies.notes: Retrospective detection, single stock.

studies.citation: Blöcker AM, Sguotti C, Möllmann C (2023) Discontinuous dynamics in North Sea cod (Gadus morhua) caused by ecosystem change. Marine Ecology Progress Series 713:133-149
studies.data_system: North Sea cod assessment and ecosystem time series; follow-up (Cecapolli, Romagnoni, Blöcker, Möllmann, Sguotti 2025, ICES JMS 82(3)) on three North Sea cod substocks
studies.outcome_definition: Regime shift / discontinuous dynamics detected with stochastic cusp models, changepoint methods and driver-state plots
studies.key_finding: Stochastic cusp / changepoint analyses indicate discontinuous dynamics in North Sea cod driven by ecosystem change; the 2025 substock analysis found contrasting regime-shift dynamics and recovery potential across Southern, Northwestern and Viking populations.
studies.notes: Single-system retrospective regime-shift detection; DOI for the MEPS paper not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Vert-pre KA, Amoroso RO, Jensen OP, Hilborn R (2013) Frequency and intensity of productivity regime shifts in marine fish stocks. PNAS 110(5):1779-1784
studies.data_system: RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database (surplus production time series)
studies.outcome_definition: Productivity regime shifts (abrupt changes between low and high productivity regimes unrelated to abundance)
studies.baseline_comparator: Model comparison among abundance-driven, regime, mixed and random-variation explanations of productivity
studies.key_finding: First assessment of the frequency and intensity of productivity regime shifts; a search summary attributes to RAM-Legacy work the finding that dynamics of nearly 70% of populations are fully or partially explained by productivity regime shifts. A PNAS letter (Szuwalski & Hilborn-group, 'Production is a poor metric for identifying regime-like behavior', PNAS 110(16):E1436) disputed the metric.
studies.notes: Attribution of the '~70%' figure to this specific paper is from a search summary, not the abstract; treat as medium confidence.

studies.citation: Szuwalski CS, Vert-Pre KA, Punt AE, Branch TA, Hilborn R (2015) Examining common assumptions about recruitment: a meta-analysis of recruitment dynamics for worldwide marine fisheries. Fish and Fisheries 16(4):633-648
studies.data_system: Worldwide marine stock-recruit time series (RAM Legacy implied, not explicit in snippets)
studies.outcome_definition: Recruitment regime shifts / non-stationarity of stock-recruit relationships
studies.baseline_comparator: Competing hypotheses: recruitment linked to spawning biomass vs. regime-driven recruitment
studies.key_finding: Tests the assumptions that recruitment is related to spawning biomass and that recruitment dynamics are stationary; addresses regime shifts in recruitment across global fisheries (specific proportions not visible in search results).
studies.notes: A 2023 Fisheries Research re-examination ('The robustness of our assumptions about recruitment') was also surfaced but details are not visible.

studies.citation: Britten GL, Dowd M, Worm B (2016) Changing recruitment capacity in global fish stocks. PNAS 113(1):134-139
studies.data_system: Global assessed fish stocks (RAM Legacy implied; not explicit in snippets)
studies.outcome_definition: Trend in recruitment capacity (ability to produce surviving offspring)
studies.key_finding: Recruitment capacity has been significantly altered by environmental change and by biological changes from overfishing, declining by about 3% of the historical maximum per decade on average.
studies.notes: Productivity-trend background; not a collapse-prediction study.

studies.citation: Free CM, Thorson JT, Pinsky ML, Oken KL, Wiedenmann J, Jensen OP (2019) Impacts of historical warming on marine fisheries production. Science 363(6430)
studies.data_system: Assessed fish and invertebrate populations (RAM Legacy implied) with temperature-linked surplus production models, 1930-2010
studies.outcome_definition: Change in maximum sustainable yield (productivity), not collapse
studies.key_finding: Hindcasts indicate MSY of evaluated populations decreased 4.1% from 1930 to 2010, with five ecoregions losing 15-35%; some species respond positively but most negatively. A Science Comment and Response followed.
studies.notes: Only the first three authors were visible in snippets; remaining coauthors are from the visible NOAA repository record header and should be verified. Productivity-regime background only.

studies.citation: Neubauer P, Jensen OP, Hutchings JA, Baum JK (2013) Resilience and recovery of overexploited marine populations. Science 340:347-349
studies.data_system: Global meta-analysis of 153 overfished fish and invertebrate stocks that declined below 50% of BMSY (RAM Legacy implied)
studies.outcome_definition: Depletion below 0.5 BMSY; recovery time to reference level
studies.baseline_comparator: Covariate model of recovery time using exploitation history, fishing and life history
studies.key_finding: Stocks subjected to moderate overfishing showed enhanced resilience and swift recovery potential, whereas prolonged intense overexploitation (especially collapsed stocks) delayed rebuilding and greatly increased uncertainty in recovery times; exploitation history is an important predictor of recovery.
studies.notes: Source of the B/BMSY < 0.5 depletion criterion that a search summary listed as an alternative 'collapse' threshold used in RAM Legacy studies.

studies.citation: Keith DM, Hutchings JA (2012) Population dynamics of marine fishes at low abundance. Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences
studies.data_system: 207 exploited marine fish stocks (104 species) stock-recruit data
studies.outcome_definition: Allee effect / depensation in standardized per-capita population growth at low abundance
studies.key_finding: Many species show strong compensation, others much weaker compensation than expected; strong evidence of an Allee effect for only 1 of 104 species at lowest recorded SSB (weak evidence for three more), e.g. Atlantic cod.
studies.notes: Meta-analytic Allee-effect detection; relevant to defining depensation-based collapse mechanisms.

studies.citation: Perälä T, Kuparinen A (2017) Detection of Allee effects in marine fishes: analytical biases generated by data availability and model selection. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 284(1861): 20171284
studies.data_system: Nine Atlantic herring populations (Bayesian stock-recruit analysis)
studies.outcome_definition: Allee effect vs compensation in recruitment dynamics
studies.baseline_comparator: Model comparison between Allee-type and compensatory stock-recruit models
studies.key_finding: Populations of the same species can show either strong evidence for Allee effects or compensation; evidence for Allee effects is strongly conditional on observations at low abundance, and earlier meta-analyses claiming rarity suffered from data-availability and model-selection limitations.
studies.notes: Related: Tirronen et al. (2022) Fish and Fisheries 'Temporary Allee effects among non-stationary recruitment dynamics in depleted gadid and flatfish populations' (https://doi.org/10.1111/faf.12623), details not visible.

studies.citation: Hutchings JA (2014) Renaissance of a caveat: Allee effects in marine fish. ICES Journal of Marine Science 71(8):2152-2157
studies.data_system: RAM Legacy SSBmsy and SSBmax for more than 130 marine fish stocks
studies.outcome_definition: Allee-effect abundance thresholds derived from reference points
studies.key_finding: On average SSBmsy ≈ 0.39 SSBmax across >130 RAM Legacy stocks; used to estimate Allee-effect abundance thresholds. Related work: Hutchings (2015) Proc B 282: 20150654 'Thresholds for impaired species recovery' and Kuparinen, Keith & Hutchings (2014) Conservation Biology 28:790-798 (doi 10.1111/cobi.12216) 'Allee effect and the uncertainty of population recovery'.
studies.notes: Reference-point-based threshold estimation; no time-series prediction.

studies.citation: Hutchings JA, Reynolds JD (2004) Marine fish population collapses: consequences for recovery and extinction risk. BioScience 54(4):297-309
studies.data_system: More than 230 marine fish populations
studies.outcome_definition: Reduction in breeding population size from known historic levels (median 83%)
studies.key_finding: Median 83% reduction in breeding population size across >230 populations; few recover rapidly and most show little change up to 15 years after collapse; reductions in fishing pressure are necessary but often insufficient, with Allee effects among the factors.
studies.notes: Collapse/recovery background.

studies.citation: Mullon C, Fréon P, Cury P (2005) The dynamics of collapse in world fisheries. Fish and Fisheries
studies.data_system: 1519 main catch series from the FAO world fisheries database over ~50 years
studies.outcome_definition: Catch-based collapse; typology of collapse trajectories (the specific 'plateau/erosion/smooth' categories were not visible in search results)
studies.key_finding: Analysis of 1519 FAO catch series to characterise the dynamics and frequency of fishery collapses; detailed collapse-type results not visible in search results.
studies.notes: Catch-based definitions only.

studies.citation: Branch TA et al. (2011) Contrasting global trends in marine fishery status obtained from catches and from stock assessments. Conservation Biology (plus Worm et al. 2006 Science and its Comment)
studies.data_system: FAO catch data vs RAM Legacy stock assessments
studies.outcome_definition: Worm et al. (2006) defined fishery collapse as annual landings < 10% of the historical maximum catch; assessment-based alternatives use biomass relative to BMSY
studies.key_finding: Critics argued the 10%-of-maximum-catch collapse definition is an artifact (no rationale for 10%/50% thresholds; maximum historic catch is often unsustainable; catch = biomass x variable harvest rate), and that increases in managed fisheries can mimic rising collapse counts.
studies.notes: Full author list of Branch et al. 2011 and the original Worm et al. 2006 DOI were not visible in search results; the ICES JMS 'Apocalypse in world fisheries?' (68(7):1375) authors also not visible.

studies.citation: Burgess MG et al. (authors not visible in search results) (2013) Forecasting fisheries collapse. PNAS 110
studies.data_system: Multispecies fishery life-history and effort information (specific datasets not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Projected overfishing (T-score > 1) or extinction risk (T-score > 2) of weak, incidentally caught stocks
studies.key_finding: Introduces a forecastable T-score for incidentally caught stocks: T<1 not at risk, T>1 projected overfished, T>2 at extinction risk; intended to trigger proactive management before collapse-and-rebuild cycles.
studies.notes: Trait/effort-based risk forecast, not a time-series EWS; first-author surname taken from PMC listing context is not visible in snippets and should be verified.

studies.citation: Boettiger C, Hastings A (2012) Early warning signals and the prosecutor's fallacy. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279(1748):4734-4739
studies.data_system: Simulation study (methodological)
studies.outcome_definition: Critical transitions in simulated systems
studies.key_finding: Conditionally selecting systems known to have transitioned, then testing EWS on them, inflates false positives (the prosecutor's fallacy); mining historical collapses without non-transitioning controls yields biased benchmarks.
studies.notes: Directly motivates including non-transitioning series and quantifying false alarms.

studies.citation: Perretti CT, Munch SB (2012) Regime shift indicators fail under noise levels commonly observed in ecological systems. Ecological Applications 22(6):1772-1779
studies.data_system: Three-species simulation model under field-like observation/process noise
studies.outcome_definition: Simulated regime shifts
studies.key_finding: A suite of early-warning indicators evaluated under noise levels typical of open ecological systems performed poorly.
studies.notes: Methodological caution for noisy survey/assessment series.

studies.citation: Litzow MA, Hunsicker ME (2016) Early warning signals, nonlinearity, and signs of hysteresis in real ecosystems. Ecosphere 7(12)
studies.data_system: Review/meta-analysis of published EWS studies plus comparative analysis of eight northeast Pacific Ocean time series
studies.outcome_definition: Ecological transitions reported in the literature; nonlinear vs linear dynamics classification
studies.baseline_comparator: Studies with linear/undetermined dynamics as comparison
studies.key_finding: Published studies demonstrating nonlinearity in ecosystem dynamics were more likely to support EWS predictions than studies with linear or undetermined dynamics; recommends identifying transition types expected to show EWS.
studies.notes: Suggests screening for nonlinearity/hysteresis before expecting CSD-based EWS.

studies.citation: Glaser SM, Fogarty MJ, Liu H et al. (2014) Complex dynamics may limit prediction in marine fisheries. Fish and Fisheries 15:616-633
studies.data_system: Over 200 time series of survey abundance and landings from two ecosystems
studies.outcome_definition: Predictability and nonlinearity (not collapse)
studies.key_finding: Fished species were more likely to show nonlinear dynamics than unfished species; landings were significantly less predictable than abundance indices; dynamics differences associated with fishing effort.
studies.notes: Relevant as evidence on predictability of survey indices vs landings and as a nonlinear-forecasting baseline reference; forecast evaluation scheme details not visible.

studies.citation: Hsieh C-h et al. (2006) Fishing elevates variability in the abundance of exploited species. Nature 443; Anderson CNK et al. (2008) Why fishing magnifies fluctuations in fish abundance. Nature 452
studies.data_system: 50-year CalCOFI larval fish record (exploited vs unexploited species)
studies.outcome_definition: Elevated abundance variability in exploited species (not collapse)
studies.key_finding: Fishing increases abundance fluctuations; Anderson et al. found no evidence that variable fishing pressure directly drives it, limited evidence for environmental tracking by truncated populations, and strong evidence that age-truncated populations have intrinsically less stable dynamics.
studies.notes: Key confound: variance/AR1 increases in exploited stocks can arise from age truncation rather than critical slowing down (also the interpretation favoured by Litzow et al. 2013).

studies.citation: Tian Y et al. (2023) Long-term variability in the fish assemblage around Japan over the last century and early warning signals of regime shifts. Fish and Fisheries
studies.data_system: Fishery, oceanographic and climatic datasets for 13 species/taxa around Japan, 1901-2018
studies.outcome_definition: Regime shifts in dominant assemblage patterns and community indices (coinciding with AMO and regional SST)
studies.key_finding: Two peaks (1930s, 1980s) dominated by sardine; regime shifts coincided with AMO and SST; autocorrelation coefficient showed ecological indicators have potential as EWS of regime shifts.
studies.notes: Assemblage-level, catch-based; retrospective.

studies.citation: Bury TM et al. (2021) Deep learning for early warning signals of tipping points. PNAS 118(39): e2106140118
studies.data_system: Classifier trained on 500,000 / 200,000 simulated series; tested on 268 empirical and model time series from ecology, thermoacoustics, climatology, epidemiology
studies.outcome_definition: Tipping points (fold, Hopf, transcritical) vs null
studies.key_finding: Deep-learning EWS achieved much greater sensitivity and specificity than generic EWS on 268 empirical and model series and can predict the normal form of the oncoming bifurcation; training limited to two-variable second-order models.
studies.notes: No fish-stock-specific application visible in search results; included as a capacity-matched-learner reference point.

studies.citation: Szuwalski CS, Aydin K, Fedewa EJ, Garber-Yonts B, Litzow MA (2023) The collapse of eastern Bering Sea snow crab. Science
studies.data_system: Eastern Bering Sea snow crab survey/assessment data, 2018-2021
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse to historical lows in 2021 (>10 billion crab lost)
studies.key_finding: A 2018-2019 marine heatwave precipitated the collapse; caloric requirements, reduced spatial distribution and body condition point to starvation; one of the largest reported losses of motile marine macrofauna to a heatwave.
studies.notes: Example of a rapid, externally forced collapse (relevant to whether CSD-type precursors can be expected).

studies.citation: Clements CF, Ozgul A (2016) Including trait-based early warning signals helps predict population collapse. Nature Communications 7: 10984
studies.data_system: Experimental populations (details not visible in search results)
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse approaching a critical transition
studies.key_finding: Composite indices including phenotypic-trait (body size) dynamics gave more accurate inference of approach to a critical transition than abundance time series alone.
studies.notes: Motivates trait-augmented EWS; not a fisheries dataset.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2026) Early Warning Signals in Ecological Time-Series. Entropy 28(6):628
studies.data_system: Review across ecosystem types including marine fisheries
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable (review)
studies.key_finding: Review stating that empirical EWS applications across major ecosystem types including marine fisheries show both successes and limitations, with performance depending on data quality, transition mechanism and system-specific dynamics.
studies.notes: Recent review; may be useful for locating additional fisheries EWS applications. Year inferred from PMC/PubMed ID range.

notes: Search limitations: per instructions, WebFetch/curl were not attempted (publisher, PubMed/PMC, bioRxiv, Dryad hosts are proxy-blocked); every fact above comes from WebSearch result snippets/summaries, so design fields are 'unknown' wherever the abstract-level snippet did not show them. Some search summaries blended sources (e.g., the Bayesian online change-point description under the 'abrupt shift' query, and the '~70% of populations explained by productivity regime shifts' figure) — attribution flagged in notes. The Science Advances 'Abrupt declines...' paper's author list and year were not explicitly visible (inferred from PMC/PubMed ID ranges and the Cano/Jensen/Dakos search context). Zhang 2020 appeared with two conflicting article numbers (106344 vs 106371); the ScienceDirect PII URL is reliable. No study was found that combines sequential (prequential) forecast origins, fixed 1-5 year horizons, a state/trend forecasting baseline, calibrated false-alarm budgets and complete follow-up for marine stock abundance collapse; the nearest items are Zhang 2020 (SD/AR1 vs productivity regime shifts in 191 populations, design details not visible), Litzow et al. 2013 (variance trends 1-4 y before crab collapses, 2 non-collapsing controls), Cano/Jensen/Dakos 2025 (whole-series classification of abrupt-prone stocks with 'moderate accuracy'), and the 2026 Science Advances paper (abrupt productivity declines precede ~25% of collapses by ~a decade, retrospective). No EWS study on FishGlob/ICES bottom-trawl survey indices and no Baltic single-stock CSD study surfaced in searches. Collapse definitions visible: BMIN < 0.2 BMSY (Pinsky et al. 2011), B < 0.5 BMSY depletion (Neubauer et al. 2013 context), biomass <= 25% of mean (Essington et al. 2015), catch < 10% of historical max (Worm et al. 2006, criticised), '<30% of maximum biomass' (mentioned in a search summary without attribution), and Yletyinen et al.'s process-based definition. Key confound literature: Hsieh 2006 / Anderson 2008 (age truncation raises variability) and Boettiger & Hastings 2012 (prosecutor's fallacy). Per hard rule (1), no EWS-outcome associations were computed or speculated.

studies.citation: O'Brien DA, Deb S, Gal G, Thackeray SJ, Dutta PS, Matsuzaki SS, May L, Clements CF (2023) Early warning signals have limited applicability to empirical lake data. Nature Communications 14:7942
studies.data_system: Multi-trophic planktonic (phytoplankton/zooplankton) long-term monitoring data from multiple lakes worldwide; examples named in snippets: Lake Kinneret (phytoplankton critical transition), Lake Washington (zooplankton abrupt non-bifurcation shift), Windermere (phytoplankton non-transition). Exact lake count not visible in search results (the 'nine lakes' figure was not confirmed; snippets say 'multiple lakes').
studies.outcome_definition: Lake dynamics classified into critical transitions vs abrupt non-bifurcation shifts vs non-transitions; classification method itself not visible in search results.
studies.baseline_comparator: Chance (0.5 probability) benchmark; classic rolling/expanding-window EWS compared against multivariate EWS and a machine-learning model (EWSNet). No state/trend forecasting baseline visible in search results.
studies.key_finding: Few instances of critical transitions found; different trophic levels often express different forms of abrupt change; predictive ability was highly processing-dependent, most indicators did not perform better than chance across true-positive and true-negative series, multivariate EWSs only weakly superior to univariate, and the ML model performed poorly. eigenMAF had highest cross-scenario ability (monthly-true=0.62; yearly-true=0.70; monthly-false=0.49). Authors argue predictive ecology should move beyond strict bifurcation-based critical transitions.
studies.notes: Warning rules visible in snippets: rolling windows - warning accepted if positive Kendall tau in 95th quantile of permuted-series taus; expanding windows - 2 SD threshold exceeded for two or more time points; EWSNet - when model predicts a critical transition. Expanding-window rule is sequential in form, but evaluation appears retrospective over whole series; explicit sequential forecast origins/fixed-horizon labels not visible. Real-world series described as having high variability and cyclicity driving false positive warnings.

studies.citation: Gsell AS et al. (2016) Evaluating early-warning indicators of critical transitions in natural aquatic ecosystems. PNAS 113(50)
studies.data_system: Long-term monitoring time series from five freshwater ecosystems selected by expert knowledge of well-described regime shifts: Lake Müggelsee (Germany), Lake Veluwemeer (Netherlands), Lake Zwemlust (Netherlands), Lake Washington (USA), Lake Võrtsjärv (Estonia).
studies.outcome_definition: Documented sudden, persistent transitions hypothesized to represent critical transitions, selected a priori by expert knowledge.
studies.key_finding: Four EWIs tested (lag-1 autocorrelation, standard deviation, skewness, density ratio). EWIs were detected in several of the long-term records, but applicability was strongly limited by the requirement for ecosystem-specific knowledge of transition-generating mechanisms and drivers to choose relevant state variables. Later work (Rohde et al. 2022 snippet) characterizes Gsell et al. 2016 among studies reporting mixed results and low detectability of EWIs prior to breakpoints.
studies.notes: Whether non-transitioning control periods/lakes or false-positive rates were assessed is not visible in search results. Full author list not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Burthe SJ et al. (2016) Do early warning indicators consistently predict nonlinear change in long-term ecological data? Journal of Applied Ecology
studies.data_system: Long-term abundance time series of 55 taxa (126 data sets) across multiple trophic levels in marine and freshwater ecosystems.
studies.outcome_definition: Significant nonlinear change in abundance time series (statistical method for detecting nonlinearity not visible in search results).
studies.baseline_comparator: None visible in search results (indicators assessed against presence/absence of nonlinear change, not against an alternative forecaster)
studies.key_finding: Time series containing true positives were uncommon (8% for variance; 6% for autocorrelation), and all but one time series also contained false classifications; variance and autocorrelation in abundance data consistently failed to predict nonlinear change. Authors recommend multivariate indicator suites with driver analysis and process understanding.
studies.notes: Series were classified by whether they showed significant nonlinear change AND significant increases in variance/autocorrelation, so series without nonlinear change (negatives) are part of the design and false classifications are counted. Exact classification scheme (per-series vs per-window) not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Carpenter SR, Cole JJ, Pace ML, Batt R, Brock WA, et al. (2011) Early Warnings of Regime Shifts: A Whole-Ecosystem Experiment. Science 332:1079-1082
studies.data_system: Whole-lake experiment: Peter Lake (Wisconsin) manipulated by gradual addition of largemouth bass over 3 years; adjacent Paul Lake monitored as reference ecosystem; high-frequency time series of chlorophyll, pH, dissolved oxygen, zooplankton.
studies.outcome_definition: Experimentally induced food-web regime shift (trophic cascade from planktivore-dominated to piscivore-dominated state); transition timing observed directly.
studies.baseline_comparator: Unmanipulated reference lake (negative control); no state/trend forecasting baseline visible
studies.key_finding: Increased autocorrelation, increased variance, and significant conditional heteroskedasticity in chlorophyll, pH, DO and zooplankton were evident in the manipulated lake more than a year before the food-web transition was complete; high-frequency monitoring of manipulated and reference lakes enabled early detection.
studies.notes: Statistics computed: variance, coefficient of variation, skewness, lag-1 autocorrelation. Single manipulated lake vs single reference lake, so false-alarm rate is only assessable qualitatively via the reference lake; formal false-alarm rates not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Batt RD, Carpenter SR, Cole JJ, Pace ML, Johnson RA (2013) Changes in ecosystem resilience detected in automated measures of ecosystem metabolism during a whole-lake manipulation. PNAS 110:17398-17403
studies.data_system: Whole-lake manipulation (trophic cascade induced by slowly adding piscivorous bass to a planktivore-dominated lake) with a nearby bass-dominated lake as unmanipulated reference over 4 years; automated sensor data for DO, pH, chlorophyll-a and derived GPP, respiration, NEP.
studies.outcome_definition: Experimentally induced trophic-cascade transition (approaching threshold).
studies.key_finding: Statistical indicators computed from automated sensor data detected the approaching threshold in the manipulated lake; sensors far less labor-intensive than manual methods.
studies.notes: Formal false-alarm quantification beyond the reference-lake contrast not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Seekell DA, Carpenter SR, Cline TJ, Pace ML (2012) Conditional Heteroskedasticity Forecasts Regime Shift in a Whole-Ecosystem Experiment. Ecosystems (see also Seekell, Carpenter & Pace 2011, Conditional heteroscedasticity as a leading indicator of ecological regime shifts, American Naturalist)
studies.data_system: Whole-lake experiment: chlorophyll-a and fish-catch time series from the manipulated lake and an adjacent reference lake.
studies.outcome_definition: Experimentally induced regime shift (trophic cascade); timing observed.
studies.key_finding: Moving-window conditional heteroskedasticity tests found significant CH at least a year prior to the regime shift in the manipulated lake but no significant CH in the reference lake.
studies.notes: The 2012 Ecosystems author list beyond Seekell/Carpenter/Pace is not fully visible in search results; the description of the moving-window CH application to chlorophyll-a and fish catches appeared in a snippet that did not clearly distinguish the 2011 Am Nat paper from the 2012 Ecosystems paper.

studies.citation: Cline TJ et al. (2014) Early warnings of regime shifts: evaluation of spatial indicators from a whole-ecosystem experiment. Ecosphere
studies.data_system: Whole-lake experiment; daily minnow-trap spatial distributions of prey fish; zooplankton and chlorophyll time series.
studies.outcome_definition: Experimentally forced food-web regime shift from abundant prey fish/small zooplankton/high chlorophyll state to predator-dominated/large zooplankton/low chlorophyll state.
studies.baseline_comparator: Not visible in search results for the spatial fish data
studies.key_finding: Increases in spatial variance and shifts to low-frequency spatial variance (discrete Fourier transform) in prey-fish catch data were observed up to a year in advance of the shift; zooplankton and chlorophyll time series also provided early warning.
studies.notes: Full author list not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Butitta VL, Carpenter SR, Loken LC, Pace ML, Stanley EH (2017) Spatial early warning signals in a lake manipulation. Ecosphere 8(10):e01941
studies.data_system: Whole-lake nutrient-addition experiment inducing a cyanobacteria bloom; fine-resolution spatial mapping of cyanobacteria via mobile sensor platform; unenriched reference lake.
studies.outcome_definition: Cyanobacterial bloom induced by nutrient enrichment.
studies.key_finding: Prior to the bloom, theoretically predicted spatial EWIs based on spatial variance and spatial autocorrelation, plus a new extreme-value index, were detected; changes in EWIs were not discernible in the unenriched reference lake.
studies.notes: Formal false-alarm rates not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Pace ML, Batt RD, Buelo CD, Carpenter SR, Cole JJ, Kurtzweil JT, Wilkinson GM (2017) Reversal of a cyanobacterial bloom in response to early warnings. PNAS 114(2):352-357
studies.data_system: Whole-lake experiment: gradual nutrient enrichment of an experimental lake while monitoring reference lakes; resilience indicators (variance, autocorrelation) of key ecosystem variables.
studies.outcome_definition: Cyanobacterial bloom (regime shift to cyanobacteria-dominated state) induced by enrichment; management action taken when indicators crossed preset boundaries.
studies.baseline_comparator: Reference lakes; no state/trend forecasting baseline visible
studies.key_finding: When resilience indicators exceeded preset boundaries, nutrient enrichment was stopped and the bloom reversed, demonstrating that monitoring resilience indicators followed by prompt action can be useful in management.
studies.notes: Closest lake study to a prospective, real-time alarm with prespecified thresholds ('preset boundaries'). Single experimental lake; false-alarm rate not visible.

studies.citation: Wilkinson GM, Carpenter SR, Cole JJ, Pace ML, Batt RD, Buelo CD, Kurtzweil JT (2018) Early warning signals precede cyanobacterial blooms in multiple whole-lake experiments. Ecological Monographs 88(2):188-203
studies.data_system: Six whole-lake experimental nutrient additions; high-frequency algal pigments and dissolved oxygen saturation; reference conditions/lakes.
studies.outcome_definition: Regime shift from clear-water to cyanobacteria-dominated state (bloom development) in each experiment; 'successful bloom experiment' wording implies not every enrichment produced a bloom.
studies.baseline_comparator: Departures from reference (lake) conditions via a quick detection algorithm
studies.key_finding: Rises in standard deviation and autocorrelation of algal pigments and DO, combined with a quickest-detection algorithm relative to reference conditions, produced at least one warning indicator preceding bloom development in each successful bloom experiment, with lead times of 1 to 57 days.
studies.notes: Whether alarms occurred in experiments that failed to bloom (false alarms) is not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Buelo CD et al. (2022) Evaluating the performance of temporal and spatial early warning statistics of algal blooms. Ecological Applications 32(5):e2616
studies.data_system: Ecosystem-scale empirical (whole-lake experimental) time series and spatial data; rolling-window SD and autocorrelation, spatial SD and Moran's I.
studies.outcome_definition: Algal bloom in a lake being pushed (by enrichment) toward a bloom vs periods/lakes not being pushed.
studies.baseline_comparator: False-positive alarm rate when the lake was not being pushed toward a bloom (no state/trend forecaster visible)
studies.key_finding: True positive alarm rates were 2.5-8.3 times higher for rolling-window SD when a lake was being pushed toward a bloom than the false-positive rate when it was not; for rolling-window autocorrelation, alarm rates were much lower and no variable had a higher true-positive than false-positive rate; spatial EWS (spatial SD, Moran's I) provided little or no warning.
studies.notes: Full author list not visible in search results. One of the few lake studies with explicit TPR vs FPR reporting.

studies.citation: Ortiz D, Palmer J, Wilkinson G (2020) Detecting changes in statistical indicators of resilience prior to algal blooms in shallow eutrophic lakes. Ecosphere 11(10):e03200
studies.data_system: Five lake-years of high-frequency monitoring (chlorophyll a, phycocyanin, DO, pH) from four hypereutrophic lakes that naturally experience algal blooms.
studies.outcome_definition: Naturally occurring algal blooms treated as regime shifts from clear-water to algae-dominated state; operational bloom definition not visible in search results.
studies.key_finding: Aimed to evaluate resilience indicators (rises in variance and autocorrelation) before natural blooms; notes hurdles such as stochastic nutrient loading, spatial complexity, and lower baseline resilience. Quantitative results not visible in search results.
studies.notes: Results section not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Rohde E, Pearce NJT, Young J, Xenopoulos MA (2022) Applying early warning indicators to predict critical transitions in a lake undergoing multiple changes. Ecological Applications 32(7):e2685
studies.data_system: Lake Simcoe, Ontario, Canada (lake recovering from eutrophication); long-term state-variable time series; mentions potential of high-frequency sensors.
studies.outcome_definition: Statistically identified breakpoints in state-variable time series.
studies.key_finding: Retrospectively evaluated agreement between EWIs (SD, autocorrelation, skewness, kurtosis) and breakpoints; notes that several studies (including Gsell et al. 2016) reported mixed results and low detectability of EWIs prior to identified breakpoints, attributed to stochastic/conservative state variables or the occurrence of nonlinear critical transitions.
studies.notes: Explicitly retrospective design per snippet.

studies.citation: Wang R, Dearing JA, Langdon PG, Zhang E, Yang X, Dakos V, et al. (2012) Flickering gives early warning signals of a critical transition to a eutrophic lake state. Nature 492:419-422
studies.data_system: Lake Erhai (China); the blog commentary title 'Flickering diatoms?' indicates a sediment diatom record, but the data type is not explicitly stated in the snippets; observed eutrophication events and algal blooms 1980-2000.
studies.outcome_definition: Critical transition to a eutrophic state around 2001, interpreted as a bistable system.
studies.key_finding: Flickering (switching back and forth between alternative states) observed up to 20 years before the ~2001 critical transition to eutrophy in Lake Erhai.
studies.notes: Single-lake retrospective case study; the 'Flickering diatoms?' blog post is a critical commentary whose content was not visible beyond its title.

studies.citation: Spanbauer TL et al. (2014) Prolonged Instability Prior to a Regime Shift. PLOS ONE 9(10):e108936
studies.data_system: Foy Lake, Montana sediment core: 109 diatom species, ~7,000-year record, 800 time-steps sampled every 5-20 years.
studies.outcome_definition: Abrupt change in diatom community structure at ~1.3 ka BP (regime shift).
studies.key_finding: Using variance, skewness, kurtosis, autocorrelation, Fisher Information and multivariate time series modelling, the study found a ~2,000-year period of declining Fisher Information/evenness beginning ~4.5 ka, interpreted as prolonged instability and resilience loss before the ~1.3 ka regime shift.
studies.notes: Single paleo record; no controls or false-positive assessment visible.

studies.citation: Taranu ZE, Carpenter SR, Frossard V, Jenny J-P, Thomas Z, Vermaire JC, Perga M-E (2018) Can we detect ecosystem critical transitions and signals of changing resilience from paleo-ecological records? Ecosphere 9:e02438
studies.data_system: Paleo records from three lakes: Roxton Pond, Quebec (echinenone pigment as total cyanobacteria proxy; abrupt eutrophication; n=73 samples, DLM analysis), Lake Anarry (myxoxanthophyll pigment, noisier eutrophication signal), Lake Geneva (composite hypolimnetic hypoxia proxy from varved cores; possible flickering).
studies.outcome_definition: Three regime-shift types: abrupt onset of eutrophic state, noisier eutrophication, and possible flickering between alternate states.
studies.key_finding: Applied rolling-window EWS and dynamic linear models (variance, autocorrelation) to paleo pigment/hypoxia proxies to test detectability of resilience change; quantitative outcomes of the detection tests are not visible in search results.
studies.notes: Author initials partially inferred from snippet listing surnames only (Taranu, Carpenter, Frossard, Jenny, Thomas, Vermaire, Perga).

studies.citation: Doncaster CP, Alonso Chávez V, Viguier C, Wang R, Zhang E, Dong X, Dearing JA, Langdon PG, Dyke JG (2016) Early warning of critical transitions in biodiversity from compositional disorder. Ecology
studies.data_system: Compositional (community) data; application to Lake Erhai diatoms not confirmed in search results (co-authors from Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology suggest Chinese lake data).
studies.outcome_definition: Critical transition in biodiversity; species-replacement sequence (canary to keystone to weedy species).
studies.key_finding: Proposes a leading indicator based on the correlation between compositional disorder (unpredictability of community composition) and biodiversity, grounded in theory of species replacement under environmental forcing.
studies.notes: Empirical test details not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Su H, Wang R, Feng Y, Li Y, Li Y, Chen J, Xu C, Wang S, Fang J, Xie P (2021) Long-term empirical evidence, early warning signals and multiple drivers of regime shifts in a lake ecosystem. Journal of Ecology 109:3182-3194
studies.data_system: Subtropical shallow lake in the Yangtze floodplain (China): 64-year multi-trophic monitoring data cross-validated with paleo-diatom records.
studies.outcome_definition: Catastrophic regime shifts with critical transition and hysteresis under warming, eutrophication and fish-stocking trophic cascades.
studies.key_finding: Reports long-term empirical evidence of critical transition and hysteresis in a subtropical shallow lake; EWS analyses are in the title but their specific results are not visible in search results.
studies.notes: Single-lake retrospective case study.

studies.citation: Lindegren M, Dakos V, Gröger JP, Gårdmark A, Kornilovs G, Otto SA, et al. (2012) Early Detection of Ecosystem Regime Shifts: A Multiple Method Evaluation for Management Application. PLOS ONE 7(7):e38410
studies.data_system: Central Baltic Sea monitoring data for copepods Pseudocalanus acuspes and Acartia spp.
studies.outcome_definition: Major ecosystem regime shift in the Central Baltic Sea (known historical shift).
studies.baseline_comparator: Multiple detection methods compared (temporal and spatial critical-slowing-down indicators, trend analysis, shiftograms); no state/trend forecaster as a matched baseline visible
studies.key_finding: Some indicators/methods gave clear early-warning signals of the Baltic regime shift while others had limited utility; proposes a multiple-method approach for management monitoring.
studies.notes: Marine community study included as a community-regime-shift comparator.

studies.citation: Litzow MA, Hunsicker ME (2016) Early warning signals, nonlinearity, and signs of hysteresis in real ecosystems. Ecosphere 7(12):e01614
studies.data_system: Review and meta-analysis of published empirical EWS studies plus comparative analysis of eight northeast Pacific Ocean time series.
studies.outcome_definition: Ecological transitions in published studies, stratified by whether nonlinearity was demonstrated.
studies.key_finding: Published studies demonstrating nonlinearity in ecosystem dynamics were more likely to support EWS predictions than studies with linear or undetermined dynamics; recommends testing for nonlinearity before applying EWS.
studies.notes: Meta-analytic; useful for outcome-definition stratification (transition type).

studies.citation: Boettiger C, Hastings A (2012) Quantifying limits to detection of early warning for critical transitions. Journal of the Royal Society Interface 9(75):2527-2539
studies.data_system: Simulation (model systems with and without approaching transitions).
studies.outcome_definition: Simulated approach to a critical transition vs null (no transition) replicates.
studies.baseline_comparator: Null (non-transitioning) simulations; ROC trade-off between missed events and false alarms
studies.key_finding: Proposed methods rarely characterize expected error rates; introduces ROC-curve evaluation of warning signals and finds that a 5% false-positive rate often corresponds to only ~5% true-positive rate, no better than a coin flip.
studies.notes: Key methodological precedent for false-alarm-budgeted evaluation, but simulation-only.

studies.citation: Perretti CT, Munch SB (2012) Regime shift indicators fail under noise levels commonly observed in ecological systems. Ecological Applications 22(6):1772-1779
studies.data_system: Simulation: three-species model under field-realistic noise.
studies.outcome_definition: Simulated regime shift.
studies.key_finding: Early-warning indicators of regime shifts fail under noise levels commonly observed in open ecological systems (low signal-to-noise).
studies.notes: Simulation only.

studies.citation: Kéfi S, Dakos V, Scheffer M, Van Nes EH, Rietkerk M (2013) Early warning signals also precede non-catastrophic transitions. Oikos 122:641-648
studies.data_system: Theory/simulation.
studies.outcome_definition: Catastrophic (fold) vs non-catastrophic transitions in models.
studies.key_finding: Critical-slowing-down EWS also precede non-catastrophic transitions, so EWS cannot by themselves diagnose that an approaching transition is catastrophic.
studies.notes: Correction: this paper is Oikos 2013, not PLOS ONE 2014 (the 2014 PLOS ONE Kéfi paper is on spatial EWS methods).

studies.citation: Hastings A, Wysham DB (2010) Regime shifts in ecological systems can occur with no warning. Ecology Letters 13(4):464-472
studies.data_system: Theory/models.
studies.outcome_definition: Regime shifts in models lacking smooth potentials.
studies.key_finding: A class of ecological models (nonlinearities plus environmental variability, no smooth potential) will show no forewarning of regime change, implying many natural systems will not display typical leading indicators.
studies.notes: Theoretical basis for expecting missed detections.

studies.citation: Drake JM, Griffen BD (2010) Early warning signals of extinction in deteriorating environments. Nature 467
studies.data_system: Laboratory experiment: 60 Daphnia magna populations; 30 subjected to gradual food deterioration, 30 controls with stable food supply.
studies.outcome_definition: Population extinction after crossing a tipping point (~270 days to tipping; extinction within a bit over a year) in deteriorating tanks; controls fluctuated but persisted.
studies.key_finding: Four statistical measures of abundance showed critical slowing down in degraded environments but not in healthy ones, up to eight generations before the extinction tipping point.
studies.notes: Replicated controls give a direct negative class, but formal false-alarm rates per indicator not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Dai L, Vorselen D, Korolev KS, Gore J (2012) Generic Indicators for Loss of Resilience Before a Tipping Point Leading to Population Collapse. Science
studies.data_system: Replicate laboratory populations of budding yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae) across dilution factors.
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse at an experimentally mapped fold bifurcation (tipping point).
studies.baseline_comparator: Populations at varying distances from the tipping point
studies.key_finding: Directly observed critical slowing down: fluctuations in population density increased in size and duration and recovery slowed closer to the tipping point.
studies.notes: Author list beyond 'Dai L, et al.' is from the query wording; only 'Dai et al.' and 'Gore' are visible in snippets.

studies.citation: Veraart AJ et al. (2012) Recovery rates reflect distance to a tipping point in a living system. Nature 481:357-359
studies.data_system: Cyanobacterial microcosm where photo-inhibition drives a tipping point at a critical light level; perturbation-recovery experiments.
studies.outcome_definition: Classical tipping point (collapse) when critical light level exceeded.
studies.key_finding: Recovery from small perturbations becomes slower as the system approaches the critical point; recovery rates can gauge resilience.
studies.notes: Full author list not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Carpenter SR, Brock WA (2006) Rising variance: a leading indicator of ecological transition. Ecology Letters 9(3):311-318
studies.data_system: Theory/simulation (lake eutrophication model).
studies.outcome_definition: Modeled regime shift (e.g., eutrophication).
studies.key_finding: Increases in variability foreshadow ecological regime shifts, though variability from impending shifts may be hard to discern from that driven by exogenous drivers.
studies.notes: Origin paper for rising variance as EWS.

studies.citation: Carpenter SR, Brock WA, Cole JJ, Pace ML (2014) A new approach for rapid detection of nearby thresholds in ecosystem time series. Oikos 123:290-297
studies.data_system: Whole-lake manipulation (gradual largemouth bass addition); spatial patterns of minnows, grazer abundance, algae, oxygen, water acidity.
studies.outcome_definition: Experimentally driven threshold crossing (trophic cascade).
studies.key_finding: Adapts Cold War 'quickest detection' methods to ecosystem time series; in the manipulated lake, variability increased in minnow spatial patterns, grazer abundance, algae, oxygen and acidity as the threshold approached.
studies.notes: DOI not visible in search results; only an Oikos blog summary was retrieved. This quickest-detection algorithm underlies Wilkinson et al. 2018's 'departures from reference conditions'.

studies.citation: Bestelmeyer BT, Ellison AM, Fraser WR, Gorman KB, Holbrook SJ, Laney CM, Ohman MD, Peters DPC, Pillsbury FC, Rassweiler A, Schmitt RJ, Sharma S (2011) Analysis of abrupt transitions in ecological systems. Ecosphere 2:art129
studies.data_system: 30-60 years of driver and biological response data from pelagic ocean, coastal benthic, polar marine, and semi-arid grassland ecosystems.
studies.outcome_definition: Abrupt transitions/state changes detected with a standardized analytical approach (framework for strong tests of abrupt transition).
studies.key_finding: Provides a synthetic framework and standard analytical approach for describing and detecting abrupt transitions, enabling comparison across case studies.
studies.notes: Relevant to outcome (transition) definition rather than to EWS evaluation.

studies.citation: Ratajczak Z, Carpenter SR, Ives AR, Kucharik CJ, Ramiadantsoa T, Stegner MA, Williams JW, Zhang J, Turner MG (2018) Abrupt Change in Ecological Systems: Inference and Diagnosis. Trends in Ecology & Evolution 33:513-526
studies.data_system: Review/synthesis.
studies.outcome_definition: Abrupt change defined as change over short periods relative to typical rates of change for a given ecosystem; only some abrupt changes are transitions between alternative states.
studies.key_finding: Abrupt changes arise from many processes, only some of which are alternative-state transitions; focusing on means of drivers/states is insufficient because changes in driver variability and disturbance regimes can produce abrupt change; long-term data and driver manipulations remain essential for diagnosis.
studies.notes: Useful for justifying an operational collapse definition that does not presume bifurcation.

studies.citation: Spears BM et al. (2017) Ecological resilience in lakes and the conjunction fallacy. Nature Ecology & Evolution 1:1616-1624
studies.data_system: Conceptual/perspective on lakes.
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable (conceptual).
studies.key_finding: Argues for careful application of stability/resilience theory to lake management, warning against the conjunction fallacy in inferring resilience loss; frequently cited by later lake EWS evaluations (e.g., O'Brien et al. 2023).
studies.notes: Content beyond abstract-level framing not visible in search results. Related viewpoint: Spears et al. 2016 ES&T 'Ecological instability in lakes: a predictable condition?' (https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.est.6b00865).

studies.citation: Bury TM et al. (2021) Deep learning for early warning signals of tipping points. PNAS 118(39)
studies.data_system: 268 empirical and model time series from ecology, thermoacoustics, climatology and epidemiology; classifier trained on simulated normal-form dynamics.
studies.outcome_definition: Approach to a bifurcation (fold, Hopf, transcritical) vs null in labeled test series.
studies.key_finding: A deep-learning classifier trained on generic normal-form dynamics provided early warnings in 268 empirical and model time series with much greater sensitivity and specificity than generic EWS.
studies.notes: Not lake-specific; included because O'Brien et al. 2023 evaluated an ML EWS (EWSNet) on lake data and found poor performance. A follow-up PNAS letter 'Deep learning for tipping points: preprocessing matters' (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2207720119) exists.

studies.citation: Deb S et al. (2022) Machine learning methods trained on simple models can predict critical transitions in complex natural systems. Royal Society Open Science 9(2):211475
studies.data_system: EWSNet trained on simulated data from simple theoretical models; applied to real-world transitions from rapid climatic change to collapse of ecological populations.
studies.outcome_definition: Catastrophic vs non-catastrophic vs no transition (three-class prediction).
studies.key_finding: EWSNet (coupled LSTM + fully convolutional network) trained on simulations reportedly predicts observed real-world transitions and distinguishes catastrophic from non-catastrophic collapses; implemented in the EWSmethods R package.
studies.notes: This is the ML model O'Brien et al. 2023 report performed poorly on lake data.

studies.notes: Illustrates EWS applied without outcome validation (no transitions observed), i.e., alarms without a false-alarm assessment.

notes: Method: 55 distinct WebSearch queries (all listed). No WebFetch/curl attempts were made given the stated egress block; all facts come from search-result snippets, so results-section details (e.g., Ortiz 2020, Taranu 2018, Gsell 2016 false-positive handling) are frequently 'not visible'. Corrections to the seed list: (1) the 'nine lakes' figure for O'Brien et al. 2023 was NOT confirmed in any snippet (snippets say 'multiple lakes'); the 'nine lakes' query instead surfaced unrelated Himalayan glacial-lake news. (2) Gsell et al. 2016 used five ecosystems (Müggelsee, Veluwemeer, Zwemlust, Washington, Võrtsjärv), not nine. (3) Kéfi 'non-catastrophic transitions' is Oikos 2013, not PLOS ONE 2014. (4) Doncaster 2016's use of Lake Erhai was not confirmed in snippets. Cross-cutting observations for Stage 0 (design only; no EWS-outcome associations computed): studies that DO include non-transitioning negatives and quantify false alarms exist in this sweep - Burthe 2016 (8%/6% true positives, false classifications in all but one series), O'Brien 2023 (true-positive vs true-negative series, chance benchmark), Buelo 2022 (TPR vs FPR for rolling SD and AR), Boettiger & Hastings 2012 (ROC; simulation), Drake & Griffen 2010 (30 control populations), and the Carpenter/Pace whole-lake series (reference lakes). This supports the project's stance of not claiming prior work ignored false positives. What was NOT visible anywhere: (a) a conventional state-and-trend or state-space threshold-crossing forecaster used as a capacity-matched baseline (Tassone et al. 2026 preprint compares metabolic EWS against directly measured temperature/chlorophyll, the closest analogue; Lindegren 2012 compares EWS with trend analysis and shiftograms but as alternative detectors, not a matched baseline); (b) calibration of alarm thresholds to a common false-alarm budget across EWS and baseline; (c) strictly sequential fixed-horizon (1-5 yr) labels with complete follow-up - Pace 2017 is the only prospective real-time alarm with preset thresholds, and it is a single lake; (d) any explicit handling of right-censored series ends. Transition definitions in lake work are mostly (i) experimentally induced and directly observed (whole-lake experiments), (ii) expert/literature-designated historical shifts (Gsell 2016, Wang 2012, Su 2021), or (iii) statistical breakpoints/classification (Rohde 2022, O'Brien 2023 classification into critical/abrupt-non-bifurcation/non-transition, Burthe 2016 nonlinear change). Bestelmeyer 2011 and Ratajczak 2018 are the outcome-definition references most cited for abrupt-change detection. Lake EWS is dominated by high-frequency (daily/sub-daily) sensor data with lead times of days to ~1 year, which differs from the annual 1-5 yr horizon in the preregistered population study; O'Brien 2023 reported performance depends on monthly vs yearly resolution.
