studies.citation: van Houwelingen HC (2007) Dynamic Prediction by Landmarking in Event History Analysis. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 34(1):70-85
studies.baseline_comparator: none (methodological paper; landmark models contrasted with joint/other dynamic-prediction approaches only conceptually in snippets)
studies.data_system: not visible in search results (event-history/clinical survival data)
studies.outcome_definition: time-to-event within a horizon window after each landmark time
studies.key_finding: Advocates landmarking: at each landmark (prediction) time, fit a model directly to individuals still at risk using only information observed by that landmark, predicting the event over a fixed horizon window; a 'landmark supermodel' smooths parameters across landmark times instead of fitting separate models per landmark. Related snippets describe building a sliding landmark dataset by truncation at the landmark and administrative censoring at the horizon.
studies.notes: Direct template for the benchmark's sequential fixed-horizon (1-5 yr) risk labels: each origin year is a landmark; label = collapse within horizon; only pre-origin data used. dynamicLM (GitHub tutorial) documents supermodel theory. Nicolaie et al. 2013 Stat Med extends landmarking to competing risks (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/sim.5665).

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results. On the Importance of a Clear Definition of Time Horizon for Time-to-Event Dynamic Predictions: A Systematic Review and a Concrete Illustration in Kidney Transplantation. Journal not visible (PMC13182843)
studies.data_system: kidney transplantation cohort (illustration); systematic review of dynamic-prediction papers
studies.outcome_definition: patient and kidney-graft survival; dynamic prediction = P(event-free until horizon | event-free at landmark)
studies.key_finding: Distinguishes two horizon definitions for dynamic predictions: a fixed final calendar horizon versus a horizon window of fixed length after the landmark; shows prognostic performance of dynamic predictions differs depending on which definition is used, so the horizon definition must be stated explicitly.
studies.notes: Year and authors not visible in search results. Relevant to preregistering whether the 1-5 year horizon is a sliding window after each origin (window) or a fixed calendar endpoint.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2023) Dynamic prediction of survival via Landmark method using the asthma prevention trial in young children. PLOS ONE (journal.pone.0293796)
studies.data_system: asthma prevention trial in young children
studies.outcome_definition: time-to-event (asthma-related) after landmark
studies.key_finding: Applied worked example of landmarking: data from each landmark time to a horizon are stacked into a sliding landmark dataset, requiring truncation at the landmark point and administrative censoring at the horizon.
studies.notes: Year inferred from PLOS article number (0293796, 2023 series); authors not visible.

studies.citation: Uno H, Cai T, Tian L, Wei LJ (2007) Evaluating Prediction Rules for t-Year Survivors With Censored Regression Models. Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(478):527-537
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: t-year survivor status (binary at fixed horizon t) under censoring
studies.key_finding: Provides inference procedures for binary classification rules that predict t-year survival from censored regression models, quantifying precision by misclassification rate, sensitivity/specificity, and PPV/NPV at a fixed horizon; the associated IPCW-weighted 'Uno C-index' is a time-dependent concordance measure weighted by the inverse probability of censoring.
studies.notes: Gives fixed-horizon sensitivity/specificity/PPV machinery under censoring; the benchmark's complete-follow-up design reduces to the uncensored special case but should cite this for any sensitivity analysis that admits censored origins.

studies.citation: Blanche P, Dartigues J-F, Jacqmin-Gadda H (2013) Estimating and comparing time-dependent areas under receiver operating characteristic curves for censored event times with competing risks. Statistics in Medicine 32(30):5381-5397
studies.baseline_comparator: paired comparison of two markers (two psychometric tests) via the proposed test
studies.data_system: French PAQUID cohort (dementia onset with death as competing risk)
studies.outcome_definition: onset of clinical outcome (dementia) by horizon t, with competing risk of death
studies.key_finding: Proposes nonparametric inverse-probability-of-censoring-weighted (IPCW) estimators of the time-dependent (cumulative/dynamic) AUC(t), derives asymptotics enabling confidence intervals and tests for comparing two markers' AUC(t), and handles competing risks. Implemented in R package timeROC; tidymodels yardstick roc_auc_survival cites this formulation.
studies.notes: Borrow: IPCW AUC(t) plus paired AUC(t) comparison test if any origins are censored; Blanche 2013 Biometrical Journal also reviews ROC estimators under marker-dependent censoring (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/bimj.201200045).

studies.citation: Blanche P, Proust-Lima C, Loubère L, Berr C, Dartigues J-F, Jacqmin-Gadda H (2015) Quantifying and Comparing Dynamic Predictive Accuracy of Joint Models for Longitudinal Marker and Time-to-Event in Presence of Censoring and Competing Risks. Biometrics 71(1):102-113
studies.data_system: not visible in search results (longitudinal marker + time-to-event cohort)
studies.outcome_definition: event within window (s, s+t] given event-free at landmark s, with censoring and competing events
studies.key_finding: Defines and estimates dynamic AUC(s,t) and dynamic Brier score for predictions made at landmark time s over horizon t, accounting for right censoring and competing risks, with methods to compare the dynamic predictive accuracy of competing models.
studies.notes: This is the closest published analogue to 'sequential origin s, horizon t' discrimination + overall accuracy metrics; the Brier score gives the calibration-sensitive companion to AUC.

studies.citation: Heagerty PJ, Lumley T, Pepe MS. Time-dependent ROC curves for censored survival data and a diagnostic marker. Biometrics (year not visible; PubMed 10877287); and Heagerty PJ, Zheng Y (2005) Survival Model Predictive Accuracy and ROC Curves
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: cumulative cases = died by time t; dynamic controls = still alive at t (C/D); incident cases = event exactly at t (I/D)
studies.key_finding: Defines time-dependent ROC(t)/AUC(t) for a baseline marker: cumulative/dynamic (cases = events by t, controls = event-free at t) and incident/dynamic (cases = events at t) variants; I/D AUC(t) can be summarized over time into a concordance index (Heagerty & Zheng 2005). Implemented in R package RisksetROC.
studies.notes: Year of Heagerty-Lumley-Pepe paper not visible in search results. The cumulative/dynamic definition matches the benchmark's 'collapse within h years vs. no collapse within h years' labels.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2019) A comparison of landmark methods and time-dependent ROC methods to evaluate the time-varying performance of prognostic markers for survival outcomes. Diagnostic and Prognostic Research
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: survival outcome; time-varying marker performance
studies.key_finding: Compares landmark-based evaluation of prognostic markers with time-dependent ROC (cumulative/dynamic and incident/dynamic) approaches for characterizing how a marker's accuracy varies over time.
studies.notes: Useful for choosing between landmark-stacked evaluation and time-dependent ROC summaries; author names not visible in results.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2025) Cumulative/Dynamic Time-Dependent ROC Analysis for Left-Truncated and Right-Censored Data: Estimators and Comparison. arXiv:2509.05693
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: C/D ROC: cases died by t, controls alive at t
studies.key_finding: Extends cumulative/dynamic time-dependent ROC estimation to data that are both left-truncated and right-censored and compares estimators (details beyond title/abstract not visible).
studies.notes: Potentially relevant because monitored populations enter the record mid-history (delayed entry). Year inferred from arXiv identifier; authors not visible.

studies.citation: Graf E, Schmoor C, et al. (1999) Assessment and comparison of prognostic classification schemes for survival data. Statistics in Medicine 18(17-18):2529-2545
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: survival status at time t
studies.key_finding: Introduces the time-dependent Brier score (and integrated Brier score) for censored survival data with an IPCW weighting scheme assuming independent censoring; the inaccuracy measures remain meaningful when predicted probabilities are misspecified and are asymptotically unaffected by random censoring; intended for computation in a validation study.
studies.notes: Full author list beyond Graf and Schmoor not visible. The IPCW Brier score is the standard overall-accuracy metric to pair with AUC(t) and calibration.

studies.citation: Suresh K, Severn C, Ghosh D (2022) Survival prediction models: an introduction to discrete-time modeling. BMC Medical Research Methodology 22:207
studies.data_system: not visible in search results (biomedical example)
studies.outcome_definition: hazard of failure event in pre-specified discrete time intervals
studies.key_finding: Tutorial on discrete-time survival prediction: expand data to a person-period dataset and model the hazard of the event in each pre-specified interval, which allows standard classification learners (including machine learning) to produce subject-specific fixed-interval risks.
studies.notes: Person-period expansion is the natural way to run capacity-matched EWS vs. state/trend learners on annual origins with 1-5 year horizons while keeping learners identical.

studies.citation: Romero-Brufau S, Huddleston JM, Escobar GJ, Liebow M (2015) Why the C-statistic is not informative to evaluate early warning scores and what metrics to use. Critical Care
studies.data_system: hospital ward monitoring (physiological deterioration; prevalence 0.02 per patient-day)
studies.outcome_definition: physiological deterioration event per patient-day
studies.key_finding: Argues AUROC/C-statistic is misleading for early-warning scores because event prevalence is extremely low (0.02 per patient-day); recommends pre-implementation reports include sensitivity plus PPV, number needed to evaluate, or estimated alert rate, reported at each individual cutoff.
studies.notes: Directly supports the benchmark's 'sensitivity at a matched false-alarm burden' design instead of AUROC alone; alert rate per unit monitoring time is the analogue of false alarms per series-year.

studies.citation: Scully CG, Daluwatte C (2017) Evaluating performance of early warning indices to predict physiological instabilities. Journal of Biomedical Informatics 75:14-21
studies.data_system: continuous patient monitoring (physiological instability events)
studies.outcome_definition: critical health event within a meaningful time window after warning
studies.key_finding: Proposes an episode-aware framework for continuous-monitoring warning indices: (1) sensitivity to notify within a meaningful time window before the event, (2) cumulative sensitivity leading up to the event, (3) whether a warning persists until the event, and (4) the distribution of warning times and the burden of additional warnings (false-alarm rate) throughout monitoring; also reports probability an event follows a given warning (PPV-like) and the warned fraction of events.
studies.notes: Template for alarm-episode metrics: lead-time distribution, persistence, and false-alarm burden per unit time, which classical sensitivity/PPV omit.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2019) A framework to characterize the performance of early warning index alarm systems for patient monitoring. MethodsX (PMC6660561)
studies.data_system: patient monitoring
studies.outcome_definition: not visible in search results
studies.key_finding: Methods-article companion describing a framework to characterize alarm-system performance for early warning indices in patient monitoring (content beyond title not visible in search results).
studies.notes: Journal inferred from ScienceDirect PII prefix S2215-0161 (MethodsX); authors not visible.

studies.citation: Gadhoumi K, Beltran A, Scully CG, Xiao R, Nahmias DO, Hu X (2021) Technical considerations for evaluating clinical prediction indices: a case study for predicting code blue events with MEWS. Physiological Measurement 42(5):055005
studies.data_system: in-hospital code blue events; Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS)
studies.outcome_definition: in-hospital code blue event
studies.key_finding: Proposes techniques and metrics for evaluating predictive alert algorithms that capture timeliness of alerts and clinical burden of alerts, illustrated with MEWS for code-blue prediction.
studies.notes: Sample size and specific metric definitions not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2023) Early Warning Scores to Support Continuous Wireless Vital Sign Monitoring for Complication Prediction in Patients on Surgical Wards: Retrospective Observational Study. JMIR Perioperative Medicine 2023;1:e44483
studies.baseline_comparator: single-parameter alarms vs. hourly sensor-based EWS
studies.data_system: continuous wireless vital-sign monitoring on surgical wards (retrospective)
studies.outcome_definition: postoperative complication
studies.key_finding: Reports alarm sensitivity of 80%-67% for hourly sensor EWS thresholds 3-5, corresponding to 2 to 1.2 alarms per patient per day with false discovery rates of 85%-83%; notes high false-alarm rates when scores are computed over shorter time spans.
studies.notes: Example of jointly reporting sensitivity with alarms-per-patient-day and FDR at each threshold; authors not visible.

studies.citation: Winterhalder M, et al. (2003) The seizure prediction characteristic: a general framework to assess and compare seizure prediction methods. Epilepsy & Behavior
studies.baseline_comparator: random/unspecific predictor (per snippets on the framework; details not visible)
studies.data_system: intracranial EEG from 21 patients with pharmacorefractory focal epilepsy (per snippet)
studies.outcome_definition: seizure onset within the seizure occurrence period (SOP) after a seizure prediction horizon (SPH) following an alarm
studies.key_finding: Defines the 'seizure prediction characteristic': terminology (seizure occurrence period = window in which the event is supposed to occur; seizure prediction horizon = minimum gap between alarm and SOP, set by the intervention time) and assessment criteria that explicitly couple sensitivity (fraction of seizures correctly predicted) with the false prediction rate (false alarms per hour of interictal time), which prior work had largely ignored.
studies.notes: Direct analogue for ecology: an alarm at origin t counts as a hit only if collapse occurs within [t+SPH, t+SPH+SOP]; false alarms are counted per unit non-collapse monitoring time. Co-author list not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Andrzejak RG, Mormann F, Kreuz T, Rieke C, Kraskov A, Elger CE, Lehnertz K (2003) Testing the null hypothesis of the nonexistence of a preseizure state. Physical Review E 67:010901(R)
studies.baseline_comparator: seizure-time surrogates (Monte Carlo randomization of event onset times) as null model
studies.data_system: EEG recordings of epilepsy patients (details not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: seizure onset
studies.key_finding: Notes that seizure-prediction performance had not been tested against a null hypothesis and introduces 'seizure time surrogates': a Monte Carlo resampling of randomized seizure onset times to test whether prediction performance exceeds chance.
studies.notes: Borrow as a null-distribution device: permute/randomize collapse times within series (respecting constraints) to obtain the chance distribution of any EWS alarm statistic.

studies.citation: Schelter B, Winterhalder M, Maiwald T, Brandt A, Schad A, Schulze-Bonhage A, Timmer J (2006) Testing statistical significance of multivariate time series analysis techniques for epileptic seizure prediction. Chaos 16:013108
studies.baseline_comparator: statistical significance testing of prediction performance (specific surrogate scheme not visible in search results)
studies.data_system: EEG (details not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: epileptic seizure
studies.key_finding: Addresses how to assess statistical significance of features extracted by multivariate time-series techniques for retrospective seizure prediction; widely cited as a methodological reference for validating prediction algorithms.
studies.notes: The 'alarm times surrogates' approach commonly attributed to this paper was not visible in search snippets; verify from full text before citing that detail.

studies.citation: Mormann F, Andrzejak RG, Elger CE, Lehnertz K (2007) Seizure prediction: the long and winding road. Brain 130(2):314-333
studies.data_system: review of EEG-based seizure-prediction studies
studies.outcome_definition: seizure onset
studies.key_finding: Review documenting that optimistic 1990s-2000 seizure-prediction results were not reproduced by later, more rigorous evaluations, prompting a debate on validity; establishes considerations for statistical validation including comparison against random predictors and appropriate assessment of predictive performance (out-of-sample, prospective-style testing).
studies.notes: Cautionary tale closely paralleling EWS-in-ecology: in-sample, transition-selected evaluations inflated apparent skill.

studies.citation: Snyder DE, Echauz J, Grimes DB, Litt B (2008) The statistics of a practical seizure warning system. Journal of Neural Engineering 5(4)
studies.baseline_comparator: chance predictor with matched proportion of time in warning (analytical expectation verified by Monte Carlo)
studies.data_system: Monte Carlo simulations of random warnings of variable duration (empirical data not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: seizure occurring during a warning period
studies.key_finding: Derives the expected performance of a chance predictor under a predefined scoring rule and uses it as the control in a hypothesis test, verified by Monte Carlo simulations generating random warnings of variable duration; proposes the test metric 'sensitivity improvement over chance' = algorithm sensitivity minus chance sensitivity given a constraint on the proportion of time spent in warning.
studies.notes: Directly provides the 'matched false-alarm burden' comparison logic: fix time-in-warning (alarm budget), then compare detected fraction against chance and against the baseline model.

studies.citation: Andrzejak RG, et al. (2026) Are seizure forecasts and cycles better than chance? What chance? Epilepsia
studies.baseline_comparator: multiple null/chance models (e.g., Poisson process) rather than a single null
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: seizure occurrence
studies.key_finding: Argues that 'better than chance' is underspecified: significance claims are usually evaluated against a single null (e.g., seizures as a Poisson process), and rejecting one null only provides evidence against that particular chance model; examines whether incorporating seizure cycles yields better-than-chance forecasting.
studies.notes: Received Dec 2025, accepted Feb 2026, issue June 2026 (per snippet). Motivates specifying several nulls (random alarms, trend-only, state-only baselines) rather than one.

studies.citation: Karoly PJ, Stirling RE, Cook MJ, Goldenholz DM, et al. (2026) Seizure forecasting: The long and winding road to clinical translation. Epilepsia
studies.data_system: mobile-app seizure diaries (per snippet)
studies.outcome_definition: seizure occurrence during high-/low-risk states
studies.key_finding: Reports time-in-state style metrics for diary-based forecasts: users spent on average 67.1% of time in a low-risk state and 14.8% in a high-risk warning state, with 69.1% of seizures occurring during high-risk states and 10.5% during low-risk states; clinical translation remains limited.
studies.notes: Illustrates reporting 'time in warning' alongside fraction of events captured, the same pair the benchmark should report per horizon.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2024) On the performance of seizure prediction machine learning methods across different databases: the sample and alarm-based perspectives. Frontiers in Neuroscience 18:1417748
studies.data_system: multiple EEG seizure databases
studies.outcome_definition: seizure within SOP after SPH
studies.key_finding: Contrasts sample-based evaluation (per-window classification metrics) with alarm-based evaluation (per-event sensitivity and false-prediction rate after post-processing into alarms) of ML seizure predictors across databases.
studies.notes: Supports reporting both per-origin classification metrics and per-episode alarm metrics; authors not visible.

studies.citation: Vickers AJ, Elkin EB (2006) Decision Curve Analysis: A Novel Method for Evaluating Prediction Models. Medical Decision Making
studies.data_system: not visible in search results (clinical)
studies.outcome_definition: binary outcome (2006); time-to-event extension per Vickers et al. 2008 (cited by dcurves)
studies.key_finding: Decision curve analysis computes net benefit of a model or test across a range of threshold probabilities (the minimum probability at which intervention is warranted), compared with treating all or none; unlike discrimination/calibration it incorporates the consequences of decisions (false positives weighted by threshold odds). The dcurves package implements binary (Vickers & Elkin 2006) and time-to-event (Vickers et al. 2008) versions.
studies.notes: Gives a principled way to weigh false alarms against missed collapses for a management threshold; the 2008 time-to-event extension's full citation was not visible in results.

studies.citation: Vickers AJ, Van Calster B, Wynants L, Steyerberg EW (2023) Decision curve analysis: confidence intervals and hypothesis testing for net benefit. Diagnostic and Prognostic Research (correction 2025)
studies.baseline_comparator: default strategies (treat all / none) and competing models
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: not visible in search results
studies.key_finding: Reviews proposals for confidence intervals and p-values for net benefit and argues that when forced to decide one should choose the option with highest expected utility irrespective of p-values; insisting on statistically significant net-benefit differences would generally be harmful and would change the criteria by which models are judged valuable.
studies.notes: Caution for the benchmark: report uncertainty for net benefit but do not gate 'usefulness' on significance; use equivalence/SESOI logic for the primary detection-fraction increment instead.

studies.citation: Van Calster B, Nieboer D, Vergouwe Y, De Cock B, Pencina MJ, Steyerberg EW (2016) A calibration hierarchy for risk models was defined: from utopia to empirical data. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: binary risk outcome
studies.key_finding: Defines a hierarchy of calibration levels for risk models (mean/'in-the-large', weak = intercept and slope, moderate = flexible calibration curve, strong) from utopian to empirically attainable; the calibration slope comes from logit(E[y|p]) = a + b*logit(p) and the intercept (calibration-in-the-large) indicates average over/under-estimation.
studies.notes: Author list per search snippet ('Van Calster and colleagues (Nieboer, Vergouwe, De Cock, Pencina, and Steyerberg)'). CalibrationCurves R package vignette gives the slope/intercept definitions.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (commonly attributed to Van Calster B et al.) (2019) Calibration: the Achilles heel of predictive analytics. BMC Medicine 17:230
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: not visible in search results
studies.key_finding: Position paper on why calibration (agreement between predicted and observed risk) is essential yet neglected; recommends assessing calibration intercept/slope and flexible calibration curves, especially at external validation where calibration-in-the-large mismatches are common.
studies.notes: Author list not visible in search snippets; verify before citing names.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2019/2020) Validation of clinical prediction models: what does the 'calibration slope' really measure? Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: not visible in search results
studies.key_finding: Shows that a calibration slope of 1 does not by itself indicate good calibration if the intercept is not also reported; calibration-in-the-large is irrelevant at internal validation (average predicted risk matches event rate) but highly relevant at external validation.
studies.notes: Year inferred from PII (2019); authors not visible. Implies the benchmark must report slope and intercept per horizon on held-out systems.

studies.citation: Riley RD, et al. (2021) Minimum sample size for external validation of a clinical prediction model with a binary outcome. Statistics in Medicine 40(19):4230-4251; and Riley RD, et al. (2022) Minimum sample size calculations for external validation of a clinical prediction model with a time-to-event outcome. Statistics in Medicine
studies.data_system: illustrative mechanical heart-valve failure model
studies.outcome_definition: binary (2021) and time-to-event (2022) outcomes
studies.key_finding: Gives closed-form and iterative sample-size calculations for external validation targeting precise estimation of O/E, calibration slope, C-statistic and net benefit; in the example, ~9,835 participants (177 events) were needed, driven by the calibration-slope criterion, and 6,443 (116 events) for net benefit at an 8% threshold; a 2022 companion covers time-to-event outcomes.
studies.notes: Use to justify the number of collapse events/origins needed per horizon for precise calibration and detection estimates; independence assumptions must be adapted for clustered origins within series.

studies.citation: Steyerberg EW, Vickers AJ, Cook NR, Gerds T, Gonen M, Obuchowski N, et al. (2010) Assessing the Performance of Prediction Models: A Framework for Traditional and Novel Measures. Epidemiology 21(1):128-138
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: binary and survival outcomes
studies.key_finding: Framework of performance measures for binary and survival prediction models: Brier score (overall), c-statistic/AUC (discrimination), goodness-of-fit/calibration, plus newer measures (survival c variants, reclassification tables, NRI, IDI) and decision-analytic measures.
studies.notes: Useful as the canonical taxonomy (overall / discrimination / calibration / clinical usefulness) for the preregistered metric list.

studies.citation: Pepe MS, Kerr KF, Longton G, Wang Z (2013) Testing for improvement in prediction model performance. Statistics in Medicine 32:1467-1482
studies.baseline_comparator: baseline risk model without the new predictor (nested models)
studies.data_system: simulation studies
studies.outcome_definition: binary outcome
studies.key_finding: Proves that null hypotheses of no improvement in performance (e.g., change in AUC) from adding a predictor Y to a nested risk model are equivalent to the null that Y's coefficient is zero; simulations show standard tests of the AUC change that ignore variability of estimated coefficients are extremely conservative.
studies.notes: Warning for nested comparisons fitted on the same data; the benchmark's out-of-sample comparison of separately fitted EWS vs. baseline models is a different (non-nested, held-out) setting, so use paired held-out AUC/detection differences with cluster-aware bootstrap instead of nested-model tests. A related result in the same search flags NRI as misleading (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12561-014-9118-0).

studies.citation: DeLong ER, DeLong DM, Clarke-Pearson DL (1988) Comparing the areas under two or more correlated receiver operating characteristic curves: a nonparametric approach. Biometrics 44(3):837-845
studies.baseline_comparator: paired competing classifiers on the same subjects
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: binary
studies.key_finding: Nonparametric test for differences between AUCs of two or more correlated (paired) ROC curves using generalized U-statistic theory to estimate the covariance matrix.
studies.notes: Assumes independent subjects; for repeated origins within series use Obuchowski (1997) or a cluster bootstrap.

studies.citation: Obuchowski NA (1997) Nonparametric Analysis of Clustered ROC Curve Data. Biometrics 53(2):567-578
studies.data_system: not visible in search results (diagnostic tests with multiple results per patient)
studies.outcome_definition: binary
studies.key_finding: Extends the DeLong structural-components method to ROC area estimation and inference when multiple test results come from the same unit (intracluster correlation), using the design-effect/effective-sample-size ideas of Rao and Scott (1992); R implementation (clusteredROC) available.
studies.notes: Directly applicable: many origins per population series (cluster) and many series per biological system; use for paired AUC(t) differences with clustering, or cluster bootstrap.

studies.citation: Robin X, et al. pROC::roc.test - Compare two ROC curves (R documentation; DeLong, bootstrap, Venkatraman methods)
studies.data_system: software
studies.outcome_definition: binary
studies.key_finding: pROC's roc.test implements paired/unpaired DeLong (via Sun & Xu 2014 algorithm), stratified bootstrap and Venkatraman tests; commentary notes DeLong covariance can be unstable in small samples (n+ or n- < 25) or with very different ROC shapes, that a paired bootstrap resamples subjects with replacement and recomputes both AUCs, and that clustered data require a cluster bootstrap rather than the exchangeable-subject bootstrap.
studies.notes: Author attribution of pROC not visible in snippets; the cluster-bootstrap caveat comes from the MetricGate explainer, not from pROC documentation.

studies.citation: LeDell E, Petersen M, van der Laan M (2015) Computationally efficient confidence intervals for cross-validated area under the ROC curve estimates. Electronic Journal of Statistics 9(1):1583-1607
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: binary
studies.key_finding: Provides an influence-curve-based variance estimator and confidence intervals for cross-validated AUC as a computationally efficient alternative to the bootstrap; implemented in R package cvAUC (ci.cvAUC, ci.pooled.cvAUC).
studies.notes: Useful for CIs on grouped-CV AUC; note that i.i.d. assumptions need adaptation for clustered origins.

studies.citation: Lakens D (2017) Equivalence Tests: A Practical Primer for t Tests, Correlations, and Meta-Analyses. Social Psychological and Personality Science; Lakens D, Scheel AM, Isager PM (2018) Equivalence Testing for Psychological Research: A Tutorial. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
studies.baseline_comparator: smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) bounds
studies.data_system: not applicable (statistical tutorial)
studies.outcome_definition: not applicable
studies.key_finding: Two one-sided tests (TOST) procedure to reject effects as large as a prespecified smallest effect size of interest (SESOI); SESOI can be justified by just-noticeable differences, cost-benefit analysis, or e.g. 33% of the effect an earlier study could detect; the tutorial also converts SESOI to an R^2 'smallest variance predicted of interest' to judge whether a predictor's contribution is above/below the SESOI.
studies.notes: Borrow for the preregistered primary test: TOST/equivalence on the EWS-minus-baseline increment in detected fraction at matched false-alarm burden, with SESOI stated in absolute percentage points of collapses detected.

studies.citation: Riesthuis P (2024) Simulation-Based Power Analyses for the Smallest Effect Size of Interest: A Confidence-Interval Approach for Minimum-Effect and Equivalence Testing. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
studies.data_system: simulation
studies.outcome_definition: not applicable
studies.key_finding: Simulation-based power analysis using a confidence-interval approach for minimum-effect and equivalence tests against a SESOI (details beyond title/abstract not visible).
studies.notes: Template for a simulation-based power analysis of the preregistered increment test using the benchmark's clustered origin structure.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results. Tests of equivalence and non-inferiority for diagnostic accuracy based on the paired areas under ROC curves (PubMed 16158400); related: A non-inferiority test of areas under two parametric ROC curves (Contemporary Clinical Trials); Hypothesis Testing in Noninferiority and Equivalence MRMC ROC Studies (Academic Radiology)
studies.baseline_comparator: paired competing diagnostic procedures with a prespecified non-inferiority/equivalence margin on AUC difference
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: binary diagnostic status
studies.key_finding: Equivalence/non-inferiority of diagnostic accuracy is assessed via two one-sided tests on the difference in paired nonparametric AUCs against a pre-specified margin (delta_0); an equivalence test equals two simultaneous non-inferiority tests; MRMC extensions cover hypothesis statement, analysis and sizing. R package mcradds::aucTest implements paired AUC tests.
studies.notes: Author lists and years not visible in search results; combine with Lakens' SESOI logic to preregister a margin for the EWS-vs-baseline AUC(t) or detection-fraction difference.

studies.citation: Dawid AP (1984) Present Position and Potential Developments: Some Personal Views. Statistical Theory: The Prequential Approach (with Discussion). Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A 147(2):278-292
studies.baseline_comparator: competing probability forecasting systems assessed on accumulated prediction error
studies.data_system: not applicable (statistical theory)
studies.outcome_definition: not applicable
studies.key_finding: Founds the prequential (predictive-sequential) approach: statistical inference exists to make sequential probability forecasts for future observations; forecasters are assessed only through their predictive distributions and the realized outcomes (prequential principle), with calibration and proper scoring as diagnostics; model selection chooses the system minimizing accumulated sequential prediction error.
studies.notes: The benchmark's 'prequential hindcast' should cite this as the source of the term and of the rule that evaluation depends only on forecast-outcome pairs emitted at each origin.

studies.citation: Gneiting T, et al. (2007) Probabilistic Forecasts, Calibration and Sharpness. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 69(2):243-268
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: not applicable
studies.key_finding: Following Dawid's prequential principle, assessment of probabilistic forecasts must rest on predictive distributions and observations only; proposes the paradigm of maximizing sharpness subject to calibration, with diagnostic tools for calibration (e.g., PIT/reliability) and sharpness.
studies.notes: Co-author names beyond Gneiting not visible in the snippets; pair with Gneiting & Raftery (2007) proper scoring rules.

studies.citation: Gneiting T, Raftery AE (2007) Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation. Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477):359-378
studies.data_system: not applicable
studies.outcome_definition: not applicable
studies.key_finding: Reviews and develops the theory of strictly proper scoring rules (e.g., Brier/log scores) on general probability spaces, which reward honest probabilistic forecasts and can be tailored as loss functions for estimation and forecast evaluation.
studies.notes: Basis for using Brier/log score as the calibration-sensitive secondary metric for fixed-horizon collapse probabilities.

studies.citation: Gama J, Sebastião R, Rodrigues PP (2013) On evaluating stream learning algorithms. Machine Learning
studies.data_system: data streams (stationary and drifting; details not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: not applicable
studies.key_finding: Defends prequential (test-then-train) error with forgetting mechanisms; proves that for stationary data and consistent learners the holdout error, prequential error, and prequential error over a sliding window or with fading factors all converge to the Bayes error; fading factors are faster and memoryless than sliding windows.
studies.notes: Practical guidance for computing and comparing sequential error curves across origins, including when the learner is refit as new years arrive.

studies.citation: Bergmeir C, Benítez JM (2012) On the use of cross-validation for time series predictor evaluation (Information Sciences); Bergmeir C, Hyndman RJ, Koo B. A note on the validity of cross-validation for evaluating autoregressive time series prediction (Computational Statistics & Data Analysis; cited as 2015 working paper/2018 article); Hyndman RJ, Cross-validation for time series (blog)
studies.baseline_comparator: competing forecasting methods evaluated over rolling origins
studies.data_system: time-series forecasting benchmarks (details not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: h-step-ahead forecast error
studies.key_finding: Rolling-origin evaluation (time-series cross-validation), where the forecast origin rolls forward through the series and each forecast is scored at a fixed horizon, is described as the most widely accepted and correct out-of-sample test for time series; standard K-fold CV is nonetheless valid for purely autoregressive models (Bergmeir, Hyndman & Koo), and tsCV can skip origins to roll forward by more than one step.
studies.notes: The benchmark's origin grid (every year, or thinned origins) maps onto tsCV with fixed horizons h=1..5. Exact years/journals of the Bergmeir papers are partly inferred from snippets.

studies.citation: Roberts DR, Bahn V, et al. (2017) Cross-validation strategies for data with temporal, spatial, hierarchical, or phylogenetic structure. Ecography 40(8):913-929
studies.data_system: simulations and ecological case studies
studies.outcome_definition: predictive error to new data/predictor space
studies.key_finding: Ignoring temporal, spatial, hierarchical or phylogenetic structure in cross-validation seriously underestimates predictive error and invites overfitting to non-causal predictors; block cross-validation (strategic rather than random splits) was nearly universally more appropriate for predicting to new data or selecting causal predictors, and should be used wherever dependence structures exist even if residuals show no correlation.
studies.notes: Justifies grouping folds by biological system/population and blocking in time; the 'ecological' provenance makes it a natural citation for reviewers in this field.

studies.citation: Takada T, Nijman S, Denaxas S, et al. (incl. Debray TPA) (2021) Internal-external cross-validation helped to evaluate the generalizability of prediction models in large clustered datasets. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology
studies.data_system: 871,687 individuals from 225 UK general practices (heart-failure risk models)
studies.outcome_definition: heart failure (per snippet)
studies.key_finding: Internal-external cross-validation (IECV): iteratively omit one cluster (study/practice), fit on the rest, validate in the omitted cluster, rotate through all clusters; cluster-specific performance measures are pooled with random-effects meta-analysis to quantify average performance and between-cluster heterogeneity. Steyerberg & Harrell proposed that models need internal, internal-external and external validation; de Jong et al. (2021, Stat Med) extend to developing generalizable models from pooled clustered data.
studies.notes: Provides the 'grouped by biological system' analysis plan: leave-one-system-out IECV with random-effects pooling of AUC(t), calibration slope, and detection-at-budget, plus heterogeneity (tau^2) reporting.

studies.citation: Kapoor S, Narayanan A (2023) Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science. Patterns
studies.data_system: survey of at least 294 papers across 17 disciplines
studies.outcome_definition: not applicable
studies.key_finding: Documents data leakage as a widespread failure mode (>=294 papers, 17 fields), defines leakage as spurious train-target relationships arising from collection/sampling/preprocessing that inflate performance, classifies eight leakage types (including temporal leakage), and proposes 'model info sheets' to detect and prevent each type.
studies.notes: Use the model-info-sheet checklist in the preregistration to certify no look-ahead in detrending, standardization, threshold calibration, or outcome labelling.

studies.citation: NOAA/National Weather Service warning verification materials (POD, FAR, lead time; Wilks 2011 contingency table); Barnes LR, et al. (2009) Corrigendum: False Alarm Rate or False Alarm Ratio? Weather and Forecasting 24(5)
studies.baseline_comparator: climatology/persistence style references (per general verification practice; specifics not visible)
studies.data_system: operational NWS severe-weather warnings
studies.outcome_definition: warned event occurrence within the warning's valid area/time
studies.key_finding: Operational warning verification is event-based via a 2x2 contingency table (hits, misses, false alarms, correct nulls; Wilks 2011): probability of detection = hits / observed events; false alarm ratio = false alarms / issued warnings (distinct from false alarm rate = false alarms / non-events); lead time = time from warning issuance to event onset; the 2009 WAF corrigendum stresses the ratio vs. rate distinction; a 2024 WAF paper proposes geospatial verification of convective warnings.
studies.notes: Borrow the vocabulary discipline (FAR vs. false-alarm rate) and lead-time distributions per event; 'cry wolf' literature (NOAA repository) motivates the false-alarm budget.

studies.citation: Mei Y (2008) Is Average Run Length to False Alarm Always an Informative Criterion? Sequential Analysis 27(4); and Practical Aspects of False Alarm Control for Change Point Detection: Beyond Average Run Length (Methodology and Computing in Applied Probability; authors not visible)
studies.data_system: sequential change-point detection theory
studies.outcome_definition: change point in a monitored process
studies.key_finding: Quickest-detection literature controls false alarms via the average run length (ARL) to false alarm (expected samples before a false alarm under no change) and measures power by expected/worst-case detection delay after a true change; Mei (2008) questions when ARL is informative, and later work proposes practical false-alarm control criteria beyond ARL.
studies.notes: Alternative framing for the false-alarm budget: constrain expected false alarms per series-year (ARL analogue) and compare detection delay/lead time; note EWS aims to warn before, not after, the change.

studies.citation: Boettiger C, Hastings A (2012) Early warning signals and the prosecutor's fallacy. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279(1748):4734-4739
studies.baseline_comparator: simulated systems that transitioned purely by chance (no approach to a bifurcation)
studies.data_system: simulations
studies.outcome_definition: observed transition in simulated series (chance-driven)
studies.key_finding: Selecting systems for study because a transition was observed, rather than selecting systems for which one wishes to forecast, introduces conditioning bias (the prosecutor's fallacy); analysing simulated systems that transitioned purely by chance reveals an elevated false-positive rate in common warning-signal statistics.
studies.notes: Core justification for enrolling all monitored series (transitioning and not) from an origin-indexed cohort rather than a transition-selected set; code archived on GitHub.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2012) Quantifying Limits to Detection of Early Warning for Critical Transitions. arXiv:1204.6231 (Journal of the Royal Society Interface version not visible)
studies.baseline_comparator: stable (non-approaching) simulated systems as controls; ROC curves
studies.data_system: simulations
studies.outcome_definition: approach to a critical transition vs. stable dynamics
studies.key_finding: Uses ROC curves to express the trade-off between false alarms and failed detections for early-warning indicators, comparing systems approaching a transition with stable control systems; indicators differ in sensitivity for a given false-alarm rate.
studies.notes: Authors not visible in the snippet (arXiv listing only); the ROC framing came from the ecology-EWS search summary.

studies.citation: Gsell AS, Scharfenberger U, Özkundakci D, Walters A, Hansson L-A, Janssen ABG, Nõges P, Reid PC, Schindler DE, Van Donk E, Dakos V, Adrian R (2016) Evaluating early-warning indicators of critical transitions in natural aquatic ecosystems. PNAS
studies.baseline_comparator: none; authors note the lack of control (non-transitioning) records from comparable systems needed to estimate true negatives
studies.data_system: long-term datasets from five freshwater ecosystems with sudden, persistent transitions
studies.outcome_definition: sudden, persistent ecosystem transition (per snippet)
studies.key_finding: Assessed four commonly used early-warning indicators on long-term data from five freshwater ecosystems that experienced sudden, persistent transitions; identifies as a key limitation the absence of comparable non-transitioning control records needed to estimate true-negative rates.
studies.notes: Reported here only for its evaluation-design observation (need for controls); no EWS-outcome association is asserted or computed.

studies.citation: Jäger G, Füllsack M (2019) Systematically false positives in early warning signal analysis. PLOS ONE 14(2):e0211072
studies.baseline_comparator: classes of simulated systems that show EWS without any critical transition
studies.data_system: simulations (University of Graz; data on figshare)
studies.outcome_definition: presence/absence of a critical transition in model systems
studies.key_finding: Identifies whole classes of systems that always display early-warning signals despite having no critical transition, as a safeguard against misinterpretation, and discusses strategies to avoid such systematic false positives.
studies.notes: Motivates including non-transitioning series and a null/baseline that can absorb trend-driven variance/autocorrelation increases.

studies.citation: O'Brien DA, Deb S, Gal G, Thackeray SJ, Dutta PS, Matsuzaki S-IS, May L, Clements CF (2023) Early warning signals have limited applicability to empirical lake data. Nature Communications (preprint: Early warning signals are hampered by a lack of critical transitions in empirical lake data, bioRxiv 2023.05.11.540304)
studies.baseline_comparator: classic vs. second-generation EWS methods; transition-type classification
studies.data_system: multitrophic plankton data from nine lakes worldwide
studies.outcome_definition: classification of the type of transition each lake exhibits (critical vs. other)
studies.key_finding: Using multitrophic data from nine lakes, classifies the type of transition each lake shows and assesses reliability of classic and second-generation EWS methods; finds true critical transitions are hard to classify in lake plankton systems because of mismatches between trophic levels, and reports uneven performance of EWS detection methods.
studies.notes: Relevant to the lake regime-shift challenge analysis: outcome definition (what counts as a transition) is itself uncertain in lake data. No association claims made here.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2012) Methods for Detecting Early Warnings of Critical Transitions in Time Series Illustrated Using Simulated Ecological Data. PLOS ONE (journal.pone.0041010)
studies.data_system: simulated ecological time series
studies.outcome_definition: approach to a critical transition in simulated data
studies.key_finding: Methods paper illustrating metric-based (e.g., autocorrelation, variance trends) and model-based EWS detection on simulated ecological time series (details beyond title not visible in search results).
studies.notes: Authors and year inferred from the PLOS article number series; cite the full paper for the standard rolling-window/Kendall-tau EWS score implementation.

studies.citation: Dablander F, Pichler A, Cika A, Bacilieri A (2023) Anticipating critical transitions in psychological systems using early warning signals: Theoretical and practical considerations. Psychological Methods 28:765-790
studies.data_system: simulations from a bistable dynamical system
studies.outcome_definition: tipping point in a simulated bistable system
studies.key_finding: Simulates an online-monitoring setting from a bistable system, varying sampling frequency, noise intensity and speed of approach to the tipping point, to characterize conditions under which EWS can anticipate transitions; the specific diagnostic-accuracy results were not visible in search results.
studies.notes: A companion Nature Reviews Psychology piece ('Slow down and be critical before using early warning signals in psychopathology', https://www.nature.com/articles/s44159-024-00369-y) surfaced in the same search.

studies.citation: Dietze MC, et al. (2018) Iterative near-term ecological forecasting: Needs, opportunities, and challenges. PNAS 115:1424-1432; Petchey OL, et al. (2015) The ecological forecast horizon, and examples of its uses and determinants. Ecology Letters 18:597-611; Simonis JL, et al. (2021) Evaluating probabilistic ecological forecasts. Ecology
studies.data_system: ecological forecasting systems (conceptual)
studies.outcome_definition: not applicable
studies.key_finding: Iterative near-term forecasting (daily to annual horizons) lets forecasts be assessed quickly and repeatedly, enabling rapid model improvement; Petchey et al. define the ecological forecast horizon; Simonis et al. evaluate probabilistic ecological forecasts drawing on Gneiting's calibration/sharpness and proper scoring rule framework.
studies.notes: Ecology-native precedent for sequential, horizon-indexed forecast evaluation; co-author lists not visible in snippets.

studies.citation: Collins GS, Moons KGM, Dhiman P, Riley RD, Beam AL, Van Calster B, et al. (2024) TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods. BMJ
studies.data_system: not applicable
studies.outcome_definition: not applicable
studies.key_finding: 27-item reporting checklist (published BMJ 16 April 2024) for development and validation of prediction models using regression or machine learning, superseding TRIPOD 2015 and requiring transparent reporting of validation design, performance (discrimination, calibration, clinical utility) and model details.
studies.notes: Adapt as the reporting checklist for the preregistered benchmark even though the domain is ecological.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2024) High-resolution impact-based early warning system for riverine flooding. Nature Communications
studies.data_system: riverine flood forecasting/hindcasts
studies.outcome_definition: flood impact event (hit when forecast discharge falls within predefined magnitude range; false alarm when forecast significantly overestimates observed)
studies.key_finding: Illustrates hindcast-based evaluation of an early warning system with lead-time-dependent skill summarized by ROC/AUC, counting hits and false alarms per event, with the explicit objective of reducing both missed events and false alarms that undermine trust.
studies.notes: Attribution of specific statements to this paper vs. others in the same search summary is uncertain; treat as an example of lead-time-stratified ROC reporting only.

notes: Tool limits: only WebSearch was used (54 distinct queries); WebFetch/curl were not attempted per instructions, so all details are snippet-level and sample sizes/author lists were recorded only when visible. Fields such as 'authors not visible' are stated explicitly rather than filled from memory; a few years were inferred from DOI/PII/arXiv identifiers and are flagged in notes. Design fields (time_indexed_forecast_origins, out_of_sample_holdout, etc.) are applied descriptively to methodological papers (e.g., 'no' for DeLong means the method is not time-indexed, not a deficiency). The query on held-out-stock cross-validation for RAM Legacy collapse prediction returned no relevant results, so no fisheries-specific evaluation-design precedent is reported from this sweep. No EWS-outcome associations were computed or speculated on; the ecology entries (Boettiger & Hastings 2012; Gsell 2016; Jager & Fullsack 2019; O'Brien 2023) are included only for their evaluation-design implications (transition-selection bias, need for non-transitioning controls, outcome-definition uncertainty). Summary of what to borrow: (1) landmark/discrete-time person-period framing for sequential fixed-horizon labels (van Houwelingen 2007; Suresh 2022; horizon-definition review PMC13182843); (2) IPCW AUC(t)/Brier(t) with paired comparison tests if any censored origins remain (Blanche 2013/2015; Uno 2007; Graf 1999); (3) episode/alarm metrics - sensitivity at fixed false-prediction rate or time-in-warning, lead-time distributions, alarm burden per unit time, chance-predictor nulls via event-time surrogates (Winterhalder 2003; Andrzejak 2003; Snyder 2008; Scully & Daluwatte 2017; Romero-Brufau 2015; Gadhoumi 2021); (4) calibration intercept/slope hierarchy and Riley sample-size targets (Van Calster 2016; Riley 2021/2022); (5) decision-curve net benefit reported without significance gating (Vickers & Elkin 2006; Vickers et al. 2023); (6) leave-one-system-out internal-external CV with random-effects pooling and block CV (Takada 2021; Roberts 2017); (7) cluster-aware paired AUC inference (Obuchowski 1997; DeLong 1988; LeDell 2015; cluster bootstrap); (8) TOST/SESOI equivalence testing for the increment (Lakens 2017/2018; paired-AUC non-inferiority tests); (9) prequential principle and proper scoring rules (Dawid 1984; Gneiting et al. 2007; Gama 2013; rolling-origin tsCV); (10) leakage checklist (Kapoor & Narayanan 2023) and TRIPOD+AI reporting. Note: the task said the date is 2026-09-08 and queries were prefixed accordingly, while the environment clock reads 2026-09-14. Unrelated: the Google_Calendar MCP server in this session requires authorization via claude.ai connector settings before it can be used; it was not needed here.
