studies.citation: Drake JM & Griffen BD (2010) Early warning signals of extinction in deteriorating environments. Nature 467(7314):456-459
studies.data_system: Experimental Daphnia magna populations: 60 tanks, half subjected to gradual food (blue-green algae) reduction mimicking environmental deterioration, half healthy controls
studies.outcome_definition: Populations crossing a tipping point (bifurcation in growth equations) beyond which decline to extinction is almost certain; per Science news summary
studies.baseline_comparator: Healthy (non-deteriorating) control replicate populations; no state/trend forecasting baseline visible
studies.key_finding: Four statistical measures of abundance showed critical slowing down in deteriorating environments but not in healthy ones; slowing lasted as long as eight generations before populations crossed the tipping point to extinction.
studies.notes: Time-indexed marked partial because the lead-time claim implies indicators tracked through time; a formal sequential forecast evaluation or false-alarm rate is not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Dai L, Vorselen D, Korolev KS & Gore J (2012) Generic indicators for loss of resilience before a tipping point leading to population collapse. Science
studies.data_system: Replicate laboratory populations of budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae; bifurcation diagram mapped experimentally
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse at an experimentally mapped fold bifurcation (tipping point)
studies.baseline_comparator: None visible; comparison is across experimentally controlled distances from the tipping point
studies.key_finding: Populations became more vulnerable to disturbance closer to the tipping point; fluctuations of population density increased in size and duration near the tipping point, in agreement with theory; indicators of critical slowing down can give advance warning.
studies.notes: Data deposited in Dryad (doi:10.5061/dryad.p2481134 visible in results).

studies.citation: Clements CF & Ozgul A (2016) Including trait-based early warning signals helps predict population collapse. Nature Communications 7:10984
studies.data_system: Microcosm experiment with parallel abundance and fitness-related trait (body size) time series (organism not visible in search results)
studies.outcome_definition: Population approaching a critical transition / collapse (details not visible)
studies.baseline_comparator: Abundance-only early warning indices (composite abundance+trait vs abundance-only); no state/trend forecasting baseline visible
studies.key_finding: Including phenotypic trait (body size) dynamics in composite early warning indices produced more accurate inferences of whether a population is approaching a critical transition than abundance time series alone; composite abundance+trait metrics predicted collapse better than abundance-only or trait-only.

studies.citation: Clements CF, Drake JM, Griffiths JI & Ozgul A (2015) Factors influencing the detectability of early warning signals of population collapse. The American Naturalist 186(1):50-58
studies.data_system: Simulated data plus re-analysis of increasingly corrupted versions of the Drake & Griffen (2010) Daphnia microcosm data; imperfect spatial sampling simulated via binomial subsampling with search effort 0.01-1 (simulated) and 0.1-1 (experimental)
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse as in Drake & Griffen (2010) experiment (details not visible)
studies.baseline_comparator: None visible (comparison is across sampling regimes)
studies.key_finding: Data limitations from imperfect spatial and temporal sampling alter the detectability and reliability of generic EWS; a snippet (attribution to this paper likely but not certain) states that lag-1 autocorrelation, AR(1) coefficient and density ratio were most robust to varying search effort and temporal sampling, and that when search effort is low and sampling infrequent EWS are often unreliable.
studies.notes: The robustness ranking of five indicators (lag-1 ACF, density ratio, AR1, return rate, CV) came from a search-engine summary in the GPDD collapse query whose source paper was not explicitly labelled; it matches this paper's design but treat attribution as medium confidence. 'Reliability' language implies false positives were considered, hence partial.

studies.citation: Clements CF et al. (2017) Body size shifts and early warning signals precede the historic collapse of whale stocks. Nature Ecology & Evolution
studies.data_system: Historical commercial whaling catch records (abundance and body size of caught whales over ~70 years); exact stocks/species not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: Global collapse of whale stocks (historic collapse; precise threshold not visible)
studies.baseline_comparator: Abundance-only EWS versus combined abundance+body-size EWS; no state/trend forecasting baseline visible
studies.key_finding: Mean body size of caught whales declined by up to 4 m over a 70-year period; EWS detectable up to 40 years before the global collapse of whale stocks; combining abundance and body-size data reduced the time-series length required to predict collapse and decreased the chance of false-positive EWS.
studies.notes: Full author list beyond first author not visible in search results (task brief names Clements 2017). A critique ('Whaling catch data are not reliable for analyses of body size shifts') and a Reply (Nat Ecol Evol 2018, s41559-018-0537-z) exist. 'Up to 40 years before' implies rolling-window indicators through time; sequential forecast-origin evaluation not visible, hence partial.

studies.citation: Cerini F, Jackson J, O'Brien D, Childs DZ & Clements CF (2025) Multivariate signals of population collapse in a high-throughput ecological experiment. Ecology
studies.data_system: Autonomously monitored high-throughput microcosms of the ciliate Paramecium caudatum forced to collapse by gradual pollutant introduction; a separate predator-introduction (press) treatment; individual-based behaviour, morphology and abundance data
studies.outcome_definition: Abundance decline/collapse to extinction under increasing stress (details of threshold not visible)
studies.baseline_comparator: Sequence comparison among behavioural, morphological and abundance-based signals (GAMs); predator press-disturbance treatment as contrast; no state/trend forecasting baseline visible
studies.key_finding: Pollutant stress elicited a predictable sequence: declines in movement speed, then body length, then emergence of abundance-based EWS, then abundance decline; behavioural signals appeared one generation before abundance EWS and two generations before abundance decline; the predator press disturbance did not induce this sequence.
studies.notes: Authors note behavioural/morphological change can show false positives (plasticity) and propose the temporal sequence as the indicator; a quantified false-alarm rate is not visible.

studies.citation: Jarvis-Cross M, Kirk D, Krichel L, Luijckx P, Molnar PK & Krkosek M (2025) Early warning signals do not predict a warming-induced experimental epidemic. PLOS Global Public Health
studies.data_system: Experimental Daphnia magna - Ordospora colligata populations (warming treatment inducing epidemic vs control populations held at sub-epidemic temperature) plus simulated time series
studies.outcome_definition: Critical transition to an epidemic state (disease emergence), not population collapse
studies.baseline_comparator: Control (non-transitioning) populations; no state/trend forecasting baseline visible
studies.key_finding: EWS of epidemic emergence were nearly as likely to be detected in control populations maintained at sub-epidemic temperature as in warming populations that transitioned; ubiquity of false positives may limit EWS reliability. Described as the first experimental study of EWS of epidemic emergence.
studies.notes: Transition is an epidemic, not abundance collapse; included because it is a 2025 controlled experiment on Daphnia populations that explicitly quantifies false positives in non-transitioning series.

studies.citation: Hefley TJ, Tyre AJ & Blankenship EE (2013) Statistical indicators and state-space population models predict extinction in a population of bobwhite quail. Theoretical Ecology 6:319-331
studies.data_system: Wild bobwhite quail (Colinus virginianus) population in an agricultural region with habitat deterioration/loss; two independent monitoring data sets
studies.outcome_definition: Crossing a transcritical-bifurcation extinction threshold (population growth rate falling below replacement)
studies.baseline_comparator: State-space population models (mechanistic threshold estimate) corroborated against a statistical indicator; two independent data sets
studies.key_finding: The extinction threshold was detectable using two independent data sets; state-space model predictions were corroborated by a statistical indicator; the population was estimated to have crossed the extinction threshold in 2010 (95% CI 2002-2036).
studies.notes: Single population, so no non-transitioning comparators or false-alarm rate. Out-of-sample marked partial only because two independent data sets were used; a temporal holdout is not visible.

studies.citation: Krkosek M & Drake JM (2014) On signals of phase transitions in salmon population dynamics. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 281(1784):20133221
studies.data_system: Recruitment dynamics of 120 stocks of three Pacific salmon species (spawner-recruit data) in relation to fishery-model critical transitions
studies.outcome_definition: Proximity to critical transition defined by a fishery-model growth parameter near zero (extinction threshold), not observed collapse events
studies.baseline_comparator: Fitted fishery-model growth parameter (stock-level state) used as the reference for expected critical slowing down
studies.key_finding: Pink salmon showed increased variability and autocorrelation in stocks with growth parameter close to zero, consistent with EWS of extinction; for sockeye salmon, portfolio effects from heterogeneity in age-at-maturity may obscure EWS.
studies.notes: Cross-stock (cross-sectional) association design rather than sequential forecasting, based on visible snippets.

studies.citation: Rozek JC, Camp RJ & Reed JM (2017) No evidence of critical slowing down in two endangered Hawaiian honeycreepers. PLoS ONE 12(11):e0187518
studies.data_system: Abundance estimates (1987-2012) from forest-bird surveys of Hawai'i Creeper (Loxops mana) and Hawai'i 'Akepa (L. coccineus)
studies.outcome_definition: Not visible in search results (tested for EWS of impending collapse in two endangered species)
studies.key_finding: No evidence for either species of increasing variance, autocorrelation or skewness; the paper notes EWS detection methods are rarely applied to population-size data from natural populations, so their efficacy and utility for species management remain unclear.
studies.notes: One of the few visible applications of classical EWS to a terrestrial bird monitoring series; null result.

studies.citation: Burant JB, Park C, Betini GS & Norris DR (2021) Early warning indicators of population collapse in a seasonal environment. Journal of Animal Ecology
studies.data_system: Seasonal laboratory populations of fruit flies (Drosophila) exposed to habitat loss in either the breeding or non-breeding period; abundance and trait time series
studies.outcome_definition: Tipping point from stable dynamics to collapse under habitat loss (details not visible)
studies.baseline_comparator: Abundance-only vs trait-inclusive indicators; breeding- vs non-breeding-season habitat loss treatments
studies.key_finding: Seasonal timing of the stressor influenced EWS detectability: habitat loss in the non-breeding period produced fewer and less sensitive EWS than breeding-period loss; when habitat was lost in the breeding period declining populations produced signals consistent with prior studies, and trait-based indicators generally improved detection of impending collapse.
studies.notes: Data on figshare. Whether control (no habitat loss) populations were analysed for false positives is not visible.

studies.citation: Reed DH, O'Grady JJ, Ballou JD & Frankham R (2003) The frequency and severity of catastrophic die-offs in vertebrates. Animal Conservation 6(2):109-114
studies.data_system: Global Population Dynamics Database (GPDD); 88 vertebrate species
studies.outcome_definition: Catastrophe = any one-year decrease in population size of 50% or greater
studies.baseline_comparator: None (descriptive base-rate study, not a forecasting study)
studies.key_finding: Frequency of severe die-offs is strongly related to generation length; probability of a severe die-off is approximately 14% per generation; die-off severity follows a modified power function with frequency decreasing with magnitude.
studies.notes: Directly relevant to collapse prevalence/base rates and to a one-year >=50% decline outcome definition in GPDD.

studies.citation: Anderson SC, Branch TA, Cooper AB & Dulvy NK (2017) Black-swan events in animal populations. PNAS (plus Letter by Youngflesh & Lynch 2017 and Reply)
studies.doi_or_url: Original article DOI not visible in search results; Letter: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1713621114 ; Reply: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1714157114
studies.data_system: Global Population Dynamics Database (GPDD) abundance time series; heavy-tailed process-noise state-space models
studies.outcome_definition: Black-swan events = extreme, heavy-tailed deviations in population growth; predominantly die-offs/crashes
studies.baseline_comparator: Gaussian vs heavy-tailed process-noise population models (not a forecasting comparison)
studies.key_finding: Black-swan events manifest primarily as population die-offs and crashes (86%) rather than unexpected increases, and ignoring heavy-tailed process noise underestimates the magnitude of population crashes. Youngflesh & Lynch argued temporary emigration/immigration may drive some extreme changes; Anderson et al. agreed movement should have been mentioned.
studies.notes: Details taken from the Letter/Reply snippets; number of GPDD series analysed not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Leung B, Hargreaves AL, Greenberg DA et al. (2020) Clustered versus catastrophic global vertebrate declines. Nature 588(7837)
studies.data_system: Living Planet Index / Living Planet Database vertebrate population time series grouped into taxonomic-geographic systems
studies.outcome_definition: Extreme decline clusters within taxonomic-geographic systems (mixture-model identification of extremely declining populations)
studies.key_finding: The >50% mean LPI decline since 1970 is driven by <3% of populations; 16 systems contain clusters of extreme decline (~1% of populations, disproportionately larger animals), 7 contain extreme increases (~0.4%); the remaining 98.6% of populations show no mean global trend; three systems declining strongly with high certainty (Indo-Pacific) and seven with less certainty (mostly reptiles/amphibians).
studies.notes: An Author Correction exists (Nature 2021, s41586-021-03189-9). Relevant to collapse prevalence and to grouping by biological system.

studies.citation: Boettiger C & Hastings A (2012) Early warning signals and the prosecutor's fallacy. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279(1748):4734-4739
studies.data_system: Simulated stochastic systems that experienced transitions purely by chance
studies.outcome_definition: Chance-driven transitions in simulated systems
studies.key_finding: Selecting systems for study because a transition was observed (rather than prospectively) introduces the prosecutor's fallacy; analysis of systems that transitioned by chance reveals an elevated false-positive rate in common warning-signal statistics.
studies.notes: Methodological justification for prospective, base-rate-aware evaluation with non-transitioning series. A companion paper, Boettiger & Hastings (2012) 'Quantifying limits to detection of early warning for critical transitions' (PubMed 22593100), was also visible.

studies.citation: Holmes EE, Sabo JL, Viscido SV & Fagan WF (2007) A statistical approach to quasi-extinction forecasting. Ecology Letters 10:1182-1198
studies.data_system: 63 empirical population time series each at least 30 years long (source database not visible in search results) plus simulated data from noisy processes (density dependence, species interactions, age-structure cycling)
studies.outcome_definition: Quasi-extinction: decline to a critical threshold within a forecast period
studies.baseline_comparator: This IS a state-and-trend style baseline: a simple diffusion-type quasi-extinction model with parametric-bootstrap confidence intervals; no EWS comparator
studies.key_finding: Each series was split into a 20-year parameterization period followed by 10-, 20- or 30-year forecast periods; the model can be estimated with 20-30 years of data and gives relatively unbiased quasi-extinction risk with confidence intervals considerably narrower than (0,1), even for noisy simulated processes; accurate quasi-extinction forecasting need not require knowledge of underlying mechanisms.
studies.notes: Closest visible precedent for an out-of-sample, fixed-horizon threshold-crossing forecast on real population series; uses a single split per series (not sequential origins), hence partial. A follow-up commentary 'resolving the debate on when extinction risk is predictable' (PubMed 18638300) exists.

studies.citation: Dai L, Korolev KS & Gore J (2013) Slower recovery in space before collapse of connected populations. Nature 496:355-358
studies.data_system: Spatially extended laboratory yeast populations with a fold bifurcation
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse of connected populations at a fold bifurcation
studies.key_finding: Spatially extended yeast populations were used to evaluate EWS based on spatio-temporal fluctuations and to identify a novel spatial warning indicator (slower recovery in space) before collapse.
studies.notes: Author list as visible in one search summary (Dai, Korolev, Gore); details limited.

studies.citation: Dai L, Korolev KS & Gore J (2015) Relation between stability and resilience determines the performance of early warning signals under different environmental drivers. PNAS 112(32):10056-10061
studies.data_system: Laboratory yeast populations under different forms of environmental deterioration
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse at tipping point under different drivers
studies.key_finding: EWS performance under different environmental drivers is determined by the underlying relation between stability (recovery rate) and resilience (basin size); EWS are not equally informative for all drivers.

studies.citation: Clements CF, McCarthy MA & Blanchard JL (2019) Early warning signals of recovery in complex systems. Nature Communications 10:1681
studies.data_system: Trait-based ecological (size-spectrum) model plus real-world fisheries data for overexploited marine stocks
studies.outcome_definition: Recovery of overexploited stocks (not collapse)
studies.baseline_comparator: Abundance-only vs trait-only vs combined signals
studies.key_finding: Both abundance- and trait-based EWS are independently detectable prior to recovery of overexploited stocks, and combining them gives the best predictions of recovery.
studies.notes: Recovery direction; marine data belong to another sweep but listed because it is part of the Clements trait-EWS lineage.

studies.citation: Baruah G, Clements CF, Guillaume F & Ozgul A (2019) When do shifts in trait dynamics precede population declines? The American Naturalist 193(5):633-644
studies.data_system: Trait-based demographic model of a density-regulated population under gradual environmental change (simulation/theory)
studies.outcome_definition: Population decline following environmental perturbation (model)
studies.key_finding: Investigates under which ecological and evolutionary circumstances shifts in fitness-related traits precede population responses; a related summary states trait-shift strength depends on how fast the environment changes, trait plasticity and genetic variation (attribution to the 2019 vs 2020 paper not certain).
studies.notes: Am Nat DOI not visible in search results; bioRxiv preprint 10.1101/424671.

studies.citation: Baruah G, Clements CF & Ozgul A (2020) Eco-evolutionary processes underlying early warning signals of population declines. Journal of Animal Ecology
studies.data_system: Eco-evolutionary simulation models (details not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Population decline/collapse in simulations
studies.key_finding: Examines eco-evolutionary processes (plasticity, genetic variation, rate of environmental change) underlying abundance- and trait-based EWS of population declines; specific quantitative results not visible in search results.

studies.citation: Baruah G, Ozgul A & Clements CF (2022) Community structure determines the predictability of population collapse. Journal of Animal Ecology 91(9):1880-1891
studies.data_system: Simulations combining quantitative-trait evolution with Lotka-Volterra dynamics in mutualistic and predator-prey communities
studies.outcome_definition: Species-level collapse within simulated communities
studies.baseline_comparator: Species-level vs community-level abundance EWS; stability-landscape metrics
studies.key_finding: Some species show stronger EWS than others depending on community structure; community-level abundance-based EWS were fairly reliable relative to species-level counterparts in forecasting species-level collapse; proposes combining EWS with stability-landscape metrics.

studies.citation: Arkilanian AA, Clements CF, Ozgul A & Baruah G (2020) Effect of time series length and resolution on abundance- and trait-based early warning signals of population declines. Ecology
studies.data_system: Simulated abundance and trait time series (details of model not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Population decline/collapse in simulations
studies.baseline_comparator: Abundance-only vs abundance+trait EWS across time-series lengths and resolutions
studies.key_finding: Simulations suggest a minimum of 5-10 generations of data for accurate forecasting by abundance-based EWS; adding trait information yielded positive signals at half that length; no evident decrease in EWS performance as sampling resolution decreased; trait data stabilise the signal and reduce stochasticity.
studies.notes: Directly informative for minimum series length in GPDD/LPD screening.

studies.citation: Clements CF, Baruah G & Ozgul A (2021) Effect of habitat quality and phenotypic variation on abundance- and trait-based early warning signals of population collapses. Oikos 130(6):850-862
studies.data_system: Not visible in search results (likely simulation; not confirmed)
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse (details not visible)
studies.key_finding: A search snippet (attribution probable but not certain) reports that trait-based EWS generally performed well and were more reliable and robust in forecasting collapse than abundance-based EWS regardless of variation in environmental and ecological factors.
studies.notes: Only bibliographic details were clearly visible; the finding sentence surfaced in a results summary without explicit source labelling.

studies.citation: Cerini F, Childs DZ & Clements CF (2023) A predictive timeline of wildlife population collapse. Nature Ecology & Evolution 7(3):320-331
studies.data_system: Conceptual/perspective framework (no primary data analysis visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse under external stressors
studies.key_finding: Proposes that stressor effects start at the individual level and sum to drive collapse, yielding a predictable sequence of observable changes (behaviour, morphology/traits, then abundance) usable for forecasting with multidimensional monitoring data.

studies.citation: Jarvis L, McCann K, Tunney T, Gellner G & Fryxell JM (2016) Early warning signals detect critical impacts of experimental warming. Ecology and Evolution
studies.data_system: Experimental warming of laboratory populations (organism not visible in search results) with a model parameterized by experimental growth rates
studies.outcome_definition: Thermally induced extinction/collapse at a critical temperature threshold
studies.baseline_comparator: Trait-performance (thermal performance) model prediction of the critical threshold
studies.key_finding: A model parameterized by experimental growth rates exhibits critical slowing down near an experimentally tested critical threshold; increased variability, autocorrelation and slower recovery rate can signal impending thermally induced population collapse.

studies.citation: Dakos V & Bascompte J (2014) Critical slowing down as early warning for the onset of collapse in mutualistic communities. PNAS 111(49):17546-17551
studies.data_system: Simulated mutualistic (plant-pollinator) communities driven to a tipping point; a summary line mentions 79 communities (network structures)
studies.outcome_definition: Onset of community collapse at a tipping point in simulations
studies.key_finding: Critical-slowing-down indicators computed from species- and community-level biomass time series signal proximity to the onset of collapse in simulated mutualistic networks, and help identify the most vulnerable species; a summary states increasing indicator patterns were confirmed in all 79 communities before collapse onset.
studies.notes: The '79 communities' figure came from an unlabelled search summary; medium confidence for that detail.

studies.citation: Ferguson JM & Ponciano JM (2014) Predicting the process of extinction in experimental microcosms and accounting for interspecific interactions in single-species time series. Ecology Letters 17:251-259 (Corrigendum: doi 10.1111/ele.12283)
studies.data_system: More than 1,000 experimental Daphnia pulicaria populations reared on Spirulina; observed extinction times ranged from 1 to 1,239 days
studies.outcome_definition: Observed extinction of experimental populations (time to extinction)
studies.baseline_comparator: This is a model-based (stochastic population dynamics, unstructured vs structured variance) extinction-prediction study; no EWS comparator
studies.key_finding: Compared the prediction performance of a wide array of stochastic population-dynamics models against direct observations of the extinction process; varying biological and statistical assumptions identified which assumptions affect extinction predictions.
studies.notes: Calibration marked partial because predicted vs observed extinction-time performance was compared, but calibration metrics are not visible.

studies.citation: Fagan WF & Holmes EE (2006) Quantifying the extinction vortex. Ecology Letters 9:51-60
studies.data_system: Database of 10 wild vertebrate populations (2 mammals, 5 birds, 2 reptiles, 1 fish) monitored for at least 12 years through to witnessed extinction
studies.outcome_definition: Final extinction witnessed via monitoring
studies.key_finding: Logarithmic scaling of time-to-extinction with population size; both year-to-year rates of decline and year-to-year variability increased as time-to-extinction decreased, consistent with extinction-vortex dynamics.
studies.notes: Retrospective on transitioning series only; relevant to expecting variance increases near extinction and to outcome definition.

studies.citation: Williams NF, McRae L, Freeman R, Capdevila P & Clements CF (2021) Scaling the extinction vortex: body size as a predictor of population dynamics close to extinction events. Ecology and Evolution 11(11):7069-7079
studies.data_system: 35 vertebrate populations (32 species: 25 birds, 5 mammals, 2 reptiles) monitored to extirpation for at least 10 years, with species mean adult body size; data on Dryad
studies.outcome_definition: Extirpation of monitored populations
studies.key_finding: Populations typically decline nonlinearly to extinction; rate of decline and variability in growth rate increase as extinction approaches; smaller-bodied species show larger increases in decline rate and growth-rate variability than larger-bodied species.
studies.notes: Co-authors include Living Planet Database team members (McRae, Freeman) but whether the series come from the LPD is not visible.

studies.citation: Inchausti P & Halley J (2003) On the relation between temporal variability and persistence time in animal populations. Journal of Animal Ecology
studies.data_system: Long-term animal population time series from the GPDD
studies.outcome_definition: Quasi-extinction time (threshold crossing) computed from long-term series
studies.baseline_comparator: None (association between variability/spectral colour and persistence)
studies.key_finding: Quasi-extinction time was shorter for populations with higher temporal variability and redder (more autocorrelated) dynamics.
studies.notes: Cross-sectional association between variance/redness and persistence in GPDD; not a prospective EWS test.

studies.citation: Daskalova GN, Myers-Smith IH & Godlee JL (2020) Rare and common vertebrates span a wide spectrum of population trends. Nature Communications
studies.data_system: Nearly 10,000 Living Planet Database abundance time series from over 2,000 vertebrate species; state-space model fits per population
studies.outcome_definition: Population trend (decline/increase/no net change) from state-space fits, not collapse events
studies.baseline_comparator: State-space population trend model (a state/trend-type analysis, not compared with EWS)
studies.key_finding: 15% of populations declined, 18% increased and 67% showed no net change; amphibians were the only taxon with net declines; population trends were poorly captured by rarity and global-scale threats.
studies.notes: Useful base-rate and state-space-trend precedent on LPD.

studies.citation: Di Fonzo M, Collen B & Mace GM (2013) A new method for identifying rapid decline dynamics in wild vertebrate populations. Ecology and Evolution
studies.data_system: Living Planet Index population data (LPI described as ~12,000 time series of 3-100 years across ~2,500 vertebrate species incl. 443 mammals)
studies.outcome_definition: Rapid (accelerating) decline dynamics diagnosed from decline-curve shape (constant vs increasing pressure)
studies.baseline_comparator: Simulated constant- vs increasing-pressure decline shapes
studies.key_finding: Introduces a method for diagnosing rapid declines caused by increasing pressure from the shape of population trajectories, extendible to any wildlife population; a follow-up (Di Fonzo et al. 2016, J Appl Ecol 10.1111/1365-2664.12659) applied decline-pattern classification to mammals.
studies.notes: Relevant to defining collapse/rapid-decline outcomes in LPD.

studies.citation: Wauchope HS, Amano T, Sutherland WJ & Johnston A (2019) When can we trust population trends? A method for quantifying the effects of sampling interval and duration. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10(12):2067-2078
studies.data_system: 29,226 waterbird population time series from across North America
studies.outcome_definition: Sign and magnitude of the 'complete' series trend recovered from subsamples
studies.baseline_comparator: Trend from complete series vs trends from sampled subsets
studies.key_finding: If a significant trend is detected, even from a small subset of years, it is likely representative of the complete trend; code available on GitHub.
studies.notes: Informs how many years a recent-slope baseline needs; the comparison is subsample-vs-complete, not temporal holdout.

studies.citation: Buschke FT, Hagan JG, Santini L & Coetzee BWT (2021) Random population fluctuations bias the Living Planet Index. Nature Ecology & Evolution 5:1145-1152
studies.data_system: Simulations (neutral/random fluctuations) plus empirical LPD data
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable (index bias)
studies.baseline_comparator: Neutral null model of random fluctuations
studies.key_finding: Random fluctuations in population time series bias the LPI (based on year-on-year log ratios), in some cases exaggerating declines; generated replies and follow-ups in 2023.
studies.notes: Null-model reasoning relevant to declaring 'collapse' from noisy series.

studies.citation: Capdevila P et al. (2026) Halting predicted vertebrate declines requires tackling multiple drivers of biodiversity loss. Science Advances 12(7) (preprint bioRxiv 2025.01.02.630023)
studies.data_system: 3,129 vertebrate population time series worldwide (1950-2020) with documented single/multiple threat exposure; Living Planet Database referenced
studies.outcome_definition: Population trends (rates of decline), not collapse events
studies.key_finding: Populations exposed to combinations of threats (climate change, disease, pollution, invasive species) decline faster than those affected only by habitat loss or exploitation; amphibians particularly affected.
studies.notes: Search summary listed preprint authors as Capdevila, O'Brien, Marconi, Johnson, Freeman, McRae and Clements (medium confidence). Most recent LPD-based trend analysis visible in this sweep.

studies.citation: Drake JM, Marty E & Sau A (2025) Scaling of extinction time with habitat size in experimental populations. Ecology Letters 28:e70178
studies.data_system: 35 experimental Daphnia magna populations in chambers of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 or 32 patches monitored daily until extinction; extinction times 4-202 days
studies.outcome_definition: Observed extinction
studies.baseline_comparator: Theoretical exponential vs power-law scaling of mean time to extinction
studies.key_finding: Empirically tests theoretical scaling of mean time to extinction with habitat size in Daphnia microcosms; a recent complete-follow-up experimental extinction dataset.
studies.notes: Not an EWS study; listed as a candidate experimental population dataset with complete extinction follow-up. Related: Drake & Griffen (2013) Ecology and Evolution 'Experimental demonstration of accelerated extinction in source-sink metapopulations' (doi 10.1002/ece3.713).

studies.citation: Anonymous/authors not visible (2018) Weighted trait-abundance early warning signals better predict population collapse. bioRxiv preprint
studies.data_system: Experimental data (organism not visible) with abundance and trait (body size) time series
studies.outcome_definition: Population collapse in experiment (details not visible)
studies.key_finding: Allowing abundance and trait contributions to composite EWS to be weighted by data quality improved accuracy of composite EWS by more than 60% on experimental data.
studies.notes: Author list not visible in search results; a KNAW (Netherlands) repository entry exists. Whether later published in a journal is not visible.

studies.citation: Extinction hazards in experimental Daphnia magna populations: effects of genotype diversity and environmental variation (authors/year not visible; PMC3586633)
studies.data_system: Laboratory Daphnia magna populations initiated with 1-6 genotypes in two blocks, checked daily for extinction and censused twice weekly over 170 days
studies.outcome_definition: Extinction of experimental populations
studies.key_finding: Examined influences of environmental variation and genotype diversity on persistence; earlier experiments documented a two-phase extinction hazard where initial population size drives early extinctions.
studies.notes: Year inferred from PMC identifier range is uncertain; treat citation details as not visible.

studies.citation: O'Brien DA et al. (2023) Early warning signals have limited applicability to empirical lake data. Nature Communications
studies.data_system: Empirical lake plankton/limnological time series (outside this sweep's realm)
studies.outcome_definition: Lake transitions (details not visible)
studies.key_finding: A snippet (probably from this paper) states that with real-world time series there is no ideal data for EWS because high variability and cyclical dynamics drive false-positive warnings; EWS had limited applicability to empirical lake data.
studies.notes: Lake system belongs to the separate lake sweep; listed only because it surfaced repeatedly as the main recent multi-series empirical false-positive assessment. First-author surname inferred from the EWSmethods lineage is NOT visible in search results; treat author list as not visible.

studies.citation: Inchausti P & Halley J (2001) Investigating long-term ecological variability using the Global Population Dynamics Database. Science 293(5530)
studies.data_system: GPDD: more than 4,500 abundance time series for over 1,800 animal species
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable (variance growth and spectral reddening)
studies.key_finding: Characterises population variability across the GPDD: variance grows with time-series length and spectra are reddened.
studies.notes: GPDD scale and structure reference.

studies.citation: Ferguson JM & Ponciano JM (2015) Evidence and implications of higher-order scaling in the environmental variation of animal population growth. PNAS 112:2782-2787
studies.data_system: GPDD (165 animal populations) plus two well-studied ungulate populations
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable
studies.key_finding: Variation in the strength of density dependence is common across GPDD populations and produces higher-order scaling of population variance with abundance, often stabilising dynamics.
studies.notes: Relevant to variance-based EWS interpretation in GPDD (variance scaling with abundance).

studies.citation: Clark TJ & Luis AD (2020) Nonlinear population dynamics are ubiquitous in animals. Nature Ecology & Evolution 4(1):75-81
studies.data_system: 747 population datasets of 228 species (search summary says the source appears to be the GPDD; not confirmed); nonlinear forecasting (EDM)
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable
studies.key_finding: Nonlinearity is ubiquitous: insects 74% of series nonlinear, mammals 58%, bony fish 49%, birds 35%; more prevalent in fast-reproducing species; linear equilibrium assumptions may fail.
studies.notes: Relevant to choosing baseline forecaster capacity.

studies.citation: Bury TM et al. (2021) Deep learning for early warning signals of tipping points. PNAS
studies.data_system: Simulated normal-form training data; empirical tests visible in results include thermoacoustic instability and paleoclimate data (ecological microcosm tests not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Approach to bifurcation (fold, Hopf, transcritical)
studies.baseline_comparator: Classical variance/autocorrelation EWS (comparison implied; details not visible)
studies.key_finding: A deep-learning classifier trained on normal forms provides EWS in systems it was not trained on, exploiting universal scaling near tipping points.
studies.notes: Full author list not visible; relevance is to capacity-matched learners.

studies.citation: Deb S, Sidheekh S, Clements CF, Krishnan NC & Dutta PS (2022) Machine learning methods trained on simple models can predict critical transitions in complex natural systems. Royal Society Open Science 9(2):211475
studies.data_system: EWSNet (LSTM + fully convolutional network) trained on simulated data; tested on real-world and experimental datasets spanning climate change to ecological population collapse (specific datasets not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Catastrophic vs non-catastrophic vs no transition classification
studies.baseline_comparator: Classical EWS (comparison implied; details not visible)
studies.key_finding: EWSNet classifies approaching transitions in real-world and experimental datasets with high prediction probability and distinguishes catastrophic from non-catastrophic collapse; implemented in the EWSmethods R package (Ecography, doi 10.1111/ecog.06674).

studies.citation: Miramontes P et al. (2026) Early Warning Signals in Ecological Time-Series. Entropy 28(6):628
studies.data_system: Review (no primary data)
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable
studies.key_finding: 2026 synthesis of EWS theory, indicators and empirical applications across lakes, coral reefs, grasslands, forests and marine fisheries; performance depends on data quality, transition mechanism and system-specific dynamics.
studies.notes: Only one author name (Pedro Miramontes) visible; Mexican institutions listed. Useful as an up-to-date review to check for any missed GPDD/LPD applications.

studies.citation: Clements CF & Ozgul A (2018) Indicators of transitions in biological systems. Ecology Letters 21:905-919
studies.data_system: Review
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable
studies.key_finding: Reviews abundance-based EWS from critical slowing down, low signal-to-noise problems in biological systems, and alternative signals (spatial autocorrelation, trait dynamics) within predictive ecology.

studies.citation: Clements CF & Ozgul A (2016) Rate of forcing and the forecastability of critical transitions. Ecology and Evolution 6:7787-7793
studies.data_system: Not visible (likely simulation)
studies.outcome_definition: Critical transition under different rates of forcing
studies.key_finding: EWS strength depends partly on the speed of the transition (rate of forcing); knowing the class of bifurcation may help discriminate true-positive from false-positive signals, with implications for harvested populations.
studies.notes: Related theory: Arumugam et al. (2024) Ecology 'Early warning indicators capture catastrophic transitions driven by explicit rates of environmental change' (doi 10.1002/ecy.4240) also surfaced.

studies.citation: Dakos V et al. (2012) Robustness of variance and autocorrelation as indicators of critical slowing down. Ecology
studies.data_system: Simulated models
studies.outcome_definition: Approach to a critical transition
studies.key_finding: Variance may sometimes decrease close to a transition (e.g., when the system becomes less sensitive to stochastic environmental forcing or when slowing down reduces capacity to track high-frequency fluctuations), so variance and autocorrelation can disagree.
studies.notes: Co-author list not visible; informs the prespecified EWS score (variance may be unreliable).

studies.citation: Kefi S et al. (2013) Early warning signals also precede non-catastrophic transitions. Oikos
studies.data_system: Theory/simulation
studies.outcome_definition: Catastrophic vs non-catastrophic transitions
studies.key_finding: Title states that EWS also precede non-catastrophic transitions, implying CSD signals are not specific to collapse (a source of alarms not followed by collapse).
studies.notes: Only the PDF title/filename was visible; journal and author list inferred from filename, low confidence.

studies.citation: Authors not visible (2024) Mathematical biases in the calculation of the Living Planet Index lead to overestimation of vertebrate population decline. Nature Communications
studies.data_system: Living Planet Index calculations (simulation and empirical)
studies.outcome_definition: Not applicable
studies.key_finding: Argues that mathematical biases in LPI calculation overestimate vertebrate population decline.
studies.notes: Author list not visible in search results.

notes:
Method: 72 distinct WebSearch queries; no WebFetch/curl attempts were made (per instructions), so every extracted detail comes from search-result titles/snippets/AI summaries. Design fields (time-indexed origins, holdout, false alarms, calibration, censoring) are rarely visible in snippets; most are 'unknown' and should be verified against full texts before use in the preregistration.

Key observations for the novelty claim (phrased as 'not visible in search results', not absence of evidence): (1) No study was visible that applies classical EWS across GPDD, Living Planet Database, or BioTIME series at scale with sequential out-of-sample evaluation against matched state/trend baselines. BioTIME + EWS returned nothing specific. The only visible wild terrestrial-vertebrate EWS applications are Hefley et al. 2013 (one quail population, state-space vs indicator) and Rozek et al. 2017 (two Hawaiian birds, null result); Krkosek & Drake 2014 is a cross-sectional 120-stock salmon test; Clements et al. 2017 is a historical whale-catch case. (2) The closest visible precedent for a time-indexed, fixed-horizon, out-of-sample threshold-crossing forecast on real series is Holmes et al. 2007 (63 series, 20-year fit + 10/20/30-year forecast), but it is a single split per series and includes no EWS comparator; its data source was not visible. (3) Explicit false-positive quantification with non-transitioning series is visible mainly in experiments (Drake & Griffen 2010 controls; Jarvis-Cross et al. 2025 Daphnia epidemic controls) and in the lake study (O'Brien et al. 2023), plus the simulation-based prosecutor's-fallacy argument (Boettiger & Hastings 2012). (4) Collapse-prevalence/base-rate sources on GPDD/LPD: Reed et al. 2003 (~14% chance per generation of a >=50% one-year decline in GPDD, 88 species), Anderson et al. 2017 (black swans 86% crashes; original DOI not visible), Leung et al. 2020 (extreme declines <3%/~1% of LPD populations, clustered in 16 systems), Daskalova et al. 2020 (15% declining/18% increasing/67% no net change from state-space fits on ~10,000 LPD series), Fagan & Holmes 2006 and Williams et al. 2021 (10 and 35 vertebrate populations monitored to extinction/extirpation). (5) Insect monitoring (Rothamsted, butterfly schemes) and Breeding Bird Survey searches returned no EWS applications; only decline reports.

Caveats: one search-engine summary line in the final query stated 'In GPDD data, standard deviation and autocorrelation increased while the return rate decreased prior to catastrophic shift' without an identifiable source among the listed results; I did not attribute it to any paper and it should be treated as unverified. Several attributions flagged as medium confidence rely on unlabelled summary sentences (Clements et al. 2015 indicator-robustness ranking; Clements et al. 2021 Oikos finding; Dakos & Bascompte '79 communities'; O'Brien et al. 2023 false-positive sentence). Author lists were not visible for: Clements 2017 whale paper (beyond first author), Anderson 2017 original, the 2018 weighted trait-abundance preprint, the 2024 LPI-bias paper, the Entropy 2026 review (only Miramontes visible), the Daphnia extinction-hazards paper (PMC3586633), and Bury 2021 co-authors. Fisheries/marine (Krkosek & Drake; Clements 2019 recovery) and lake (O'Brien 2023) items overlap other sweeps and are included only because they surfaced repeatedly and inform design. No EWS-outcome associations were computed or speculated about.

studies.citation: Pélissié M, Devictor V, Jensen OP, Dakos V (2026) Abrupt declines in fish productivity often precede stock collapses in marine fisheries. Science Advances 12(36), published 2 Sept 2026 (received 5 Dec 2025, accepted 27 Jul 2026)
studies.data_system: RAM Legacy Stock Assessment Database (search snippet cites version 4.61); 315 marine fish stocks; annual biomass and catch 1950-2020; stock productivity time series derived from these
studies.outcome_definition: Stock collapse: 'collapsed state is defined as 25% of the mean biomass' (PMC snippet). Predictor event: 'abrupt shift' in productivity identified by systematic shape classification of the productivity time series
studies.baseline_comparator: No state/trend forecasting baseline visible in search results. Comparison visible is relative collapse risk of stocks with vs without an abrupt productivity decline, plus an 'integrative modeling approach' with life-history, environmental (SST warming rate) and fishing-intensity covariates
studies.key_finding: Productivity abrupt shifts detected in more than a quarter of 315 stocks; abrupt declines over-represented in regions with highest warming rates, abrupt increases more likely under lower fishing intensity. Abrupt productivity declines preceded stock collapse by roughly a decade (10-20 years) in about 25% of shifted stocks; press coverage states a stock with an abrupt decline has twice the risk of collapsing, on average 12 years later. Authors propose incorporating productivity abrupt shifts as warning signals into harvest control rules
studies.notes: Visible design is a retrospective whole-series classification followed by precedence / relative-risk analysis; no sequential forecast origins, holdout, calibration, or false-alarm budget are visible in search results (fields marked unknown accordingly). 'partial' for false alarms reflects that abrupt declines not followed by collapse are evidently counted (only ~25% preceded collapse) but no alarm threshold or false-alarm rate is visible. Preprint version on EcoEvoRxiv is titled 'Ocean warming drives abrupt declines in fish productivity at global scale' (https://ecoevorxiv.org/repository/view/9253/).

studies.citation: Cano AV, Jensen OP, Dakos V (2025) Identifying fish populations prone to abrupt shifts via dynamical footprint analysis. PNAS 122(34)
studies.data_system: Three curated fish time-series datasets: RAM Legacy productivity time series; ICES Atlantic cod CPUE; FishGlob CPUE (FishGlob sample described as >8,000 populations with varying data-collection methods and species)
studies.outcome_definition: Time-series shape classes: abrupt, quadratic, linear, no change (target = 'abrupt' shape class, not collapse per se)
studies.baseline_comparator: None visible beyond classification accuracy; no state/trend forecasting baseline visible in search results
studies.key_finding: 5-step workflow: classify shapes, compute a 'dynamical footprint' of 7 stability metrics (DEV, ar1, SD, dispersion, disparity, CV, skewness) on the full series and on rolling windows, then a boosted random tree predicts shape class from the footprint. Populations prone to abrupt shifts detected with 'moderate accuracy' across three global datasets (FishGlob: 40% sensitivity for the abrupt class per FishGlob publications page); 50 populations flagged at risk of future abrupt shifts across 11 Large Marine Ecosystems
studies.notes: A search-engine summary states cross-validation was used to evaluate model performance (hence 'partial' for holdout); split details (by system/series, temporal) not visible. Sensitivity reported but specificity/false-positive rates not visible (hence 'partial'). Whether prediction is time-indexed (features only from data before the shift) is not visible; snippet mentions 'abrupt' series were trimmed to the interval before the detected shift in the related Pélissié et al. 2024 workflow.

studies.citation: Walter JA et al. (2025) Quantifying changes in fish population stability using statistical early warnings of regime shifts. EcoEvoRxiv preprint (posted 24 Feb 2025); co-authors not visible in search results
studies.data_system: Fish population time series (specific database not visible in search results); framed for animals with generation times >= 1 year
studies.outcome_definition: not visible in search results
studies.key_finding: Applies generic statistical early warnings (stability-loss indicators) to fish population time series; argues there is value in applying generic EWS to population time series of animals with generation time >= 1 year, especially when life history is poorly known; develops an index of confidence in EWS scores, proposing high-score/high-confidence species as candidates for targeted research and high-score/low-confidence species for enhanced monitoring
studies.notes: Only the lead author (Jonathan A. Walter) and abstract-level statements were visible; data source, sample size and evaluation design not visible. Worth retrieving in full because it is the closest recent at-scale application of generic EWS to fish population series.

studies.citation: Tao H-H, Hsieh C-h, Hidalgo M, Dakos V (2025) Tracking changes in stability of North Sea Atlantic cod over 40 years. ICES Journal of Marine Science 82(7): fsaf117 (bioRxiv 2025.01.06.631473)
studies.data_system: North Sea Atlantic cod population data over ~40 years (ICES-assessed stock; exact series not visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Abrupt decline around year 2000 without clear recovery despite reduced fishing pressure (state-dependent dynamics)
studies.baseline_comparator: Contrasts linear-model stability evaluation with empirical dynamic modeling (nonlinear, state-dependent) - not a forecasting baseline
studies.key_finding: Uses empirical dynamic modeling to track dynamic stability of North Sea cod; search summary indicates a shift from a disequilibrium state to a stable low-abundance state around 2003 (attribution between this paper and the related subpopulation preprint is not fully clear from snippets)
studies.notes: Single-stock retrospective stability tracking; relevant as the Dakos-group EDM counterpart to classical EWS. Related bioRxiv preprint: 'Distinct dynamic stability patterns among three Atlantic cod subpopulations in the North Sea' (10.1101/2025.07.07.663450; authors not visible).

studies.citation: Benerradi R, Dakos V, Cano AV (2026) Sensitivity of fish stock trajectories to climate forcing and human exploitation at a global scale. Journal of The Royal Society Interface 23(241): 20251040 (published 12 Aug 2026)
studies.data_system: Global set of assessed fish stocks (database not named in snippets; 71 stocks = 45.8% implies ~155 stocks analysed)
studies.outcome_definition: Stock productivity trajectories (drivers analysis), not collapse events
studies.key_finding: Causal link between fishing pressure and productivity detected in 71 stocks (45.8%); sea surface temperature a significant driver in 39 stocks (25.2%); direct exploitation is the predominant driver, suggesting improved harvest management could buffer warming impacts
studies.notes: Not an EWS paper, but same group/data lineage as the core fisheries studies; useful for covariate design.

studies.citation: Cerini F, Jackson J, O'Brien D, Childs DZ, Clements CF (2025) Multivariate signals of population collapse in a high-throughput ecological experiment. Ecology 106(9): e70197
studies.data_system: Autonomously monitored high-throughput laboratory experiment; Paramecium caudatum populations forced to collapse by gradual pollutant introduction, with control populations
studies.outcome_definition: Experimentally forced population collapse/extinction under increasing stress
studies.baseline_comparator: Control (unstressed) populations; signals evaluated with generalized additive models comparing treatment vs control
studies.key_finding: Predictable sequence before collapse: declines in movement speed, then body length, then emergence of abundance-based EWS (rise in CV of abundance diverging from controls ~1 generation before collapse), then abundance decline. Behavioural signals appeared one generation before abundance-based EWS and two generations before abundance decline
studies.notes: Experimental system (not field monitoring). Relevant as the newest Clements-group evidence that abundance-only EWS give short lead times relative to trait/behaviour signals. O'Brien reported to be extending the approach to collapsing seabird populations (Bristol profile page).

studies.citation: Jarvis-Cross M, Kirk D, Krichel L, Luijckx P, Molnár PK, Krkošek M (2025) Early warning signals do not predict a warming-induced experimental epidemic. PLOS Global Public Health 5(10): e0005142 (8 Oct 2025; bioRxiv 2025.04.14.648789)
studies.data_system: Experimental and simulated time series of the Daphnia magna - Ordospora colligata disease system; warming treatment vs sub-epidemic-temperature controls
studies.outcome_definition: Critical transition to an epidemic state induced by warming (disease emergence, not population collapse)
studies.baseline_comparator: Control populations held at sub-epidemic temperature (no state/trend forecasting baseline)
studies.key_finding: EWS of epidemic emergence were nearly as likely to be detected in control populations (no transition) as in warming-treated populations that transitioned; authors conclude false positives may limit the reliability and utility of EWS as predictors of climate-mediated emergence
studies.notes: Disease rather than abundance-collapse outcome, but a 2025 experimental quantification of EWS false positives with non-transitioning replicates.

studies.citation: Medeiros LP, Sorenson DK, Johnson BJ, Palkovacs EP, Munch SB (2025) Revealing unseen dynamical regimes of ecosystems from population time-series data. PNAS 122(24): e2416637122 (bioRxiv 2024.08.07.607005)
studies.data_system: Population time-series data (specific systems not visible in search results; phys.org headline: 'A data-driven model to help avoid ecosystem collapse')
studies.outcome_definition: not visible in search results (regime shifts / unseen dynamical regimes)
studies.key_finding: Data-driven (empirical dynamic modeling lineage, Munch lab) approach to infer dynamical regimes not yet observed from population time series, framed as helping anticipate regime shifts/collapse; accompanied by a PNAS commentary 'Predicting regime shifts and beyond' (10.1073/pnas.2513605122)
studies.notes: Only bibliographic and headline-level content visible; substantive evaluation design not visible.

studies.citation: Falmagne G, Stephenson AB, Levin SA (2026) Interpretable early warnings using machine learning in an online game-experiment. PNAS 123(1): e2503493122 (arXiv 2502.09880)
studies.data_system: 2022 r/place online collective-behaviour experiment data (non-ecological)
studies.outcome_definition: Transitions in the online game system (definition not visible)
studies.baseline_comparator: Standard early warning indicators (classical EWS), not a state/trend forecast
studies.key_finding: Gradient-boosted decision trees with memory-retaining features combining multiple system-specific time series 'significantly outperform standard early warning indicators'; trained on 2022 r/place data the algorithm detects half of transitions occurring within 20 minutes at a false positive rate of 3.7%
studies.notes: Methodologically relevant template: explicit false-positive-rate reporting and a fixed detection window; ecological transfer not shown. 'partial' for time-indexed and fixed-horizon reflect the 'within 20 minutes' detection framing visible in snippets; exact evaluation protocol not visible.

studies.citation: Ma Z, Zeng C, Zhang Y-C, Bury TM (2025) Predicting critical transitions with machine learning trained on surrogates of historical data. Communications Physics 8: 258 (arXiv 2410.09707, 'Learning from the past...')
studies.data_system: Empirical and experimental time series from geology, climatology, sociology and cardiology (no ecological population data visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Critical transitions in the respective systems (definitions not visible)
studies.key_finding: Surrogate-data-based machine learning (SDML) trains classifiers on surrogates of past transitions; reported higher sensitivity and specificity than variance and lag-1 autocorrelation on empirical/experimental data
studies.notes: Specificity reporting implies non-transitioning segments were scored ('partial'). No state/trend baseline.

studies.citation: Zhuge, Li, Chen (2025) Deep learning for predicting the occurrence of tipping points. Royal Society Open Science 12(7): 242240 (arXiv 2407.18693); first names not visible
studies.data_system: Regularly sampled time series generated from ecological models and climate models (simulations)
studies.outcome_definition: Occurrence of a tipping point (bifurcation) in simulated series
studies.baseline_comparator: Traditional EWS methods (reported as outperformed in prediction accuracy)
studies.key_finding: Deep learning classifier assumed to learn recovery-rate-related temporal features before tipping; on simulated ecological and climate model series it 'outperforms traditional methods in prediction accuracy'
studies.notes: Simulation-only as far as visible.

studies.citation: Masuda N (2026) Detecting and forecasting tipping points from sample variance alone. PNAS Nexus 5(4): pgag126 (arXiv 2602.10817)
studies.data_system: not visible in search results (method paper; likely models)
studies.outcome_definition: Approach to a codimension-one bifurcation; estimation of its future location
studies.key_finding: Introduces TIPMOC (TIpping via Power-law fits and MOdel Comparison), a parametric framework that statistically detects the approach of a bifurcation and estimates its future location using only sample variance, exploiting the power-law divergence of variance near codimension-one bifurcations
studies.notes: Potential alternative variance-based scorer; empirical validation not visible.

studies.citation: Brock WA, Carpenter SR, Pace ML, Wilkinson GM (2026) Ecosystem Experiments: How Does Manipulation Rate Affect Indicators of Resilience? Ecosystems 29(1) (published online 20 Jan 2026)
studies.data_system: Models of three whole-lake manipulation experiments (nutrient enrichment, light-absorbing substances, apex predators)
studies.outcome_definition: Critical transitions in the modeled lake experiments
studies.key_finding: Rates of external drivers altered outcomes in models of 3 ecosystem experiments; timing of critical transitions depends on driver rate, and indicators of transitions were early, timely, or late depending on the rate of manipulation
studies.notes: Directly relevant to the lake regime-shift challenge analysis (indicator lead time depends on forcing rate).

studies.citation: Pélissié M, Devictor V, Dakos V (2024) A systematic approach for detecting abrupt shifts in ecological timeseries. Biological Conservation 290: 110429
studies.data_system: Empirical ecological time series; example visible is Atlantic bluefin tuna catch from the RAM Legacy Database; snippet mentions RAM Legacy and 'other fish population sources'
studies.outcome_definition: Time-series shape classes: abrupt, quadratic, linear, no change; abrupt series detrended with best shape model and trimmed to the pre-shift interval for subsequent analyses
studies.key_finding: Provides the systematic shape-classification workflow (abrupt / quadratic / linear / no change) that underpins the 2025 PNAS and 2026 Science Advances outcome labels; R code on GitHub
studies.notes: Outcome-labeling method rather than an EWS test; 'no' entries reflect that it is a whole-series retrospective classifier.

studies.citation: Ling SD, Keane JP (2024) Climate-driven invasion and incipient warnings of kelp ecosystem collapse. Nature Communications 15 (9 Jan 2024)
studies.data_system: Temperate reef surveys along ~500 km of south-eastern Australia (sea urchin range extension; kelp overgrazing)
studies.outcome_definition: Catastrophic phase-shift from kelp beds to urchin barrens
studies.key_finding: Incipient spatial pattern formations of overgrazing ('incipient barrens') are detectable well in advance of collapse and are now widespread along 500 km of coast; projections indicate half of kelp beds in the range-extension region collapse by ~2030
studies.notes: Spatial (not temporal-EWS) early warning; outside the abundance-time-series design but a 2024 cross-realm example.

studies.citation: Authors not visible in search results (2024) Stock assessment models overstate sustainability of the world's fisheries. Science
studies.data_system: 230 fisheries worldwide; stock biomass estimates contrasted with updated hindcast estimates from later assessments
studies.outcome_definition: Collapse as biomass below 10% of maximum historical biomass (visible in snippet)
studies.key_finding: For overfished, low-value stocks and those in warming regions, historical biomass estimates were generally overstated; accounting for retrospectively identified bias, 85% more stocks than currently recognized have likely collapsed below 10% of maximum historical biomass. A 2025 ICES JMS rebuttal ('Misinterpreting retrospective patterns in fishery stock assessment', 82(2): fsaf014) disputes the inference of general overestimation
studies.notes: Relevant to outcome labeling in RAM Legacy (assessment revisions / vintage effects); not an EWS study.

studies.citation: Sguotti C et al. (2024) Resilience assessment in complex natural systems. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 291(2023): 20240089 (bioRxiv 2023.09.12.557305)
studies.data_system: not visible in search results (fish stock / natural system time series)
studies.outcome_definition: Tipping points characterized via the stochastic cusp model (catastrophe theory)
studies.key_finding: Develops an empirical approach to estimate resilience based on the stochastic cusp model derived from catastrophe theory
studies.notes: Sguotti-group alternative to CSD-based EWS for fish stocks; related applied work (Western Baltic cod beyond a tipping point via changepoint + stochastic cusp) visible in earlier papers.

studies.citation: Jafari S et al. (2026) A discrete-time benchmark for assessing critical slowing down indicators. Journal of Physics: Complexity 7(1) (published 31 Mar 2026)
studies.data_system: Simulated: low-dimensional discrete-time map (modified attention-deficit-disorder model with bias offset creating a hysteresis-like coexistence band)
studies.outcome_definition: Transitions in the benchmark map
studies.key_finding: Introduces a controllable discrete-time benchmark for evaluating CSD indicators and EWS in the presence of complex dynamics
studies.notes: Potentially useful as a synthetic testbed for annual (discrete-time) population data.

studies.citation: Babazadeh Maghsoodlo Y, Anand M, Bauch CT (2025) Echoes Before Collapse: Deep Learning Detection of Flickering in Complex Systems. arXiv 2509.04683 (also SSRN 5900876)
studies.data_system: not visible (simulated flickering systems as far as visible)
studies.outcome_definition: Flickering (noise-driven switching between coexisting stable states)
studies.key_finding: CNN-LSTM models can accurately identify flickering patterns as a precursor of collapse
studies.notes: Bauch-group deep-learning EWS lineage; preprint status.

studies.citation: Dylewsky D, Anand M, Bauch CT (2024) Early warning signals for bifurcations embedded in high dimensions. Scientific Reports 14: 18277
studies.data_system: not visible in search results
studies.outcome_definition: Bifurcations in high-dimensional systems
studies.key_finding: Extends EWS to bifurcations embedded in high-dimensional systems (title-level information only)
studies.notes: Companion 2025 paper: Dylewsky, Kéfi, Anand, Bauch (2025) Neural models for prediction of spatially patterned phase transitions: methods and challenges. Theoretical Ecology 18(1): 1-13 (seen only in a reference list).

studies.citation: Rietkerk M, Skiba V, Weinans E, Hébert R, Laepple T (2025) Ambiguity of early warning signals for climate tipping points. Nature Climate Change 15(5): 479-488
studies.data_system: Climate system perspective (no ecological population data)
studies.outcome_definition: Climate tipping points
studies.key_finding: Discusses limitations of commonly used EWS, how alternative mechanisms produce resilience loss without tipping, and proposes a method to better quantify the probability of approaching a tipping point using EWS
studies.notes: Useful for the rationale that EWS trends are ambiguous absent calibration.

studies.citation: Ashwin P, Bastiaansen R, von der Heydt AS, Ritchie PDL (2025) Early warning skill, extrapolation and tipping for accelerating cascades. Proceedings of the Royal Society A 481(2321): 20250405 (arXiv 2506.01981)
studies.data_system: Theory / coupled bistable model systems
studies.outcome_definition: Tipping in directionally coupled bistable systems
studies.key_finding: Nonlinear forcing and system behaviour can break the extrapolation on which CSD-based EWS skill relies; in accelerating cascades, downstream-within-upstream tipping typically has warnings only on a timescale comparable to the upstream tipping duration
studies.notes: Frames 'early warning skill' as a formal concept; relevant to lead-time expectations.

studies.citation: Diekert F, Heyen D, Nesje F, Shayegh S (2025) Do early warning signals of tipping points lead to better decisions? Journal of The Royal Society Interface 22(225): 20240864 (1 Apr 2025)
studies.data_system: Theoretical decision model
studies.outcome_definition: Tipping point in a stylized managed system
studies.key_finding: Models an early warning system as a tipping indicator plus a trigger value; EWS information can balance tipping risk but can also induce riskier behaviour when no signal is received
studies.notes: Relevant to justifying an explicit alarm threshold / false-alarm budget framing.

studies.citation: Zhang H, Li H, Huo S, Yang Z, Wu F (2025) Navigating tipping points: A complex systems framework for anticipating lake ecosystem collapse. Fundamental Research 6(2): 592-603 (online 25 Jul 2025)
studies.data_system: Review (lake ecosystems)
studies.outcome_definition: Lake regime shifts / collapse
studies.key_finding: Synthesizes catastrophic risk in lakes through complex adaptive systems; temporal, spatial and network EWS can foreshadow tipping but require context-specific validation because lakes respond heterogeneously to interacting stressors
studies.notes: Background for the lake challenge analysis.

studies.citation: Miramontes P, Alvarez-Martinez R, et al. (2026) Early Warning Signals in Ecological Time-Series. Entropy 28(6): 628 (2 Jun 2026); full author list not visible

notes: SEARCH LIMITS: 74 WebSearch queries were executed (all listed verbatim in queries_run). The session's WebSearch budget (200 calls shared across the session) was then exhausted; the following 10 planned queries were submitted but NOT executed and returned no results: (1) "Global Marine Fishery Stock Productivity Under Climate Change" Global Change Biology 2026 authors; (2) "Early warnings are too late when parameters change rapidly" Scientific Reports 2025 authors; (3) "A novel multispecies approach for the detection of regime shifts in a plankton community" Ocean Science 2025 authors; (4) "Predicting regime shifts and beyond" PNAS 2025 commentary Medeiros authors; (5) "early warning signals" 2026 wild populations empirical abundance "Journal of Animal Ecology" OR "Global Change Biology" OR "Ecology Letters" OR "Conservation Biology"; (6) bioRxiv 2026 "critical slowing down" OR "early warning signals" population collapse OR extinction time series; (7) "critical slowing down" test across hundreds OR thousands "wild populations" OR "natural populations" time series 2024 2025 2026 evidence; (8) "early warning signals" "Breeding Bird Survey" OR "butterfly monitoring" OR "waterbird" population declines 2024 2025 2026; (9) lake "early warning" cyanobacteria OR "algal bloom" forecast operational "false alarm" OR "false positive" 2025 2026 Buelo OR "resilience indicators" high-frequency; (10) machine learning predict fish stock collapse OR "population collapse" 2026 "time series" out-of-sample OR "cross-validation" ecology preprint. No WebFetch/curl attempts were made (blocked per instructions), so all design fields come from search-result titles/snippets and search-engine summaries; snippets may paraphrase. GAPS: no 2024-2026 study was found that applies EWS at scale to the Living Planet Database, BioTIME 2.0, or GPDD (queries 11, 12, 35, 53, 57, 70 returned only older Clements-group experimental work and LPI-methodology papers); no 2024-2026 study was found that benchmarks EWS against a state/trend forecasting baseline with a shared false-alarm budget in a prequential design; no ESS Open Archive EWS preprint was found (query 37). The closest at-scale fisheries EWS applications are Pélissié et al. 2026 (Science Advances, RAM Legacy, 315 stocks; retrospective precedence/relative-risk design, collapse = 25% of mean biomass), Cano et al. 2025 (PNAS; RAM Legacy + ICES cod + FishGlob; shape-class classifier with cross-validation, moderate accuracy, 40% sensitivity for the abrupt class in FishGlob) and the Walter et al. 2025 EcoEvoRxiv preprint (generic EWS on fish population series with a confidence index; evaluation details not visible). Recent explicit false-alarm quantification with non-transitioning controls appears in experimental (Jarvis-Cross et al. 2025; Cerini et al. 2025) and non-ecological ML (Falmagne et al. 2026: 3.7% FPR) settings rather than field population monitoring. Per hard rule 1, no EWS-outcome associations were computed or speculated about for any dataset. One author-list caution is flagged inside the EWSmethods entry (co-authors beyond O'Brien and Clements were not visible in results).
